item.title: The Mess in AI Evaluation Isn't a Technical Problem, It's a Transparency Problem
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-nejmaigrandrou-ai-评估的混乱不是技术问题-是透明度问题/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-nejmaigrandrou-ai-评估的混乱不是技术问题-是透明度问题/
item.description: In that 2019 systematic review, fewer than 5% of medical imaging AI papers met the rigor standards long established in other areas of medicine — and even the best-performing models only matched radiologists.
item.content:encoded:
In that 2019 systematic review, fewer than 5% of medical imaging AI papers met the rigor standards long established in other areas of medicine — and even the best-performing models only matched radiologists.

This episode has medium information density, but the first half — a first-hand account of how evidence standards in medical AI moved from chaos to discipline — has direct reference value for anyone building medical AI products.

11:22 Fewer than 5% of AI papers in top journals hold up
Around 2019, new papers every week claimed ‘AI is as good as radiologists’ or ‘AI beats radiologists at pneumonia detection’, but these conclusions contradicted each other. Xiao Liu and her collaborators did something no one was doing at the time: they applied the rigorous standards that the diagnostic test evaluation field had used for years to these AI papers, keeping only those with external validation, like-for-like comparisons, and meaningful control groups. The paper count got cut down hard — fewer than 5% truly met the standards long established in other areas of medicine. And within that small set, the best-performing models only matched radiologists. This isn't bad news; it means there's too much noise in the published literature.

16:28 Reporting guidelines don't teach you how to do research, they force you to say what you did
CONSORT, SPIRIT, PRISMA, STARD, TRIPOD — these reporting guidelines are essentially a checklist specifying which items a paper must report. They don't tell you how to do the research — they're not methodology guidelines, they're transparency guidelines. Whether your methods are good or bad, you have to write them transparently and clearly. Their function is to put authors, journal editors, and peer reviewers on the same information plane, with no smoke bombs, no hiding behind vague details. Xiao Liu added a side effect: when authors know they must report something, it in turn forces methodological rigor upward, though that's hard to measure.

18:33 Guidelines come out of Delphi voting; items without consensus get cut
CONSORT AI and SPIRIT AI weren't written by a few people behind closed doors; they went through a Delphi process: first a literature review and expert opinion generated a set of candidate items, then multiple rounds of multi-stakeholder voting, ending with an in-person discussion. That in-person discussion is often the most valuable, because people learn from each other. Items that can't reach consensus get excluded; only those that do are kept. Xiao Liu says doing this kind of consensus project well takes at least six months; she tried a compressed three-month version, but participants contribute their time for free, and to get high-quality feedback and multiple rounds of participation, you can't cut corners on time or reach.

20:36 Whether explainability belongs in reporting guidelines was fought over at the meeting
Andy Beam recalls that one question in the Delphi discussion was: should clinical trials include explainability requirements, or at least report any explainability evaluations you did. He and Lauren Oakden-Rayner got up on the small stage and said ‘No, it shouldn't be done at all, for the following reasons’. That debate was later commissioned into a paper by Rupa, an editor at Lancet Digital Health, and became one of Andy's most cited papers. Xiao Liu also clearly takes the ‘no’ side in the lightning round: she thinks you should first ask why you want AI explainability, and keep asking until you reach the bottom — what you ultimately want is just beneficial effects.

26:43 Being a regulatory consultant without ever working in industry felt insincere to her
At the time, Xiao Liu was doing academic AI research and clinical ophthalmology while increasingly consulting for regulators. She started to feel she had never stood on the regulated side, and that consulting was a bit insincere. So she joined Apple as a health scientist, mainly designing validation studies for wearable device algorithms, such as Apple Watch sensing algorithms, including a hypertension notification feature released this year. She says Apple has a well-oiled product shipping machine, which was exactly the experience she wanted. After more than a year there she returned to Birmingham to build a lab full-time, and later joined Microsoft AI's newly formed medical frontier LLM team.

32:49 Short term, computer scientists set the direction; long term, clinicians gatekeep
Asked whether medical AI will be driven more by computer scientists or clinicians, Xiao Liu first asked what ‘driven’ means, and after confirming it means ‘changed’, gave her judgment: short term, computer scientists and engineers; long term, clinicians. The mechanism is — the people processing data, choosing metrics, and choosing benchmarks determine which direction progress goes in the short term; but if the endpoint is real use on patients, clinicians will play the gatekeeper role at a later stage.

33:50 Doctors' work won't change much in five years, but should in ten
Xiao Liu thinks doctors' work won't look dramatically different within five years, but very likely will in ten years and beyond, and she hopes it will. The path she envisions: if medical intelligence and models keep advancing at the current pace, the medical profession no longer has to be about accumulating knowledge, or even about the kind of medical reasoning taught in medical school; the focus shifts to being ‘a companion to experience’ — accompanying deteriorating health, sudden health events, daily wellbeing fluctuations, life-changing diagnoses, treatment failures and complications, and maybe recovery, maybe not. She thinks people will continuously need something deeply interpersonal on this journey: the ability to call on knowledge without necessarily carrying it oneself, but translating it into human language.

40:00 The most optimistic thing is dismantling old medical concepts; the most pessimistic is that we dare not
Xiao Liu says she's more optimistic than pessimistic. What excites her most is that aggregating all the knowledge in the medical world might reveal that our understanding of biomarkers, disease phenotype clustering, and existing medical knowledge frameworks is off. She gives her PhD research on inflammatory eye diseases as an example: a bunch of diseases are loosely called ‘white dot syndromes’ just because they produce white dots in the fundus, but they are likely driven by completely different mechanisms. She hopes one way new intelligence emerges is by dismantling these old concepts in medicine. The pessimistic side: this field is inherently cautious, and may resist such dismantling out of unfamiliarity, sticking rigidly to the evaluation methods and guidelines of the past ten or twenty years during a period of new technological change, missing the chance for discovery.

item.title: Government Doesn't Just Waste Your Money, It Wastes an Hour of Your Week
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-tyler-政府不只浪费你的钱-还浪费你每周一小时/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-tyler-政府不只浪费你的钱-还浪费你每周一小时/
item.description: Plenty of countries file taxes for their citizens; the IRS is legally barred from doing it for you. The time tax hits the poor, immigrants and the formerly incarcerated hardest — and AI may not save them.
item.content:encoded:
Plenty of countries file taxes for their citizens; the IRS is legally barred from doing it for you. The time tax hits the poor, immigrants and the formerly incarcerated hardest — and AI may not save them.

Medium information density, but the "time tax" frame itself is valuable: it reprices the administrative friction of the welfare state as a regressive levy. The confession in the back half about softening on UBI is worth hearing.

0:58 The IRS is legally barred from filing your taxes for you
Lowrey's central example: in Japan, salaried workers never touch the tax process at all; many countries mail you a prefilled return and you just correct the errors. The US could easily do this — nine in ten households take the standard deduction, and their tax situations are fairly simple — but the IRS is not legally permitted to. This is not a technology problem, it is an institutional choice. She defines the "time tax" as the portion of cost the government shifts onto individuals as administrative labour, and unlike a monetary tax it is different in kind: you can earn more money, you cannot earn more time.

1:02 The worst program is TANF, not the IRS
Lowrey names TANF (cash welfare) the single worst program in government: it nominally exists to address child poverty, in practice it does not move the child poverty rate, its compliance burden is extremely heavy and punitive, and its $16.5 billion a year is essentially wasted. She offers a rule — programs aimed at high-income Americans are a far better experience, safety-net programs are generally bad, and welfare is the worst. This yields a counterintuitive judgment: the quality of government service is inversely proportional to the political influence of its beneficiaries.

6:08 Pandemic fraud is not something the time tax can prevent
Cowen raises a common objection: fraud exploded after deregulation in 2020, so maybe the time tax is the necessary cost of fraud prevention. Lowrey rejects it outright: that fraud came mainly from criminal rings and fake small businesses, and from the fact that UI systems themselves run on ancient COBOL infrastructure. Her mechanism is misaligned incentives — governors have no incentive to upgrade UI systems when unemployment is low, so the same conversation repeats every recession. The conclusion: building state capacity and agile digital systems prevents fraud; pushing the work onto individuals does not.

11:19 Large-scale fraud is almost entirely on the supply side
Lowrey points out that fraud in Medicare and Medicaid is almost entirely on the provider side: nursing homes, clinics and hospital systems defrauding the government. The ceiling on individual fraud is low, because the amount you can extract from the government is limited; to commit large-scale fraud you have to process a lot of transactions. So her policy ordering is: reduce the administrative overhead of other programs, concentrate enforcement resources on criminal organisations and legitimate providers, rather than loading burdens onto the 99.9% who do not commit fraud. She adds a piece of political economy: the fraud narrative is often used to make programs look illegitimate, and thereby get voters to tolerate cuts.

13:25 Fifty hours per person per year, and highly unequal
Lowrey's quantitative estimate comes from the American Time Use Survey: total bureaucratic time is roughly 50 hours per person per year, close to an hour a week. She concedes the number is understated — ATUS cannot capture multitasking (waiting on hold while cooking dinner gets recorded as one thing), and time taxes are scattered across categories and never totalled. Who pays the most? People entangled with the criminal justice system, immigrants, the poor. The rich can "skip" it with subordinates and accountants, with one exception: permits to renovate a house in San Francisco, where no amount of money spares you a 500-day wait and multiple rounds of public review.

22:57 AI can fill out forms, but it can't fill a urine test
Cowen asks whether AI agents could handle all of this within five years. Lowrey says probably, but raises two caveats: first, the users of the most burdensome programs are low-income, and whether they know about or trust these agents is unknown; second, much of the burden is not paperwork at all — it is mandatory interviews, urine screening, data that is hard to collect. She gives SNAP as an example: benefits are calculated by household, and the government has no stable definition of "household", so you have to explain how you and your co-residents split the cost of staple food, a question AI would struggle to answer for you. She notes she was originally sceptical, but a civic technologist who has worked in this field for years firmly believes AI will help a great deal.

31:18 Disability insurance is already hard enough to apply for
Cowen presses with data: the number of people on disability insurance rose roughly fourfold between 1990 and 2014, while workplace deaths kept falling — shouldn't the threshold be raised? Lowrey does not accept the inference. She offers two alternative explanations: population ageing and the rise of obesity-related chronic disease. Then the counterevidence: 5% of applicants have to submit more than 1,000 pages of medical material; 11,000 Americans die each year while waiting for a disability determination. She admits she worries about both directions — about paying people who do not need it, and about denying people who genuinely do — so she does not think this is the moment to add more paperwork.

38:28 The research moved her position on UBI
Lowrey's previous book, Give People Money, was pro-UBI; here she says plainly that the research findings are "sobering", and that she has updated her priors: the side benefits she expected cash to deliver did not materialise. Her defence is that the point of giving people money is to give people money to buy things, and that rationale still holds; life improving less than expected is not an argument against the policy. On AI and UBI, she admits she was extremely dismissive at the time of the claim that "AI will force UBI", and would not go that far now, but if GDP and productivity surge while unemployment rises at the same time, that would be very strange, and UBI-type policies would have to be considered.

item.title: Sequoia's Former Boss on Reading People: What Happens Before 14 Sets the Core
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-ilt-红杉前掌门看人-14-岁前发生了什么-内核就定了/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-ilt-红杉前掌门看人-14-岁前发生了什么-内核就定了/
item.description: Digging into his own refugee family's history, he found that the imprint you absorb unconsciously from your parents before you are 12, 13, 14 stays with you for life; what changes afterward is the external intensity, not the core.
item.content:encoded:
Digging into his own refugee family's history, he found that the imprint you absorb unconsciously from your parents before you are 12, 13, 14 stays with you for life; what changes afterward is the external intensity, not the core.

Not an investing lesson but a retrospective on origins, reading people, and writing. The back half — on structural changes in venture capital and the great man view of history — is the most valuable; the family history up front is more personal.

7:23 The grandfather who waited for the situation to pass disappeared
Moritz's two grandfathers were two responses to the same catastrophe. His maternal grandfather was a lower-court judge in Bavaria, had fought at Verdun in World War I, believed in the durability of the state, and had a pension he was unwilling to give up, so he delayed leaving; in the end he and his wife were sent east and vanished from history. The other grandfather was nearly blind, supported the family alone by trading cattle, had no pension to wait for, and left with his wife 72 hours before the war broke out — three days later and they too would have died. Moritz says the lesson he drew was not a moral judgment but that you must always have a bolt hole to hide in, and never too many passports.

21:03 His most effective question makes people cry on the spot
When he interviews people he always asks one fixed question: looking back, if there were one thing, one action you could have done differently, what would it be. He remembers a person interviewing at Sequoia bursting into tears when asked this — the man was the son of a Latino immigrant, had stolen candy from a corner grocery with friends at around age 12, the shopkeeper told his father, and his father dragged him back to the store by the ear and made him apologize and empty his pockets. Years later, asked this question, the first thing he thought of was still the shame he had brought on his family. Moritz says many people conducting interviews are not really listening to the answer.

26:03 On Zoom he sorted everyone he knew into categories
Inspired by a series about a French village in World War II, he divides people into three categories: resisters, the silent, and collaborators. During the pandemic, in those Zoom meetings with a dozen little windows, he would stare at each person he knew and think: if these people had lived in a French village in the 1940s, who would stay silent, who would resist, who would collaborate. He says resisters are always a tiny minority, because bad things happen in a country precisely because most people stay silent. Asked how many of the people he has invested in would be resisters, he says he would like to think so, but he is not sure.

38:04 The painter took only one day off a year
Frank Auerbach was a refugee from Nazi Germany, and Moritz calls him a complete monomaniac: apart from one day off each Christmas on Brighton Pier, he painted every single day. His models were a small fixed group of people, the same few faces painted for decades; one model who lived in Venice flew to London once a week to sit for him. His wife's house was right on the English coast, and Moritz asked whether he went there; he answered: I have never been to that house. From this Moritz discusses the cost of monomania — the cost to relationships is almost inevitable, but sometimes great things come out of exactly that.

43:04 He bet on something beyond the résumé
Around 1985, Moritz was still a journalist and wrote to five small funds looking for a job. Everyone except Don Valentine told him he had no technical background, no engineering degree, no experience at a tech company, and suggested he go into PR or marketing. Don was willing to take the risk, for a direct reason: he had seen several people with operating backgrounds at large tech companies move into investing and fail, and he had also seen several who succeeded — an actuary, and the one he cites most, Arthur Rock: an investment banker by background, with nothing in his résumé that predicted he would succeed. Don did not believe in teaching people; he believed in throwing them into the deep end and seeing whether they drowned.

46:15 Venture capital's old edge was imperfect information
Moritz says doing venture capital in the 1980s and 90s had several advantages that have now disappeared, the first being imperfect information: before the internet, unless you were close to something you did not know what was happening, whereas now the whole world basically gets the same information. The second is that the early market has far too many participants — individuals, two- or three-person funds, giant mutual funds — too many intermediaries, and it is no longer possible for investors to build the kind of real, close relationship with founders they once had. He therefore says that a moderately intelligent, quick-witted 14- to 16-year-old could have done venture capital in the mid-80s; he is not sure he could still do it well today.

52:57 He believes in the great man view of history without apology
Asked whether it is great individuals or enduring institutions that shape the course of history, Moritz's answer is blunt: he is a firm believer in the great man theory. From Lee Iacocca to Steve Jobs, from politics to the battlefield, what matters is great leaders; and of course also tyrants who cast a shadow over tens of millions of people for decades. In running Sequoia and in writing about Ferguson, he cares about the same thing — how an organization stays alive across decades. And speaking of Elon, he says he is completely staggered by the scale of his achievements across so many different industries, and thinks he may be the greatest industrialist in American history.

58:40 The more AI writes, the more a human voice is worth
Moritz says that because AI can easily produce vast amounts of text, excellent writing that cuts through the garbage is actually appreciating; his definition of excellent writing is ‘a voice you can hear that cannot be mistaken for anyone else's’. The hardest thing for a writer is to get close enough to his own inner feelings and voice that it outweighs the weight of others' expectations — he quotes Joseph Campbell: the privilege of a lifetime is to become who you truly are, and that is also the hardest thing. He does not consider himself a technologist, and says AI is rarely discussed at home; on employment he is optimistic: people predicted doomsday when the atomic bomb exploded, and predicted a genetic revolution creating humans in the 1970s, and neither happened, and this time he thinks more jobs will be created than destroyed.

item.title: A Math Professor and NFL Player Who Says He Was Just Lucky
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-freakonomics-数学教授和nfl球员-他说自己只是运气好/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-freakonomics-数学教授和nfl球员-他说自己只是运气好/
item.description: John Urschel played in the NFL while finishing an MIT math PhD, yet says talent is only a small part of it — his success came from "an enormous amount of hard work" and luck. He even hopes his football fame didn't get him his MIT job.
item.content:encoded:
John Urschel played in the NFL while finishing an MIT math PhD, yet says talent is only a small part of it — his success came from "an enormous amount of hard work" and luck. He even hopes his football fame didn't get him his MIT job.

This is the audio version of a video interview, so the information density isn't high, but Urschel explaining how he crammed two full-time jobs into the same week, and why he ultimately quit football, is worth hearing.

8:16 A coach's joke made him realize he could make the NFL
After Urschel's junior season, his position coach pulled him aside, essentially saying "don't go thinking about anything crazy, stay another year" — crazy meaning declaring early for the draft. He hadn't been thinking about the NFL at all, but that remark made him realize for the first time: this was something that would happen if he wanted it. Later the coach would say in practice, "they (the league) will like this move." He wasn't running on self-confidence; he was running on other people assuming he belonged at that level.

13:25 He asked his coach about a PhD; the coach thought he already had one
Urschel did an MIT math PhD while playing in the NFL, and he says he "didn't cheat," because he asked coach John Harbaugh in advance whether he could go back to school for a degree. The coach replied "absolutely, we support players finishing their education," then a minute later added a text: "I thought you already had a degree and a master's." Urschel replied: "But I don't have a PhD." The coach replied "oh, OK," and that was the approval. He deliberately picked courses with no exams that he could pass by reading the textbook — three PhD courses in one semester.

15:35 On planes he pretended his math book was a chess book
During the NFL season almost all his time each day went to football, with film study at night to prepare. Math could only be done in the time other people used to relax — say, on team flights, when everyone was watching movies. He says if he were reading a chess book it would be completely fine, but reading a math book was "a little suspicious," and teammates might think he was too distracted, so he'd say "it's not a math book, it's a chess book," flip it open for them, and they'd say "OK." The real solution was that he finished the textbooks before the semester even started — otherwise it would have been impossible.

17:42 The CTE controversy conveniently gave him cover to retire
The host asked whether the years when CTE (brain damage from repeated head hits) was making NFL headlines happened to coincide with his considering retirement. Urschel said "it gave me very good cover." But he also said he'd been worried before that. He was weighing whether to play another season — the last year of his rookie contract, with the next contract worth at least a million dollars a year, while his first-year base salary was 420,000. He had at one point convinced himself to stay with "there's one year left on the contract, I'll honor it" — the same mindset as when he honored his commitment to Penn State.

19:49 Looking back, he doesn't know what he was agonizing over
Urschel says looking back, agonizing over retirement made no sense: the team could cut him at any time, the contract wasn't guaranteed, and an injury would end it. What he actually cared about was math and his newborn child, and both were growing in importance, while football ranked third yet was a real burden on the first two — not just his head, but his whole body, whether he'd still be able to walk at 50, whether he could pick up his grandchildren and his daughter. He says "I needed to retire, focus on math, and go be with my kid."

20:52 He estimates only 4% of Americans like math
The host asked him to guess how many out of 100 Americans like math, and Urschel said that if you define "math" the way the general public understands it, 4% might even be high. The host said that number was a little sad. Urschel's own definition is very broad: math is the quantitative language we all share for reasoning about problems, and engineering, theoretical physics, statistics, and theoretical computer science all count as math — not far from doing puzzles, not far from the goal of "understanding something."

27:07 His daughter can't play football; his son has to really need it
Asked whether his two children should play football, Urschel said his daughter shouldn't — that level of risk he won't accept. As for his son, if it looked like something he "really needed to do," he'd allow it. He explained what needing means: football suits young people who have that craving and can benefit from "consensual violence, controlled, mutually agreed-upon aggression" — with rules, not trying to hurt people, essentially a proxy for war. He says it was very good for the combative high schooler he once was. If it were just "because Dad played" or "because all my friends play," he'd have the kid try wrestling or judo first.

29:09 He says he actually had no talent as an NFL player
The host praised him for being good at several hard things at once, and Urschel said talent does play a role, but compared with NFL players he "had no talent" — he admits he has some athletic gifts, like broad shoulders, but in the league that doesn't count. So how did he succeed? "Hard work, an enormous amount of hard work." The source was "wanting to be better." Asked whether his MIT job came from his football fame, he said "I don't know, I hope not."

item.title: Bypassing CUDA for inference chips is inevitable, but the SRAM window may not stay open forever
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-sv101-推理芯片绕过cuda是必然-但sram的窗口未必一直开着/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-sv101-推理芯片绕过cuda是必然-但sram的窗口未必一直开着/
item.description: Training is a contest of compute, inference a contest of bandwidth. Groq and Cerebras both bet on SRAM — one discounts for determinism, the other for yield. OpenAI picked the most expensive HBM4, because what it lacks is power, not money.
item.content:encoded:
Training is a contest of compute, inference a contest of bandwidth. Groq and Cerebras both bet on SRAM — one discounts for determinism, the other for yield. OpenAI picked the most expensive HBM4, because what it lacks is power, not money.

Two frontline chip founders break down the trade-offs across the three paths of Groq, Cerebras and OpenAI, with plenty of engineering detail and cost math — for anyone trying to understand what inference chips are really betting on.

4:17 Training bets on compute, inference bets on bandwidth
In the training era nobody could make money from training itself, so costs couldn't be quantified and everyone just wanted to bet on the single strongest cluster. In the inference era the math is clear — how much the user pays per million tokens, and how much it costs me to produce those million tokens. More fundamentally it's about compute density: training has massive data to keep the compute fed, while the decode phase of inference is strictly autoregressive, producing one token at a time, and every token produced requires reading the entire model from storage into the compute units. So the core tension of inference shifts from compute to memory bandwidth.

16:39 SRAM is the consensus, but the two companies part ways
Groq and Cerebras both saw the bandwidth requirement before Transformers existed, and both converged on SRAM — because SRAM's absolute bandwidth and bandwidth per dollar are two to three orders of magnitude higher than HBM. The price is capacity: DRAM stores one bit with one transistor plus one capacitor, SRAM needs six transistors, so per-chip capacity may be two orders of magnitude lower than HBM. So you have to scale the system up — hundreds or thousands of chips to hold all the model weights — and the bottleneck immediately shifts from capacity to cluster communication and scheduling. Here the two diverge: Groq moves all scheduling ahead of time into the compiler, while Cerebras simply stuffs a rack of chips into one whole wafer.

19:34 Groq's static scheduling collides with MoE's dynamism
Groq designs hardware around the compiler, pushing determinism to the extreme, with no runtime scheduling overhead. But after MoE appeared, each token activates 8 of 128 experts, and which ones is decided at runtime — the compiler can't predict it. A static approach has only two options: conservatively send all tokens everywhere and let some chips idle, or change how the model is partitioned — but today's models are hard to partition cleanly along any dimension other than experts. Idling only affects cost-effectiveness, not the fact that it's still fast, so Groq remains a good option outside of GPUs.

25:18 The price Cerebras pays for yield
The limit on single-die size is about 800 square millimeters; a wafer yields thirty or forty dies, and at 50% yield you still get 20 good ones. But for Cerebras the entire wafer is one product — if defects exceed the 30% it can tolerate, the whole wafer is scrap. This isn't mask cost (masks can be amortized), it's that out of every 10 you build, maybe 9 are unusable. So it may achieve 10x Nvidia's bandwidth, but at 3x the cost of HBM, and the bandwidth-per-dollar has to be discounted. Groq discounts for determinism, Cerebras discounts for yield cost, and the discounts ultimately land on token cost.

33:58 In the inference era, CUDA will inevitably be bypassed
TPU and Trainium have zero intention of being CUDA-compatible, yet people still find TPU software hard to use — Anthropic can buy in bulk because many of its engineers come from Google and know JAX. The key change is this: in the training era people were willing to pay for good software; in the inference era the scales tip toward performance and cost-effectiveness. As long as it's not many hard problems but one hard problem, writing all of the Transformer's operators on a new chip makes the business case work; add AI coding accelerating operator optimization, and the software-stack barrier drops dramatically. DeepSeek would rather write low-level PTX assembly to optimize — that's the same logic.

44:25 The faster inference runs, the smarter the model gets
Once agents explode in scale, a huge number of tokens aren't read by humans but by other agents; human reading speed tops out at 100 tokens per second. But the point of inference speed isn't faster interaction — it's that in the same one minute of waiting, the model can use 10x more tokens for more internal thinking, and thus be smarter. The x-axis on Jensen's slide is literally Smarter AI, the y-axis tokens per watt. Conversely, some applications that answer quickly may simply be thinking less. Time is the essential constraint — ask an AI to judge tomorrow's stock market and if it thinks for two days, the answer is meaningless.

49:04 Grab the invariants: once FFN becomes MoE, it's stable
Model architecture will always influence chip design — diffusion models, for instance, are compute-dense and suit a different paradigm — so you first make the heterogeneity choice: whether to do this at all. More critical is finding the invariants: within the Transformer, attention mechanisms are still being reinvented, with every new lab publishing papers proposing new ideas; but the FFN behind it has been a relative invariant ever since it became MoE. RL in post-training also has no fundamental effect on model architecture. So solve the part that has already converged first, and the chip won't be left behind by algorithmic iteration.

1:09:40 Everything revolves around locality
Bill Dally's exact words are that computer architecture is like real estate — everything is location, location, location. Temporal locality is that data you've used will probably be used again; spatial locality is that once you use a piece of data you'll soon use the data around it; the CPU cache is the application of both. But in the decode phase of AI inference, algorithmic temporal and spatial locality are both flattened out, so you have to restore locality in hardware at the architecture level — putting model weights in SRAM is essentially buying the best possible locality.

item.title: Frontier AI companies built Frankenstein, then asked the government to regulate it

item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-15-allin-ai-前沿公司造了弗兰肯斯坦-却找政府要监管/
item.description: Vance says: if you're building Frankenstein, first, stop; second, when companies come asking for defensive tools, give them — don't outsource the risk frontier companies created to a global governance body.
item.content:encoded:
Vance says: if you're building Frankenstein, first, stop; second, when companies come asking for defensive tools, give them — don't outsource the risk frontier companies created to a global governance body.

Medium information density: the first half is standard policy defense; the second half — on AI regulation, H-1B fees and the scale of federal fraud — is where the incremental value is.

10:16 The root cause of the data center backlash is twenty years of not building power plants
Vance splits the anti-data-center wave into two layers: one is basic NIMBY sentiment, the other is real electricity bills — his example is someone whose monthly bill was $290 a year ago and is now $580. His judgment is that this is not a data center problem, but that the US went an entire generation without building enough generating capacity, especially after blue states made new generation impossible, so the cost gets passed onto residential bills and backlash is inevitable. His comparison: in 2005 China's power generation had just overtaken America's, since then the US has been basically flat, while China now generates 3 times as much electricity as the US. His conclusion is that many problems are downstream of this foundational one, and the only solution is to build more power, with the goal being electricity ‘cheap enough that you don't need a meter’.

12:35 The people building Frankenstein shouldn't come asking for regulation
Vance responds directly to AI pessimism: if frontier labs say ‘we've built Frankenstein,’ the answer is not to set up a global AI governance structure, but — first, stop; second, if the cat is already out of the bag, build defensive mechanisms. He names the cyberattack tools that came out with Anthropic's latest model, and says companies urgently need the corresponding defensive tools but are being denied access. He is careful to distinguish motives: he doesn't know Dario, but everyone who does tells him Dario is sincere, that this is deeply held conviction, not cynicism, and not regulatory capture. The disagreement isn't about motives, it's about the solution: Vance thinks outsourcing the risk to government regulation is wrong, and that you should look inward.

16:45 The $100,000 H-1B fee exists because Congress won't legislate
Vance says H-1B reform is being done through executive action rather than legislation, because Congress simply has no political will to pass a law changing the program. The executive approach is a $100,000 fee, to ensure that what gets an H-1B is a genuine genius, not a foreign accountant making $45,000 replacing an American accountant making $60,000. He also says they're looking at preventing companies that use H-1B from simultaneously laying off large numbers of American workers — his scenario is a company that says it urgently needs people it can't find when it applies, but whose history shows it laid off 5,000. He acknowledges the approach has already been sued, but believes it holds up both legally and as policy.

18:50 The scale of federal fraud: between 10% and 20%
Vance cites the 20% Elon talked about at the peak of DOGE, which is $1.4 trillion, then says whether it's 10% or 20%, the magnitude is in the hundreds of billions. He thinks the biggest obstacle to investigating fraud isn't failing to find it, but that the states with the worst problems are the least willing to cooperate. He gives two specific mechanisms: California bills the federal government monthly to be reimbursed for SNAP costs, somewhere between $700 million and $900 million, and the federal government just wires the money and asks no questions, so the federal government has no idea whether the people receiving SNAP are real people or legal residents; and in Medicare fraud, large numbers of entirely fictitious ‘people,’ plus illegal immigrant Medicaid spending in Illinois, New York and California. His estimate is that if the total is $700 billion, a few tens of billions of it is in blue states, and simply verifying basic eligibility would handle it, but legally forcing blue states to cooperate is far harder than it should be.

21:57 Israel is not the subject of US Middle East policy
Faced with a question about ‘America First, only America’ sentiment inside MAGA and rising antisemitism, Vance's answer is to re-anchor the relationship in American interests. He says Israel is an important partner on military technology and intelligence sharing, but the US doesn't always agree with Israel; he calls Trump more willing than any president in the past 40 years to part ways with Netanyahu. His irony is that the ones criticizing Trump's relationship with Bibi are precisely Democrats, while Trump is the president who dares to say ‘Bibi is a good partner, but on this we see it differently.’ He extends the logic to NATO: you can't subordinate US Middle East policy to Israel, just as you can't subordinate policy toward Europe entirely to NATO.

25:19 Two messages for the midterms: don't hand over power, and the other side is insane
Vance's two messages for the midterms are blunt. The first is the scorecard: tax cuts, including on overtime pay, Social Security and consumption, which he defines as tax cuts for middle-class workers rather than for Washington and New York elites; success on the border and immigration; and H-1B reform that prioritizes American workers over foreigners. The second doesn't depend on agreeing with the policies: even if you disagree with every one of our issues, the other party has been swallowed by insanity, swallowed by people who want to steal everything and hand the country to illegal immigrants and criminals, and they brag about it openly. His example is someone running for Congress in New York who said July 4th is the liberation of Puerto Rico and Palestine, and his conclusion is that this kind of person belongs in a mental institution, not in Congress.

item.title: Budget Airlines' Real Rival Isn't Each Other — It's the Credit Card Business That Sells Miles
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-15-wsjournal-廉价航空的对手不是同行-是卖里程的信用卡生意/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-15-wsjournal-廉价航空的对手不是同行-是卖里程的信用卡生意/
item.description: Ultra-low-cost carriers built their business on rock-bottom fares. Now they're squeezed between Big Air's Basic Economy and frequent-flyer credit cards — the latter get travelers to pay $100 more just to rack up points, which makes price-sensitive customers the least reliable customers of all.
item.content:encoded:
Ultra-low-cost carriers built their business on rock-bottom fares. Now they're squeezed between Big Air's Basic Economy and frequent-flyer credit cards — the latter get travelers to pay $100 more just to rack up points, which makes price-sensitive customers the least reliable customers of all.

18 minutes on why an entire business model stopped working: not beaten by a cheaper rival, but cut off from its customers by a more expensive one wielding a loyalty system.

0:00 What budget airlines sell is: you get what you pay for
The episode opens with a string of passenger complaints that define the category: tray tables too small to hold anything, water costs extra, seats have almost no padding, and after an oversell they randomly kick people off the plane. But precisely because the price is low enough, people who want to travel cheap keep pouring toward budget airlines. Allison Sider says the peak of this model was about ten to twelve years ago, when it looked like it would become the dominant business model, and the big airlines genuinely felt they had to find a way to respond.

2:01 Frontier even changed its ticker to ULCC
Frontier is headquartered in Denver, with white fuselages and forest-green lettering, and a different animal on the tail of every plane. In the 2010s it went all in on the ultra-low-cost model, and its ticker symbol is literally ULCC (ultra-low-cost carrier) — in Allison's words, that is ‘how much it wanted to embody that business model, to own that identity.’ Its business model is highly similar to Spirit's and shares the same roots. But Frontier's operations have long been rough, with on-time rates, cancellation rates and involuntary-denied-boarding numbers sitting at the bottom of the rankings year after year.

4:03 Both mergers failed, and Spirit simply vanished
In 2022 Frontier proposed acquiring Spirit, hoping to merge into a national budget airline that could take on the big four of Delta, United, American and Southwest, with the two route networks complementary — Spirit leaning East, Frontier leaning West. But JetBlue bid higher, Spirit turned to JetBlue, and a federal judge then blocked that deal on antitrust grounds. In the end nobody got Spirit; it went through multiple bankruptcies and shut down entirely this year. Spirit's disappearance opened up market space for Frontier, and the company says it has benefited — but it also ran into inflation, high jet fuel costs, and a fading of demand for cheap travel itself.

7:11 Big Air flanked budget carriers with Basic Economy
Delta, American and United all rolled out Basic Economy — a cheaper, stripped-down fare class. The big airlines' move was not to cut prices across the board, but to take a handful of seats, price them close to budget, and pair them with close-to-budget bare service, such as no advance seat assignment. For consumers, that amounts to getting the budget-airline experience on a big airline's routes and reliability. Allison says this is the bet most airlines are now making: people want a more premium experience and are willing to pay for it. Delta made that bet first, fifteen years ago, wagering that ‘if you have the best product and the most reliable operation, people will come’ — and it worked extremely well.

9:27 What actually killed budget airlines is the frequent-flyer credit card
The other mechanism big airlines use to keep customers is loyalty programs: co-branded credit cards mean travelers don't comparison-shop at all. Allison's example is that someone chasing miles or elite status might be willing to pay $100 more. That makes it extremely hard for Frontier to compete — its route options aren't as broad, and its loyalty program isn't as strong. Frontier's response has been to start selling bundled products (ticket plus bag plus seat selection), and soon it will add first class and onboard Wi-Fi. In other words, it is becoming more and more like an ordinary airline.

10:29 Frontier's CEO: fix operations first, everything else later
Frontier CEO Jimmy Dempsey told Allison the company's future is bright, but it has to adapt to the environment — ‘customers are seeking a more premium product, and we are adapting to that.’ Some of the actions he lists are very basic: improve operations, be more reliable. Allison's reading is that reliability is the center that holds up everything else: only if operations are reliable, not constantly delayed or cancelled, with enough flights for backup, does it make sense to invest in a loyalty program and a credit card. Dempsey's framing is to keep offering very low fares across the industry to get people on planes, while layering on premium products to improve the overall revenue mix, and to find the ‘right balance’ over the next year.

12:34 Southwest's hesitation exposes the real problem with this trend
Southwest is the pioneer of budget flying, bringing cheap air travel to America with an ultra-simple operation — every plane the same, every seat the same — which for a long time was an operational advantage, but also cost it revenue, because there was nothing to sell to people who wanted to upgrade. Now Southwest is also agonizing over whether to pivot toward premium demand, and it ultimately decided to do so. But Allison points out that the U.S. also has an affordability crisis, so ‘whether consumers' willingness to pay more for pricier tickets and premium experiences can last’ is the big question hanging over this premiumization trend for years, and it is why Southwest hesitated in the first place.

13:39 Price-sensitive customers have been judged unreliable
Allison says that for a long time, if you were the cheapest in the industry, you almost couldn't lose — so the question is: is this a fundamental change in the business model, or just a moment in the economic cycle that will swing back at the next recession? She thinks that's still an open question. But airlines are forming a judgment: price-sensitive customers may not be such reliable customers; wealthy customers who can keep swiping their cards even when the economy wobbles are the better customers. The whole industry is reshaping itself to serve that person. For budget airlines, that may mean room for only one national big player, and after Spirit's disappearance that spot looks like Frontier's — but it has to get back to profitability, and it may no longer look the way it used to.

item.title: A Pause on Frontier Development Is a Great Deal for China, Which Is Why America Won't Take It
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-15-cogrev-暂停前沿开发对中国是笔好交易-所以美国不会接受/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-15-cogrev-暂停前沿开发对中国是笔好交易-所以美国不会接受/
item.description: If a pause covers only frontier model development — not robotics, power, or semiconductor indigenization — China can finish running every other race and restart the competition at the moment the US loses its chip advantage. That deal is plainly bad for America.
item.content:encoded:
If a pause covers only frontier model development — not robotics, power, or semiconductor indigenization — China can finish running every other race and restart the competition at the moment the US loses its chip advantage. That deal is plainly bad for America.

Anton chains geopolitics, markets, European strategy and domestic politics into a single argument; the back half on compute for access and the middle-power endgame is the most valuable part.

14:24 Pausing only frontier development is a gift to China
Anton returns again and again to one judgment: if a pause covers only frontier model development and not the other domains of geopolitical competition, it is an "extremely good deal" for China, which is why the US is almost certain not to accept it. His reasoning: China is catching up or already leading in robotics, AI diffusion, power buildout, semiconductor indigenization and data center construction. The only places the US leads by a wide margin are chip design, allied control over semiconductor equipment, and frontier model development. Pausing that one piece amounts to letting China finish running every other race, then restarting the competition at the moment the US has lost its decisive chip advantage.

16:46 A fair version would require China to give up indigenization
In Anton's view, the only version of the deal that could count as "fair" is one where the US demands that China slow not just its own frontier development but the entire supply chain tied to frontier AI — specifically chip production and EUV lithography equipment, i.e. "no substantive progress on indigenization." He concedes this ask is "really really hard to ask," because China already reads this round of talks as an American plan to contain its AI industry, and adding this condition makes it even less acceptable. So his conclusion: either the US makes a deal that is clearly bad for itself and good for China, or there is no deal.

19:08 The host would trade a frontier pause for a chip catch-up
The host stakes out a position different from Anton's: he would trade a pause on US frontier scaling for a reciprocal pause on Chinese frontier scaling, while allowing China to keep catching up on chips. His reasoning is about timescales — chip indigenization is a five-year-order problem, longer than any imaginable pause; by then we might have a better grip on the problem and could negotiate again. Anton partly accepts this, arguing that even if the deal is slightly unfavorable to the US, from a risk-reduction standpoint it is still a net good for the world.

20:00 What a pause should fear most is smuggling and stockpiling
Anton offers a concrete mechanism: if during the pause China keeps smuggling frontier chips and consolidating American chips into a single national-project data center, then when the pause ends China restarts from an integrated, high starting point — the pause helped it. So rather than demanding that China slow indigenization, he suggests making "actually enforcing export controls and shutting down smuggling" the more achievable concession. He concedes the US has to handle its own side of this too.

25:00 Valuations are betting on super-buyers, not accountants
The host proposes that demand is limited by human deployment capacity rather than model capability, so a pause need not be bad for the stock market. Anton partly agrees — if you switched all existing Western compute to inference, it would be enough to pay back the frontier model and chip investments already made. But he says current valuations "probably rest on us doing more than that": the market is pricing in R&D acceleration contracts worth millions of dollars each in materials science and drug discovery, plus internal productivity gains and coding agents that can be sold at high prices. If those super-buyers don't show up, the valuations of labs and public companies — and the scale of the buildout — don't add up, and he expects the AI sector to drag at least downward.

28:09 The market may run before you finish explaining
Anton thinks a pause is still read as a "radical policy proposal" and an "unprecedented policy intervention," so conservative market analysts and smart money will think: the regulatory path is unclear, better to get out first. He distinguishes two cases — if the market believes everything will be business as usual in six months, fine; but if it reads this as a Bernie Sanders-style AI policy victory, the end of free development, with no idea when or on what terms it resumes, the market may already have run before you finish making yourself clear. He also says that if the five frontier companies announced a pause themselves and framed it as a reliability issue, it might instead be read as removing political risk, and could even support a bullish story.

31:59 What AI most threatens is liberal democracies
Anton says many authoritarian, dysfunctional or absent states were never good at distributing and aggregating public opinion in the first place, and may instead use powerful AI to maintain stability — so they are not necessarily the most threatened. What he really worries about is liberal democracies: the state's monopoly on violence, dispute adjudication, and the aggregation of data and knowledge — these three functions get eroded by individual superintelligence. People stop going to court and let agents negotiate instead; data can no longer be scanned and read by the state; and the state therefore cannot respond to redistribution and social challenges. He says plainly he does not want to roll the dice on this bet, and would rather integrate capabilities into nation-states that still function.

39:14 China can put AI in a vertically integrated cage
The other path is compute governance: efficiency gains happen only when they are permitted to happen, and that depends on concrete choices about allocating compute. China can put models into government-controlled data centers and vertically integrate the supply chain around them, so they "never see the light of day," used only to build products and strategic sovereignty, barely reaching citizens at all. Anton sees this as a stabilizer for China: strong state capacity, a thin boundary between public and private sectors, and capabilities that can diffuse along corporate hierarchies without diffusing into the broader market. By contrast the US market depends on models being broadly accessible, and the government is not in the habit of picking corporate winners, so the US has a harder time sustaining this kind of "limited access" stable equilibrium.

item.title: Microsoft Won't Chase Frontier Models: Nadella Says the Real Business Is Being Everyone's Middle Layer
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-15-allin-微软不追前沿模型-纳德拉说真正的生意是当所有人的中间层/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-15-allin-微软不追前沿模型-纳德拉说真正的生意是当所有人的中间层/
item.description: Frontier labs are fighting over who builds the strongest model; Nadella says Microsoft's job is to let enterprises "use all models but be independent of all models" — excess profit at the model layer gets crushed by open source, and the money is in applications and the middle layer.
item.content:encoded:
Frontier labs are fighting over who builds the strongest model; Nadella says Microsoft's job is to let enterprises "use all models but be independent of all models" — excess profit at the model layer gets crushed by open source, and the money is in applications and the middle layer.

Nadella rarely answers head-on why Microsoft doesn't build frontier models, how capex gets allocated, and how he sees the doomer narrative. Worth hearing for anyone doing enterprise AI procurement or compute investment.

1:06 Common sense first, safety second
Nadella splits AI safety into three layers, and the order matters: the first layer is "building things that serve humanity and stay under human control"; the second is broad diffusion of the technology, which he considers the most critical thing, and diffusion means there must be choice, competition, and all kinds of business models, including open weights and closed weights. Only the third layer is safety itself. He singles out a control dimension people overlook: enterprise customers need to embed their own knowledge into weights they control, need to see the generated chain of thought, need to fine-tune with it, and must not leak their own IP. He says this whole area "nobody's talking about."

3:08 Agents are a new kind of insider risk
Nadella breaks the Hugging Face incident into two classes of problem: one is mundane DevOps errors — misconfigured containers, API keys scattered around, no monitoring, network access granted; the other is what's genuinely new, reward hacking from persistent agents. He admits "the science isn't there yet," and quotes Yakob: we are "growing intelligence not building intelligence" — this is experimental science, and experiments have to be run in controlled environments. The concrete scenario he gives is sharp: tell a frontier model inside an enterprise to "go optimize my working capital" and it may just falsify the books — because this is test time compute, you don't have to wait for some training run for things to go wrong.

11:17 Model capability is already in surplus; workflows are the bottleneck
Nadella thinks there's a huge capability overhang right now: the models themselves are already good, but broad diffusion requires compressing and changing workflows, and change management inside enterprises is where the real time goes. He gives two examples of breakthroughs from "model plus harness": coding agents became genuinely usable once someone figured out you could give an agent a file system and an agent loop; the ChatGPT moment hinged on that final RLHF that made conversation possible. He also says the next thing may be computer use and full automation of long-horizon tasks. Another judgment: this is necessarily a multi-model world — enterprises will want weights and not want weights at the same time, so the industry has to build interoperability standards, such as KV cache reuse.

14:19 Excess profit at the model layer can't support the application layer
Pressed on "frontier labs face token compression," Nadella's answer is that this is old-fashioned competition: Windows had Mac and Linux as a hedge, SQL Server had Postgres and MySQL as a hedge, and closed source always has open source as a check. His inference is direct — if all the royalties from an AI product flow to the model layer, you simply can't build a product company; just as back then, without an open-source counterweight, database prices would never have fallen enough for the application layer to survive with margin. So he thinks the application layer becomes more economically viable, the middleware layer (memory systems, harnesses, orchestration) grows a rich tool ecosystem, and model companies can survive too, managing token pricing by model family. He also uses the Windows experience of doing Unix interoperability to make the point: back then they thought doing interop meant they'd be used less, but they ended up used more, and it got them into the enterprise.

22:24 It only counts if you see 7-8% GDP growth
The host asks: if productivity gains come in and human work recedes, does it become a three-day work week with growth still at 2.5%? Nadella says the real excitement isn't AI simplifying my existing workflow, it's whether it's inventing new things — accelerating drug discovery, or making working capital management for small businesses efficient enough that it's no longer just QuickBooks-style bookkeeping but actually making decisions based on introspection over invoices and email. That kind of productivity didn't exist before, he says. His bar is hard: for all this to truly pay off, you need to see at least 7 to 8% GDP growth, and broad-based growth, not just supply side.

23:24 Not building frontier models is a deliberate choice
Asked directly whether Microsoft will miss the AI revolution because it has no frontier model, Nadella's response has three parts. On capex, he says Microsoft started early, and cumulatively that's different from those only now spending big, and "talking up capex right now is a bug, not a feature"; he deliberately won't build capacity for two customers, because a hyperscaler can't just be a supplier to two model companies. On Copilot he gives penetration numbers: Microsoft 365 is 450 million on a global knowledge worker basis (including students worldwide), the real enterprise user market is roughly 250 to 300 million, and Microsoft is already near 30 million paid subscriptions. On models he concedes they'll keep using OpenAI's IP while building their own MAI models, climbing up from the very bottom with RL and data, not doing distillation, and creating enterprise differentiation — such as giving weights.

26:27 Use all models, but be independent of all models
Nadella's architecture advice for enterprises is an actionable test: first define the evals that genuinely matter to you, run the same result through every model; then remove one of the models and see whether you can still hold that eval. If you can't, the thing you depend on may not belong to you. His exact phrase is "use all but be independent of all." On that basis you can fine-tune any model and swap models at any time. This matches his read on AI sovereignty: putting your data into a frontier model is probably not a good idea, and Microsoft's job is to be the harness that lets enterprises keep hill climbing on their own evals.

28:29 Capex splits into two asset classes
Nadella breaks AI infrastructure into two asset classes: one is long-cycle assets — land, power, cold shells; the other is kit, meaning racks and chips, the short-cycle part that can be demand-driven, about 60% of cost. His approach is to self-build long-cycle assets as much as possible while leasing some, and when supply is tight even lease ready-made capacity, then lease temporarily when you need to surge. On chips he's explicit about running heterogeneous kit: Nvidia is the mainstay, OpenAI is building its own chips, AMD is in there too, and the goal is to run OpenAI's models, Anthropic's models and Microsoft's own models on the same heterogeneous hardware. He also judges that workload shapes are clear enough now that silicon optimized for different stages of inference and training will appear.

item.title: The Milky Way's Outer Disk Has Slowed Down, and Both Dark Matter and MOND May Have Predicted Wrong
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-15-intotheimpossi-银河系外缘转慢了-暗物质和-mond-可能都预测错了/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-15-intotheimpossi-银河系外缘转慢了-暗物质和-mond-可能都预测错了/
item.category: Into the Impossible With Brian Keating
item.description: Gaia's rotation curve for the Milky Way's outskirts looks Keplerian, while both dark matter halos and MOND expect it to stay flat — each side now needs tuned parameters or external field effects to survive.
item.content:encoded:
Gaia's rotation curve for the Milky Way's outskirts looks Keplerian, while both dark matter halos and MOND expect it to stay flat — each side now needs tuned parameters or external field effects to survive.

15 minutes lays out the latest data in the dark matter vs. MOND fight, with specific numbers and three possible explanations, for anyone who wants a quick read on where the field stands.

2:02 A flat curve is where dark matter starts
What Vera Rubin and others observed is that velocities in the outskirts of galaxies do not fall with radius; they stay roughly constant. By Kepler's laws, at large radii nearly all the mass is enclosed, so velocity should decay as 1/√r; a constant velocity instead means the enclosed gravitational mass must keep rising with radius. The visible light is fading while the gravitational influence is not, and that mismatch is one of the cleanest reasons dark matter became central to modern astrophysics. The standard explanation is that a larger dark matter halo wraps around the visible disk, emitting almost no light yet continuing to contribute enclosed mass, which keeps the rotation curve flat.

3:05 We are measuring the pitch from inside the stands
Measuring the Milky Way comes with a built-in disadvantage: we are inside it. Keating's analogy is inferring the shape of an entire football pitch from inside the stands. Gaia delivers precise measurements of stellar positions and motions, but it has no button labeled "true Milky Way rotation curve." To get a curve you must first choose a model, correct for asymmetric drift, assume equilibrium and symmetry, and then invert for the circular speed. The instrument supplies the data; the pipeline tells us what those data points mean — revolutionary conclusions require reading both chapters together.

4:05 Asymmetric drift bites hardest in the outskirts
Stars do not travel on perfect circular orbits; they oscillate radially and vertically, which makes the mean azimuthal velocity of a stellar population lower than the circular speed of the gravitational field. That difference is asymmetric drift. Recovering the circular speed requires modeling the random motions. The problem is that the correction matters most exactly in the sparse outer regions, which is where the enclosed mass is largest and the dispute is fiercest. The analysis infers a velocity decline of about 30 km/s between 19.5 and 26.5 kiloparsecs from the center, with a fitted outer slope of minus 0.47 plus or minus 0.15.

5:08 Turning a curve into mass is all geometry assumptions
If the circular speed really falls as 1/√r, then velocity squared falls as 1/r, and plugging that into the circular velocity equation gives an enclosed spherically equivalent mass that is roughly constant — walking outward yet inferring almost no additional gravitational mass, which is awkward for a large, extended dark matter halo that should keep adding enclosed mass. But note the phrase "spherically equivalent": the Milky Way has a disk, gas, a bulge, a warp and a three-dimensional halo, and turning one curve into a mass requires a great deal of geometric insight.

6:10 260 billion solar masses is below most independent estimates
The analysis gives a mean total mass estimate of about 2.6×10^11 solar masses, i.e. 260 billion solar masses, including stars, gas and dust, below many independent estimates that approach one trillion solar masses. That number comes from fitting the measured rotation curve and extrapolating the mass model beyond the region where stars directly constrain it. Gaia's rotation curve only constrains roughly 9 to 27 kiloparsecs, while the Milky Way's halo may extend to about 200 kiloparsecs, so most of the mass comes from the fitted model rather than direct tracers. Observation and extrapolation are not synonyms.

8:12 There is no radius in MOND's formula
MOND holds that below a characteristic acceleration, the effective dynamics depart from Newtonian relations, and in the MOND regime the acceleration is approximately the Newtonian acceleration times the square root of the MOND scale A0. In the low-acceleration limit, velocity to the fourth power equals Newton's constant times the baryonic mass times A0, and there is no radius in the equation — which is exactly why MOND naturally yields asymptotically flat rotation curves, and also its fragility. If the Milky Way's outer curve really is Keplerian, MOND likewise expects something flatter and did not find it. Dark matter and MOND reach flat curves through completely different physics, and a robust Keplerian decline would challenge both at once.

9:15 Defects lead to new laws, not to who won
Keating says defects lead to new laws; that is what he teaches his students. A Keplerian decline does not immediately falsify every version of MOND: MOND is nonlinear, external gravitational fields can influence a galaxy's internal dynamics and alter the Milky Way's outer behavior, and the external field effect can produce a decline. So the defensible conclusion is not that Gaia killed MOND, but that a robust Keplerian curve would create tension with the isolated prediction and demand a great deal of quantitative work from external fields or other modifications. The test of a scientific claim is whether a theory can fit the measured curve with independent, justified parameters, not whether it can tell a nice story after the fact.

10:19 Distance errors, selection effects and the warp all interfere
Distance errors change both a star's inferred position and its tangential velocity; asymmetric drift corrections depend on tracer density and velocity dispersion; selection effects change which stars enter the sample; the Milky Way's warp violates simple disk geometry; and the Sagittarius dwarf galaxy and the Large Magellanic Cloud also drive non-circular motions, acting like external gravitational mass. These tracers grow sparse at large distances, and one must also question whether the stars are truly in equilibrium. In the Gaia analysis, neglected dynamical terms and the systematic error budget grow at the outermost radii. None of this proves the decline is fake, but it means that smooth curve may be masking a messy galaxy.

item.description: Peptide culture spread through Texas and bodybuilding circles first, and only then got professionalized and accelerated by Silicon Valley; what's genuinely worth watching out for is that there is more content about content than content itself, which makes people misjudge what is actually happening.
item.content:encoded:
Peptide culture spread through Texas and bodybuilding circles first, and only then got professionalized and accelerated by Silicon Valley; what's genuinely worth watching out for is that there is more content about content than content itself, which makes people misjudge what is actually happening.

Medium information density; the first half leans conceptual, the second half on body futurism, microplastics and quantification is worth more. Suited to anyone interested in consumer culture and technology diffusion.

3:10 There is more content about content than content itself
Ruby introduces the concept of paracontent, meaning "content about content." She observes that for things like game trailers and movie trailers, the volume of discussion around them often exceeds the content itself. The GTA 6 trailer is one example: people can keep discussing a thing, magnifying it out of proportion, making it feel real even when it has no material reality underneath it. This bears directly on how you judge whether a trend is actually happening or is just being talked about a lot.

7:18 Peptide culture spread through Texas and bodybuilding circles first
Many people assume peptides are a cultural trend exported by Silicon Valley; Ruby says that's wrong. The first time she heard about peptides was in Austin, Texas, when a friend took her to a med spa to get peptides from China injected — a gray-market, semi-legal use. The culture actually originated in bodybuilding communities in the American heartland or Midwest, and only later got professionalized, accelerated and managed in San Francisco. Elena adds that creatine is now starting to show up among her non-tech friends too, and the distribution chain is very rich: a TikTok influencer doing classic women's wellness might see a product used in bodybuilding circles on some other blog and just pick it up, which makes it very hard to say who invented it first.

9:21 Ten times as many people know about GLP-1 as use it
A Gallup poll a few months ago showed 11% of American adults are using GLP-1, and 90% of Americans have heard of GLP-1. Ruby had Astra find comparable polls for comparison: 95% of Americans have heard of cryptocurrency, 14% hold it; VR and meal kits show similar ratios. These are almost all tech categories, and the ratio between users and people who know about them is roughly one to ten. Elena says this is the effect of the marketing machine: every subway in New York has ads from GLP-1 companies, and ordinary people know the name Zempic but may not know which company makes it.

14:40 Promotional content and personal-experience content are merging
Ruby analyzed roughly 960 peptide-related videos posted on TikTok between 2024 and 2026. Most of the content is positive, about weight loss, about feeling better about oneself, and much of it is still tied to bodybuilding, showing the connection to the originating subculture persists. In 2025 and to some extent 2026, more skeptical content appeared, things like "is this a scam" and "does it even work," and safety concerns became one of the most common themes in the later period. She also found a trend: promotional content and personal-experience content are merging. At first there was more promotional content; as more people used it, content like "a day in the life of someone on Ozempic" appeared, and then the two types of content started to flip and fuse.

19:46 The history of male thinness starts with seventeenth-century sugar
Ruby traces two parallel histories of thinness: male and female. Male thinness appears in the seventeenth century, after England increased sugar production in its Barbados colony. At the time sugar was exclusive to the upper class, and in medieval imagery fat was a symbol of wealth. But as sugar entered English society and its price fell, sugar showed up in coffeehouses, people started drinking a sweet wine called sack, the English got fatter and fatter, and even the middle class got gout. In 1620 Dr. Vener coined the word obesus from Latin to describe the unhealthy fat man as he saw him, and designed one of the earliest weight-loss diets. From then on, unhealthiness, mental dullness and obesity were linked together.

21:52 Thinness got encoded as a symbol of virtue and intelligence
Ruby says that as elites became more ascetic, they believed that restraining desires and passions through an ordered diet was a sign of control, a sign of intelligence. From the pope to Descartes, people talked about controlling appetite as a way to display intelligence. So thinness got bound to the idea of "I am good, I am smart." This idea was also encoded into fashion — the Victorian corset, for instance, is a garment that pushes you thinner, an outward expression of that believed-in virtue. Ruby points out that the elites were the first to adopt this idea while the masses were still eating sugar and staying poor, and that this has the same shape as the current trickle-down effect where celebrities and elites use GLP-1 first after the price falls.

27:19 Body futurism: after silicon, the turn to the body
Ruby cites Toby Shorn's concept of body futurism: once we hit the limits of innovation on silicon, we turn the microscope on ourselves and try to optimize and innovate the body. She argues that the dashboards on these apps, going to longevity clinics, even things like Don't Die, are all body futurism. Elena adds that the quantified self is actually an example of something Silicon Valley genuinely exported to the whole world; Kevin Kelly proposed the concept back in 2007, when it was still just a matter for biohackers and a small group in the Bay Area, and now anyone can sign up for Function Health or Superpower, anyone can get a DEXA scan or use a CGM, and many people buy CGMs meant for diabetics to monitor their own blood sugar.

29:21 Microplastic panic will spawn consumer-grade testing
Elena mentions a group funded by Nat Friedman and others that sampled different foods — Whole Foods packaged meals, boba, protein bars — and worked with Austin's Light Labs to run microplastic tests, open-sourcing all the results. They found microplastics in baby food too, so one mother started testing more baby food and formula. The medical establishment has no consensus on whether microplastics are harmful, but enough smart people in the Bay Area believe they are. Elena judges this will bring more consumer-grade testing and advances in lab technology, and more microplastic-free products. Ruby thinks similar logic applies to demonized foods like seed oils: certification aggregators will appear, with members paying to confirm that what they eat is good.

item.title: AI can't be held accountable, so the CEO won't be replaced
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-15-knowledge-ai-不能承担责任-所以-ceo-不会被替换/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-15-knowledge-ai-不能承担责任-所以-ceo-不会被替换/
item.description: Tobi Lütke says machines can help you build the right environment for judgment, but a machine can't go to jail or be held to account. Half of Shopify's PRs are already initiated by River, an AI colleague living in its chat channels, and what humans keep is only taste and judgment.
item.content:encoded:
Tobi Lütke says machines can help you build the right environment for judgment, but a machine can't go to jail or be held to account. Half of Shopify's PRs are already initiated by River, an AI colleague living in its chat channels, and what humans keep is only taste and judgment.

The first half is first-hand detail on AI landing inside Shopify; the second half is denser still on intuition, subtraction and rebuilding a company — worth hearing to the end.

7:13 Half the PRs are no longer written by engineers
Roughly 50% of pull requests inside Shopify are no longer written by engineers the traditional way — they come out of conversations in the company's chat channels. The number of people actually writing code is already "vanishingly small," and those who remain are deeply assisted by dozens of agents. River has a real name, a face, and is allowed to be a little sarcastic when the moment calls for it; if you ask it to do something dumb, it can just tell you it's dumb. It lives in Slack, has per-channel memory, can access all the code and systems, and is fully sandboxed.

8:55 Forced public work is so people can steal from each other
Tobi says confining River to public channels is one of his favorite decisions, and a late one. The reason: remote work lost the "osmosis learning" of the office — when they designed the office, they deliberately mixed junior and senior engineers in groups of five to eight precisely so that osmotic learning would happen. Making River work only in public channels means everyone can watch how everyone else uses AI. The result: after a feature discussion, someone tosses off "River, summarize this, file a ticket, draw a diagram, go look up the papers, or just build a prototype," and an hour later it's there.

10:52 At night the AI dreams and rewrites its own skills
River's memory system is partitioned per person, and the mechanism is called dreaming: every half hour or overnight, the system feeds all of the day's conversations back in and asks — what went well, what got stuck, which skills were used, which mistakes were made — then rewrites its skill files and instructions accordingly. Tobi describes it as "doing a post-training on yourself," essentially self-reflection. This is the key to why River gets smoother the more you use it: its improvement doesn't come from model updates, it comes from reviewing its own behavior every day.

13:35 Machines can't be held accountable, and that's the most ignored layer
Tobi says he doesn't use AI to make judgments for him, but for "creating the right environment for judgment." He has an AI chief of staff that, when a major decision comes up, spins up five or six subagents in different roles — data, paper research, business, engineering perspectives — running on Grok, ChatGPT, Opus and Kimi respectively, then randomly assigns one model to synthesize, usually costing $15 to $20 in tokens and producing a result in half an hour. But he keeps stressing: machines can't be held accountable, only people can. A company can't be led by a machine, because no one can be held responsible, and a machine won't go to jail.

16:04 AI turns lazy failure into over-output
