item.title: An AI-native organisation isn't everyone using AI — it's assuming the organisation doesn't exist and rebuilding it
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-14-cn18b4d2-ai-原生组织不是人人用-ai-是假设组织不存在重写一遍/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-14-cn18b4d2-ai-原生组织不是人人用-ai-是假设组织不存在重写一遍/
item.description: Locke merged HR and IT into HARO, put a technical founder type in charge of people and AI; circle leads hold the bonus-pool allocation power, and hiring requires proving AI can't do the job.
item.content:encoded:
Locke merged HR and IT into HARO, put a technical founder type in charge of people and AI; circle leads hold the bonus-pool allocation power, and hiring requires proving AI can't do the job.

A 12-year hardware company's founder on the concrete mechanics of organisational rewrite: HARO, circles, AI management trainees, how FDEs actually land — with details and the pits he fell into.

4:01 AI-native starts by assuming the organisation doesn't exist
Chen Bin's definition of an AI-native organisation is not ‘everyone should use AI well’ but starting from AI and asking again: can AI do this thing, and can we avoid having a person do it. The harsher step is to assume the original organisation and processes don't exist — ‘they shouldn't even exist’ — and go back to the state of a one-person startup to redesign roles and processes. So this is not accelerating existing processes; it is tearing the processes down first and rebuilding them. He concedes this is mainly aimed at the core organisation builders, not a slogan shouted at everyone.

6:04 HARO's head comes from technology, not HR
Locke merged HR and IT into HARO (Human AI Resource Office), but Chen Bin stresses it is not an ordinary HR+IT: the head must understand the business, and the person chosen is an old partner who started the company with him and has done technology, product, CEO, R&D, brand and IT. The logic is inverted — the old HR head leaned toward people and was insensitive to AI, so now a technology-oriented person runs it, with HR BPs who are sensitive to people assigned to him. Under this department sit the AIO (the former IT team, which will build Agent Builders) on a solid line, and FDEs reporting on a dotted line.

10:04 Agent Builder and FDE are two kinds of people in the short term
Chen Bin draws the line clearly: an Agent Builder leans technical and can build an Agent; an FDE has to go into the business front line, map out supply, planning and procurement processes, and is best a business expert. Long term one person might cover it; short term it must be two kinds of people working together. They did not copy Anker's approach of pulling people out of work and locking them up for a month, because they don't have that much slack; instead they let business people spend 30% to 50% of their energy doing AI-ification alongside their day jobs. The company also set up AI proficiency levels L1 to L4, with L2 and above called ‘AI navigators’ and above that ‘pilots’.

16:06 Circles erase functional power; circle leads hold the bonus pool
Locke's circles differ from project teams and Huawei's matrix: the matrix is product line plus function on two axes, while a circle is a small team around an end-to-end value loop, deliberately erasing functional power and boundaries so the circle lead's power grows. The company gives a circle a bonus pool, and the circle lead decides how to split it — even how much to give himself. HR and functional departments only have an advisory voice. Chen Bin says at this stage the ‘fighting’ line dominates; the functional line may in future become something like a technology committee, but within the first half year to a year of the change, the front line decides.

20:36 Experience can become a burden instead
Chen Bin says AI management trainees naturally started using AI from university in 2023, have no fear when doing things, and use it more than the veterans. His exact words: ‘sometimes experience instead becomes a burden’. The worst is the half-baked — experience hasn't arrived but they think they are very experienced and can't change. Veterans have framework thinking and systematic thinking as their foundation, but on which processes and which roles can be removed, the clear-eyed judge more easily. The threshold for AI management trainees is internal AI level L2 or above, requiring skill use and Agent building; only L3 can author workflows.

23:23 R&D turns fast, marketing turns slow
Chen Bin admits transformation speed varies a lot by department: technical R&D tied to software and coding is easiest, because writing code every day gives positive feedback; marketing and branding are slow, because after publishing more content they ask ‘so what’ — did it bring revenue growth and bonus increases. He also mentions a real conflict: people doing design and content feel AI can only accelerate quantity, not improve quality, and that 60-point output doesn't stick. His response is to give everyone an operating mindset: whether content brings conversion is the standard.

35:32 Three rounds of sign-ups: stand up again, sit down again
Locke ran three internal rounds of sign-ups: the first for incremental roles, such as the company-level ten or twenty Agents and their Agent Builders and FDEs; the second for roles missing after circles formed, such as a content marketing Agent Builder; the third to keep filling gaps. Applicants first do a self-assessment to find what they are good at, then give a three-to-five-minute defence; after the judges score, AI is used to analyse the meeting minutes and the talk for matching. Of a hundred applicants, twenty or thirty may be chosen. Chen Bin says both the mechanism and the results are very good.

42:16 Hiring requires proving AI can't do the job
After a department's people are picked off by circles, if the boss wants to backfill, logically there are only two channels: find AI management trainees, or use more AI tokens. If you really must hire again, it goes to Chen Bin for special approval, and you have to explain why a trainee can't do it and why AI can't do it. Chen Bin says ‘logically he has no channel left’. They plan to hire 50 AI management trainees by year-end, and are already close to 20. Xiaofei's role at Locke is like a strategic HR, a CHO as a service, doing the AI-native transformation together with Chen Bin.

item.title: He Unlocked the Chains of the Insane, Then Built Psychological Ones
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-14-stuffmissed-他解开了精神病人的锁链-却造出了心理锁链/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-14-stuffmissed-他解开了精神病人的锁链-却造出了心理锁链/
item.category: Stuff You Missed in History Class
item.description: Pinel cut Bicêtre's annual mortality rate from 50% to under 13% in a single year, mostly through cleanliness; but he denied organic brain causes, and Foucault accused him of replacing iron chains with psychological ones.
item.content:encoded:
Pinel cut Bicêtre's annual mortality rate from 50% to under 13% in a single year, mostly through cleanliness; but he denied organic brain causes, and Foucault accused him of replacing iron chains with psychological ones.

A crossover case of medical history and social reform, suited to anyone who wants to see how a humanitarian reform gets amplified by institutions; but the controversy only arrives in the back half, and the early biography is flat.

4:07 No license is what forced the case-file system into existence
The medical degree Pinel earned in Toulouse only allowed him to practice in Toulouse, so once he reached Montpellier and then Paris he could not practice directly. During his four years in Montpellier he instead visited hospitals repeatedly, talked with patients at length, and took copious notes, organizing the information into detailed records. Because he followed the same group of patients over a long period, he could observe how illnesses evolved and thereby identify patterns in their course. This ‘observe—record—track’ method was later carried to Bicêtre, where it became the prototype for building a file on every patient, recording age, temperature, diagnosis, and even comparing patient temperatures against the temperature of the building.

8:19 Classifying the insane with botanical taxonomy
The seventh ward at Bicêtre held 200 men judged to be insane, many chained in extremely small rooms, with chains long enough only to let them shuffle around inside. Pinel communicated closely with the director, Jean-Baptiste Poussin, gathered as much information on patients as he could, organized it into tables, and transferred his knowledge of plant classification over to the problem, trying to build finer diagnostic categories rather than simply lumping people together as ‘mad.’ He did not call patients ‘mad’ or ‘insane’ but said they were in a state of ‘mental alienation’—that is, estranged from their own reason.

9:21 Mortality fell from 50% to under 13%
Pinel put a concrete set of practices in place at Bicêtre: moving patients out of prison-style confinement and into rooms with as much natural light as possible; no longer using chaining as a routine measure; establishing hygiene standards for the institution; having patients take hot baths regularly; and providing what today would be called occupational therapy to help patients overcome the obstacles of daily life. Within a year, the institution's annual patient mortality rate fell from 50% to under 13%. The show states plainly that this was largely just a matter of keeping patients and their environment clean—where disease is spreading, without cleanliness there is no control. In addition, a considerable share of patients were able to return to life outside the institution, whereas at the time the expectation for most people entering an asylum was to die inside it.

19:43 He measured skulls to prove phrenology was garbage
Pinel recorded age, temperature and diagnosis for every patient, and also measured skulls. This was not because he believed in phrenology—quite the opposite: phrenology was just taking shape during his main working period, built on the craniology that originated in Austria in the 1790s, which held that a person's tendency to violence or madness could be read off the shape of the head. Pinel considered the whole thing useless, and he collected skull measurements precisely in order to falsify it. He later wrote that the data seemed to confirm his earlier view: strong mental emotions are the most common cause of insanity, and the skulls of the mad have no special conformation that cannot be found in any other skull picked at random.

21:46 He did not unlock everyone's chains
The image of ‘Pinel breaking the chains of all his patients and turning prisoners into patients’ needs discounting. A famous late-19th-century painting by Tony Robert-Fleury depicts him removing chains, and it shows the women's institution. But he did not release every patient bound in irons: where he judged that loosening them would create danger, patients remained confined and tethered. In the paper he read in 1794 he gave several cases of men he called ‘agitated and violent,’ one of whom had been chained for more than forty years. He described their behavior in detail to explain why irons were needed, and wrote that one of the basic principles for dealing with the insane was ‘a judicious mixture of kindness and firmness,’ avoiding unnecessary coercion and using only as much force as was needed to restrain them.

27:53 He denied brain pathology, and that is a real flaw
One of the long-standing criticisms of Pinel's work is that he ignored the physiological causes of mental health problems. His writing discusses at length how life events worsen mental conditions, yet never considers bodily causes—which is strange, because writing on the physiological causes of mental illness goes back to Hippocrates and Galen, and in Pinel's own time Lavoisier, along with his university colleague Michel-Augustin Theret, were already discussing brain chemistry. In 1801 Pinel explicitly argued against bodily causes of madness, writing that ‘the derangement of the intellect is generally regarded as the result of an organic lesion of the brain, and therefore incurable, a supposition contradicted by anatomical facts in a great number of instances.’ The show says directly: he was completely wrong on this point.

30:56 That ‘Citizen, I am convinced’ story may be invented
In 1849 Chambers' Edinburgh Journal published a story about Pinel, sourced to Pinel's son Scipion Pinel—who also became a psychiatrist. The story goes that during the Terror, the Paris Commune official Georges Coudon came to Bicêtre hunting for ‘traitors feigning madness,’ and after seeing the chains, the filth and the mad howling with his own eyes, asked Pinel whether he had gone mad himself to want to unchain these people. Pinel is said to have replied: ‘Citizen, I am convinced that these madmen became so unmanageable only because they were deprived of air and liberty.’ The show says this sounds very cool and very clever, but whether the story is true we do not know—it may be family legend, or it may have been made up by an editor. It certainly added bricks to Pinel's 19th-century legend.

32:59 Foucault: the iron chains were swapped for psychological ones
Pinel's writing and work have been argued over almost continuously for nearly two hundred years. Supporters point out how progressive his work was and how many of his ideas still matter today. One particularly forceful critic was the 20th-century philosopher Michel Foucault. Foucault argued that Pinel may have removed the physical shackles from patients, but only replaced them with psychological shackles, describing his work as a form of ‘moral imprisonment’ in which patients were manipulated in subtler ways during treatment. By Foucault's logic, in becoming obedient to the doctor, patients became estranged from themselves. The show also notes that this line of argument in Foucault has problems of its own.

item.title: Charged Black Holes Emit Charged Particles, and Quantum Gravity Corrections Barely Matter
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-14-instituteforad-带电黑洞发射带电粒子-量子引力修正几乎不起作用/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-14-instituteforad-带电黑洞发射带电粒子-量子引力修正几乎不起作用/
item.description: Quantum corrections to near-extremal black holes drastically rewrite the Hawking spectrum for photons and gravitons, but switch to charged particles and the corrections nearly vanish — because the particles are mostly produced in the throat, far from the horizon, where they cannot feel the metric fluctuations near the horizon.
item.content:encoded:
Quantum corrections to near-extremal black holes drastically rewrite the Hawking spectrum for photons and gravitons, but switch to charged particles and the corrections nearly vanish — because the particles are mostly produced in the throat, far from the horizon, where they cannot feel the metric fluctuations near the horizon.

A high-energy theory session: dense derivations, high terminology barrier; worth listening for those interested in black hole information and quantum gravity, for everyone else the information density is on the low side.

1:20 Near-extremal black holes are actually quantum objects
In classical general relativity a black hole is characterized by three parameters — mass M, charge Q, angular momentum J — and solutions exist only when M is greater than or equal to Q; the case of exact equality is an extremal black hole, and near-equality is a near-extremal black hole. Over the past few years, via the Euclidean gravitational path integral, it was discovered that near-extremal black holes receive very large fluctuations from the quantum metric, and many textbook properties are thereby rewritten. This is precisely the motivation for this talk: since so many properties have changed, the standard story of Hawking radiation should be run through again as well.

10:29 The Schwarzian mode is one-loop exact
Write the metric as a classical solution plus fluctuations and the gauge field as a classical field plus fluctuations, then expand the action, and you can compute the fluctuations. In the past this was done only at quadratic order, to compute the logarithmic correction to the entropy; the new development is the identification of a special class of metric fluctuations confined deep in the ADS2 throat, namely the Schwarzian modes. Their effective action is proportional to temperature divided by some energy scale, vanishes at zero temperature, and contributes enormously when the temperature is far below that energy scale. More crucially, this action as a whole is the Schwarzian theory, and it is one-loop exact: computing only the quadratic term automatically includes all higher-order interaction terms.

20:50 The neutral-particle spectrum is rewritten by quantum corrections
For the S-wave of a massless scalar, the Hawking formula gives the energy flux. Taking the initial energy to be 100 times the breaking scale, the quantum rate and the semiclassical curve nearly coincide; but pushing the initial energy down to one tenth of the breaking scale, the two curves diverge enormously, and the quantum rate does not allow the black hole to radiate more energy than the amount by which it exceeds extremality. This is the evidence that quantum gravity corrections matter in the neutral-particle story, and it is the benchmark against which charged particles are to be compared later.

26:56 Charged particles were previously uncomputable because the dimension goes complex
In parameter space, in the region where both mass and charge are large (the QED region) as well as in the massless charged region, the scaling dimension of the scalar field in ADS2 becomes complex, the techniques used for neutral particles do not apply, and this is why charged particles long remained incompletely understood. The only corner where similar techniques carry over is the ‘lightly charged field’ corner: add a tiny charge to the massless field so that the particle charge times the black hole charge is far less than 1, and the scaling dimension is about 1. In this corner, adding a little charge makes the deviation from the semiclassical answer shrink dramatically.

33:27 The Hawking computation and the Schwinger computation are equivalent
There are two perspectives in the literature for computing black hole electron production: one is Hawking-style, canonically quantizing on a curved background and evaluating the particle number operator at infinity; the other is Schwinger-style, treating the black hole as a background electric field and computing pair production via the Schwinger mechanism. The former is the correct computation and implicitly includes Schwinger pair production, but it is extremely hard; the latter is much easier. This talk proves that as the temperature goes to zero, the Hawking computation and the Schwinger computation give nearly identical results, the only difference being that Hawking decomposes in spherical angular momentum modes with quantized angular momentum, whereas Schwinger uses a flat-space approximation with no quantized angular momentum.

43:34 One electron kicks the black hole back into the safe zone
The backreaction is very violent: if the black hole sits in the near-extremal, highly quantized region, then emitting a single electron (which carries away a large amount of energy and charge) leaves the black hole's final state back in the completely safe semiclassical region. This explains why quantum gravity corrections to charged-particle emission are unimportant — the produced particle itself pushes the system out of the quantum region.

50:38 The superradiance boundary is where particles just barely cannot escape
Reinterpreting the Hawking spectrum in the Schwinger picture, it can be divided into three segments. Near the superradiance boundary (the green region): in the point-particle approximation, if a particle is produced too close to the horizon it falls in and cannot escape, so the rate drops sharply to zero at the superradiance boundary; the peak corresponds exactly to the position of the point particle's unstable minimum, push a little to the left and it escapes, push a little to the right and it falls into the black hole. The middle purple region: particles are produced in the long ADS2 throat or the flat-space part, and Schwinger is an excellent approximation. The leftmost red region: particles would have to be produced at infinity in an infinitely weak electric field, the rate is essentially zero, and so an essential singularity appears.

53:38 Quantum corrections cannot reach most of the particles
In a certain gauge the metric fluctuations are localized near the Euclidean horizon, whereas charged particles are mostly produced in the throat or even farther out in the flat-space region, far from these fluctuations, unable to feel them, so the rate is naturally unaffected. What might receive large corrections is the green region hugging the superradiance boundary, but that region is small and its contribution to the total rate is limited. The author states explicitly that tools are currently lacking to compute precisely how the green-region rate is modified, so no precise answer can be given.

item.title: Obeying Incentives Is for Losers: You Should Decide Right and Wrong for Yourself
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-14-econtalk-遵守激励是失败者行为-你该自己判断对错/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-14-econtalk-遵守激励是失败者行为-你该自己判断对错/
item.description: Economists say fix the incentives and you fix the world. Mastroianni says that misses half of it: even if you have a reason to do something bad, you still shouldn't do it. Outsourcing your value judgments to an incentive structure is abandoning the core task of being a person.
item.content:encoded:
Economists say fix the incentives and you fix the world. Mastroianni says that misses half of it: even if you have a reason to do something bad, you still shouldn't do it. Outsourcing your value judgments to an incentive structure is abandoning the core task of being a person.

Medium information density; the early stretch gets tangled up in Omelas and Rube Goldberg, and the real stuff is the big fish, Sumner, and high pay selecting the wrong people in the middle and back half.

8:07 Having a reason to do wrong doesn't mean you should
Mastroianni first grants that incentive analysis beats ‘people are bad, so they do bad things’: it at least admits people have reasons, and change the reasons and you may change the behavior. But he adds a premise economists often miss — if you do it because an external reward structure tells you it's good, because it will pat you on the head or give you a little treat, that's loser behavior. His words: even if you have a reason to do something bad, you still shouldn't do it. He jokes that this is an obvious point, but some points are so obvious that no one thinks to say them.

12:21 The real Omelas is a Rube Goldberg machine
In Le Guin's Omelas, the whole city's happiness rests on a tortured child in the basement, and some people choose to walk away. Mastroianni says that story was in his head when he wrote the piece, but he cut a section: in the story you have some metaphysical connection to the child, whereas in reality the connection is more like a Rube Goldberg machine — you aren't the one torturing the child, you're three warehouses away, just the hammer that swings down, hits the ball, the ball rolls down the slope, lights the match. The bad thing is far from you, you didn't do it with your own hands, but you're in the causal chain. That makes ‘walking away’ much harder and far less heroic: it doesn't look like brushing the dust of Omelas off your feet, it looks like ‘I'm not going to be VP of brand partnerships for Philip Morris.’

17:27 Outsource your value judgments and the wicked deputize you
Russ asks: are you saying we should encourage people to be more moral? Mastroianni says he doesn't think that can be centrally organized, mandated, compelled or cultivated by government — when government tries, it tends to go bad fast. His goal is to produce the kind of person who does the right thing even when it's inconvenient, even when it's costly. He offers a chain: if you only do what you're rewarded for, you can start out amoral and end up deputized for the immoral. His judgment: the wicked are few; what's plentiful is people with no strong sense of right and wrong, and those people can be turned into an army by the wicked.

20:33 The big fish finds you; you decide whether to look
The ‘big fish’ comes from Lovecraft's Dagon: a man sees a fish god, is never right again for the rest of his life, and finally jumps out a window. Mastroianni uses it as a metaphor — everyone has a fish inside them, and if you really take it seriously you have to overturn your entire life. His own fish was the 2020 Society for Personality and Social Psychology conference in San Francisco: the venue was in the Tenderloin, and inside people ate canapés and talked about reducing implicit bias a tiny bit, possibly just noise, while outside people huddled with fentanyl in their veins. He specifically mentions the 1970s seminary student experiment: randomly assigned to speak on the Good Samaritan or on career opportunities, then randomly told they were late or on time, and the only thing that determined whether they stopped for the man lying by the road was whether they were in a hurry. He says one of the most famous findings in the field, known to everyone in that room, and no one felt any conflict over it — that was the fish he saw.

31:28 Sumner took the cane blows and went back to provoking
Charles Sumner is the man whose statue Mastroianni walked past every day in grad school. He came from a poor Boston family, his father was illegitimate; the place where he grew up was home to large numbers of formerly enslaved people. He went to France, and at the Sorbonne he saw Black and white students studying together as equals, and wrote in his diary: the difference between people is obviously not caused by nature, it can only be caused by education. He became a radical abolitionist, arguing not just for abolition but for racially integrated schools and Black suffrage — things that only became common sense more than a century later. As a senator he gave a fierce anti-slavery speech, and days later a Southern congressman walked up to his desk and beat him with a cane until he was nearly dead, trapped in his desk, soaked in his own blood, and it took him more than a year to recover. After recovering he kept provoking, and pushed Lincoln to issue the Emancipation Proclamation two years early. His new biographer says Sumner is cited 40 times in the brief for Brown v. Board.

40:20 Desperate to join the club of people you don't respect
Russ cites Adam Smith: we want to be loved and to be lovely, so we should surround ourselves with good people whose approval we want. Mastroianni goes harder: he and the people close to him have spent their whole lives desperately seeking opportunities from people they don't respect, landing them in an absurd position — ‘I think they're bad people, I think they're completely wrong about what's good and bad, but I really want them to let me into their club.’ Into it for what? You will inevitably become more like them, and you can't control it. He says the moment you can say ‘I distrust this person's judgment so much that even if he could give me success, I'll go do something else’ is the moment of freedom he described earlier: that person has no power over you anymore.

50:15 High pay doesn't buy you better professors
Russ says he made about $18,600 a year when he graduated, and is glad he didn't go into finance or a big company's chief economist office. He asks: economics professors can make $500,000 or even $750,000 a year — with more money, is it harder to maintain the norms of honesty and truth-seeking that founded the discipline? Mastroianni says this looks more like a selection effect than a corruption effect: the people attracted by $750,000 are often not the people who can be good professors; the consequence of high pay isn't corrupting people who might have been good, it's attracting people who shouldn't be there and making them compete with each other. Russ presses: if you pay $750,000, shouldn't you get the best professors? Mastroianni answers: the professor you want is someone who puts truth above everything, and once the money is big enough, what comes is people who don't put truth first — and our selection procedures can't tell who's in it for truth and who's in it for the salary, especially since many of the people doing the selecting came for the wrong reasons themselves.

57:37 Status is harder to separate from knowledge than money is
Mastroianni says what attracts the wrong people in most places isn't money, it's status: being called professor feels good, so many people want it, so few get it. And status markers are harder to distinguish from knowledge markers than money markers are, because they claim to be knowledge markers — ‘you published in a good journal, so it must be good work.’ He says we've reached the point where people talk about writing a specific paper for a specific journal, and call papers pubs or A-pubs, and he finds it vile and disgusting, like defacing a cross. He says this is why he isn't in academia: he was willing to earn less to study what he thought mattered, to tolerate job insecurity, to move all over the world, but if after all that it's still ‘why don't you publish a pile of garbage papers’ and ‘why don't you massage the statistics a little’, then it isn't worth it.

item.title: OpenAI Declares the AGI Era, but There Isn't Enough Compute to Go Around
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-14-a16z-openai-宣布进入-agi-时代-但算力不够分给所有人/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-14-a16z-openai-宣布进入-agi-时代-但算力不够分给所有人/
item.description: Greg Brockman says Astra can run coherently for 24 hours on a task, so you can reasonably call it AGI; the real bottleneck isn't model capability but compute and safety alignment — no matter how strong the model gets, it may not reach everyone affordably.
item.content:encoded:
Greg Brockman says Astra can run coherently for 24 hours on a task, so you can reasonably call it AGI; the real bottleneck isn't model capability but compute and safety alignment — no matter how strong the model gets, it may not reach everyone affordably.

Greg rarely goes into how OpenAI internally uses 10,000 agents to solve math problems, how it killed Sora, and how it pulls 25% of production engineers into defense — the mechanism details are worth more than the conclusions.

0:00 AGI isn't a moment, it's a fuzzy spectrum
Greg says AGI is no longer a point in time but a fuzzy spectrum. His judgment is that Astra has ‘hit something’ and can reasonably be called AGI: it can use a computer, take on long-horizon tasks, and OpenAI has seen it run coherently for 24 hours straight to complete a task, across a very broad range of domains. But he stresses the model is still jagged — writing is ‘the first time it's not slop’, but it isn't good yet; in some places it's just a little more polish away from being great, and right now it's just short of that. He cites the jagged-boundary diagram from Twitter and says the place you actually want to get to is stability across every dimension, not exceptional strength in a few.

4:08 Not enough compute: a strong model still can't reach everyone
Greg frames ‘pacing the frontier’ as two things: one is model capability itself, which he believes is achievable; the other is distributing that capability to everyone, which he thinks is the massively underrated challenge. In his words the model will be strong enough, but ‘we won't have enough compute to serve it all’ — it's very hard to deliver it to everyone affordably. He also calls safety, security and alignment almost the bottleneck on progress — not something you patch after the model is done, but a standard you must continuously up-level, or it becomes the thing holding back the schedule.

9:25 The Hugging Face incident is the alarm clock for the defense window
Greg splits the Hugging Face incident into two layers: one is how OpenAI itself monitors, sandboxes and controls models during evaluation, which led the team to change a large number of internal standards; the other is that it previewed what broad capability diffusion into the hands of threat actors looks like — an AI that can both escape a secure environment and hack into a company's production environment, and what it found was quite sophisticated. His conclusion is that defenders have a window right now: frontier capability is still in the hands of a few companies, defenders have differential access, and they should use this time to raise their own security waterline with frontier models, so that when capability diffuses they get pulled up along with it. Ben Horowitz adds the flip side: we have 50 years of code and architecture that wasn't designed for this world, plus a pile of consumer-data honeypots sitting on the internet.

12:31 10,000 agents cracked Navier-Stokes
Ben raises the upside: being able to deploy 10,000 agents, let them communicate with each other and self-organize to do work. Greg confirms OpenAI used 10,000 agents to attack the Navier-Stokes problem, and formalized it in Lean so the AI writes verifiable code. He gives the significance two layers: the problem itself has applications to fluid dynamics and ocean currents; more importantly it represents AI creating new knowledge, potentially opening a whole wave of scientific and drug discovery. That connects to what he says later about ‘formally verifying all software’ — something that never took off because it was too infeasible for humans, and now that AI has proof capability, it becomes possible again.

13:32 OpenAI pulls 25% of production engineers to play defense
Greg describes OpenAI's own approach: pulling 25% of production engineers off their projects, telling them everything is paused and their job now is defense — using models to find holes in their own systems. They found a batch of serious issues and fixed them. He also describes a convergence process: take Astra and scan your own systems, find new problems, but eventually it saturates — Astra is smart enough that it has basically found all the P0s it can find, and then you wait for the next, stronger model to open a new round. From this he proposes the ‘defense factory’: end-to-end automation from vulnerability discovery, triage, remediation, deployment to verification, and if you can do it at machine speed, defenders gain a very large advantage.

18:47 Codex found 13 vulnerabilities in 15 minutes
Greg tells the story of his own site, gregbrockman.com: a very simple static site, and he had Codex do a penetration test. It came back in 15 minutes with 13 findings — an SPF record set up so someone could forge email, some requests going over HTTP without forcing HTTPS, and so on. Individually none of them is a big deal, but he says if AI can chain many small vulnerabilities into one big one, that's different. Then he had Codex just fix them: over 45 minutes it opened cloud service control panels, clicked around, set various headers, migrated to Cloudflare Pages, and kicked off the DMARC process (which has a 48-hour window). He says after those 45 minutes he felt ‘so protected’.

30:07 US AI sentiment is lowest because nobody tells people the upside
Ben asks why AI sentiment is higher in Asia and Europe than in the US. Greg's answer: the industry and companies need to do a better job explaining to people ‘why you benefit’, not just that this is a strategic asset for the country. He offers a set of usage numbers: ChatGPT has roughly 1.1 billion weekly active users, about 100 million of them in the US, close to a third of the population using it weekly. He tells a story about a friend: in the hospital, a doctor about to inject a certain antibiotic, she typed a question to ChatGPT, and ChatGPT said absolutely do not use that, you had that condition a year ago and it could be fatal; she showed the response to the doctor, who said that's exactly right, I only have five minutes to read your chart. Greg says stories like this aren't told enough and need to enter the public consciousness.

43:50 Sora was killed to get the business moving
Greg says this year's theme is focus, because ‘we can't do it all’. The test is working backward from the mission: if deployment and productization strengthen the mission, keep it; if not, cut it. He states plainly that Sora was the highest-profile of the canceled projects, and ‘very painful’, but it had to be done to unlock the business. Another move was merging the consumer and enterprise chat into chat work. He admits that in the first half many metrics were pointing the wrong way, and the team had to be repeatedly told to get back to basics, quoting “The Score Takes Care of Itself”: you can't affect the outcome, only the inputs, and winning the Super Bowl comes down to blocking and tackling. His own focus over the past two years shifted from data centers, infrastructure and machine learning engineering to the business this year.

item.title: After AI Takes the Talent, Crypto's Only Opportunities Are Six Tokens
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-14-empire-ai-抢走人才后-加密的机会只剩六种代币/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-14-empire-ai-抢走人才后-加密的机会只剩六种代币/
item.description: Delphi's Yan Liberman says crypto VCs make one deal a year because AI has sucked up all the smart people; the only things that can actually make money are a handful of tokens with real revenue that don't depend on the crypto market.
item.content:encoded:
Delphi's Yan Liberman says crypto VCs make one deal a year because AI has sucked up all the smart people; the only things that can actually make money are a handful of tokens with real revenue that don't depend on the crypto market.

A frontline crypto VC publicly lays out his six positions and his reasoning, including why he no longer does crypto venture and why he has given up on the gaming vertical. High information density, but you need a bit of crypto background.

1:02 This rally has no obvious buyer
Yan says the market was caught off guard by ‘QE in the form of long-end bond curve control’, which triggered a short squeeze, but he personally finds it hard to see new highs in the short term, because it would take a lot of new money, and the obvious buyer historically (Sailor) isn't buying now — instead he's cashmaxing and paying down preferred stock. He thinks leverage hasn't built up excessively, and this sequence of slow grind, pause, alt rotation is actually healthy. Another structural change is that the alt market has gotten shallower, money concentrates more easily into a few assets, so you don't need a whole new cohort of buyers to move the market — it has become a ‘stock picker's market’.

5:06 Buy the ones that look like hot coins but aren't as crowded
Yan admits there are only about 10 to 15 investable liquid tokens right now, and every crypto fund is already positioned in those 15. His conclusion: you should look for names that ‘look and smell like these coins, but aren't as crowded to trade’. Hyperliquid is a long-term bull, but going to 200 within four months would be a surprise; if you want short-term outperformance, you have to look at less obvious names. Santi adds that with 15 investable coins, any liquid fund going on a show repeats the same five names.

7:08 Crypto venture does one deal a year
Yan says only one of their newest venture fund's five investments is crypto, and over the past year they did just one crypto venture deal. The reason is that crypto venture's value capture and defensibility are now clearer, so you can quickly screen out a large number of projects, but the thesis that ‘crypto gets broadly adopted across multiple verticals’ has been pushed to the sidelines, and AI is a major factor in drawing away talent, attention and capital. His one crypto investment is Tori Finance, a tokenized Turkish lira carry trade, USD-hedged, about 10.5% organic yield, no incentives.

18:18 The six tokens share one thing: revenue that doesn't come from crypto
Yan's six public tokens are Hyperliquid, Zcash, Lighter, Venice, Grass, Aerodrome. He says he prefers projects with a ‘revenue story’ that don't depend heavily on crypto activity, because that makes them more resistant to drawdowns and gives a stronger TAM story. He goes deep on Grass: projected $70 million revenue, $40 million operating profit, doing residential IP network data scraping, customers are frontier labs, token market cap $330 million, unlocks finish in October, about 30% of supply is with the foundation, no equity only a foundation, and if valued as a pure equity non-crypto business, the private market could probably raise $1 to 2 billion.

23:22 Crypto's return requirements have already changed
Yan says he no longer anchors on annualized return rates, but instead sets individual price targets, stop losses and invalidation conditions, and keeps a reserve of money to handle a ‘total collapse’ scenario. He admits he just likes volatility. Santi says he now doesn't do crypto venture that can't at least 10x, that Ethereum at $300 billion has no clean 10x, and that the downside asymmetry is far greater than the upside. Yan responds that comfort comes from holding ‘productive assets’ rather than ‘reflexive assets’, and the key to a productive asset is the durability of its earnings and how much it depends on reflexive assets.

30:30 The gaming vertical has been given up
Yan says gaming as a whole is a hard vertical to invest in, because games as a business have too short a lifecycle, and once you run the NPV the long-term value story is hard to sustain. They tried Gunzilla, a big bet, and the result was bad, which he attributes to management and spending issues rather than game quality — the game itself is AAA level, on par with Call of Duty, PUBG, Fortnite. He says this may be their last attempt at AAA level, and after that gaming as a broad category will be hard, with only small-scale games doing well. They now think the only truly investable vertical left is basically ‘financialized applications’.

37:39 Aerodrome is a classic catch-up trade
Yan says Aerodrome originally planned to migrate to mainnet in mid-July and support multichain, but it was delayed, and the price suffered as a result; the launch is now set for the second half of September, migration to ETH and ARC has been announced, and whether it migrates to Robin Hood is unconfirmed. He sees this as a huge opportunity for TVL, volume and fees, and many people treat it as a catch-up trade. The prior problem was the relationship between emissions and revenue — emissions go to LPs, revenue goes to stakers, and it was criticized as using emissions to offset revenue. Now they want to make emissions dynamic, tied one-to-one to trading volume, so price up means emissions down; at the same time they're adding multiple revenue lines, estimated to contribute an extra 40% of revenue with no emissions offset. Currently OI relative to market cap is not a large position.

44:50 The investment committee now weighs founders most
Yan says if he could pick only one change, it's the weight given to founder due diligence. In early crypto it was obvious what needed to exist, so investing was more about the idea and defensibility, with lower founder weight. But once you move into other professional verticals, you can't really diligence the idea and moat, and the only repeatable, scalable thing is the founder side. They now ask ‘what is your earliest memory, then walk us through your life’. He also mentions the ‘chip on the shoulder’ from childhood trauma and the desperate desire to win as factors that are actually valuable, and gives Athena's Guy as an example, saying he will do whatever it takes to win.
