item.description: Usable AI data center capacity is about 15 GW at the end of 2026 and races to 45-55 GW by the end of 2027, a 30-40 GW increment. At $50 billion of revenue per gigawatt, the two giants would have to produce $750 billion to $1.5 trillion, and that number does not hold up.
item.content:encoded:
Usable AI data center capacity is about 15 GW at the end of 2026 and races to 45-55 GW by the end of 2027, a 30-40 GW increment. At $50 billion of revenue per gigawatt, the two giants would have to produce $750 billion to $1.5 trillion, and that number does not hold up.

The first half is on-the-ground reporting from Hot Chips and Semicon Taiwan; the second half is the real value of this episode: a bottom-up arithmetic of compute supply and demand, plus the judgment that anti-AI sentiment could swing elections.

3:05 The window for new AI chips has reopened
The author wrote last year that ‘the window for new AI chips has closed, except for Google's TPU’, and here he explicitly takes it back and says he was wrong. The trigger was OpenAI unveiling its in-house chip Jalapeno at Hot Chips, a short talk with high information density. Outside the hall a ring of new AI chip startups was gathered: Etched, MatX, Posetron, Fractile. Etched gave no talk but built presence by handing out hats and having its founder ask questions all over the Q&A. The author reminds us these are hardware companies: they do not just design chips, they have to build their own racks and systems and get into the lab and do the work, and recruiting top talent and execution are hard barriers. His survival test borrows Nathan Bedford Forrest's controversial line: get there first, and with the most men.

6:08 Semicon Taiwan is really TSMC's request for proposals
First-timers are surprised: neither TSMC nor ASML has a booth. But TSMC dominates the whole show — its teams walk the hall visiting new suppliers and scouting new technology, and many information sessions have TSMC executives on stage laying the company's problems out in public. The author's conclusion is that Semicon Taiwan is essentially an RFP that TSMC issues to the entire semiconductor industry. The technical throughline is clear: future manufacturing has to go big. AI chips are hitting existing limits, most typically the reticle limit, which determines how large an area a lithography machine can print. TSMC had a slide showing the ‘battleship-class’ chip it plans to build spanning 14 reticles, and the industry responded quickly, as usual.

7:10 Glass panel packaging has moved from PPT to the show floor
Two years ago the author made a video on panel level packaging, which was the theme of Semicon Taiwan 2024, and at the time it was all talks and slideshows. Now AI systems are so large that the industry wants to use square, glass panel interposers to carry chiplets and memory, replacing silicon interposers. The author's attitude is reserved: can TSMC make them without warping or cracking? ‘I'll believe it when I see the chip.’ But the ecosystem is already moving, and equipment such as handling robots adapted to square panels appeared in the hall. He judges this wave of ‘chipmaxing’ will be one of the most far-reaching technology transitions in semiconductor history, roughly on the scale of the move to 300 mm wafers.

8:12 The spot market has vanished, and VCs now help portfolio companies find GPUs
When the author was last in the Bay Area in September 2025 the picture was completely different. Since then long-running agentic AI has swept Silicon Valley, triggered in part by stronger models such as Anthropic's Opus 4.5 around November 2025 and by Open Claw. In February 2026 prices began to rise, everyone scrambled to lock up compute, and Anthropic led the way signing big deals with SpaceX, Google and others. The author was told that by the time of this trip the spot market had completely disappeared. For Neoclouds (a term coined by semi-analyst Dan Nishbal in April 2024 for pure cloud vendors that resell AI training and inference compute, such as Coreweave and Nebius) this is a huge boon, and they are confident the shortage will last at least another one to two years. The author met several people who did not know each other and each wanted to start a Neocloud. For AI startups this is a business risk: imagine telling investors the product has to wait until mid-2027 because there is not enough compute. The new way VCs help portfolio companies is to go find compute, and he heard of people scraping together a thousand GPUs here and there, even hunting in unexpected places like Eastern Europe.

9:12 Two giants are feasting while compute is still being wasted
By contrast, Anthropic and OpenAI are feasting internally. Dylan recently said on Dashpod that these two AI giants each have about 5 GW of compute. The author infers from this that a considerable share of all that compute may be wasted, and anecdotes he heard confirm this ‘rolling in it’ is not being used as efficiently as possible. He also asked every AI insider he talked to one question: will Google return to the frontier? The general consensus is no, though the explanations are vague. Several people pointed out that Google's decision to sell a large amount of compute to Anthropic is itself equivalent to not believing in itself. This is a big reversal from the period when Gemini 3 made some people think OpenAI was finished. What the author heard is that Google suffered severe talent drain, plus a culture unfriendly to frontier AI.

11:15 Neolabs are venture capital that treats compute as money
What fascinates the author most is the Neolab: a research startup with basically no revenue that raises money to explore an interesting AI idea, whose founders are often elite researchers and whose business plan is close to nothing beyond ‘discover a completely new architecture’. The most famous and earliest, Safe Superintelligence, raised a billion dollars and has yet to release a product or model. The label is fuzzy, covering recursive intelligence, Humans, Core Automation, Flapping Airplanes and others; among those with products are Japan's Sakana AI, Thinking Machines, Reflection AI, plus a batch in verticals such as materials science, world models and robotics. The first reaction is that these assets are dumb: no revenue, no plan to monetize soon. But the author can understand it: historically breakthrough science came from research universities, government labs or Bell Labs, and now university funding is being cut and talent is being sucked into industry. AI is probably the first major technology in the past 50 years to emerge without government involvement, and in this era research is closed and secretive. So let Nvidia, with compute and cash in hand, plus a pile of VCs, fund these asymmetric bets. OpenAI and Anthropic are locked into the transformer paradigm and are unlikely to spend money researching these directions. The probability of failure is high, but most of the money is given in the form of compute anyway; if someone really strikes gold and forces the giants to pivot (say, to a more data-efficient architecture), the giants will most likely buy the discoverer at an eye-watering price, and one such deal pays for everything. The author thinks this is a better use of cash than continuing buybacks, and names Apple.

14:15 Tokens are burning, and nobody has measured ROI
Customers really are burning tokens, but are they getting ROI? The author asked across the ecosystem and the answer remains vague: don't know, nobody has measured it, it is all anecdote. He believes lower barriers to coding will hit knowledge work — financial firms used to hire a pile of reporting analysts to keep management on top of positions, and now two smart young analysts plus Claude writing a dashboard is enough, which he has seen with his own eyes. But for other AI capabilities, such as making spreadsheets and making presentations, the things marketing usually pushes, he has seen no obvious impact. Maybe it just needs more time, maybe it is a problem of intelligence itself. OpenAI recently published a blog on how agents accelerate internal research, but still frames AI's capability as intern level: it can execute routine tasks, and is far from a real AI researcher. What he heard is that AI still lacks human research taste, though some believe sufficient scale can achieve it. And one thing holds true for everyone in San Francisco: people are working harder than before. If the models are really that capable, why does everyone say they have more work than ever? Maybe AI does not kill our work for us, but gives us more work.

15:17 Compute flips from shortage to glut in 2027
Everyone is saying shortage, shortage, two more years of shortage, and the author instead suspects things will not go as expected. His arithmetic is not complicated: usable AI data center capacity at the end of 2026 is estimated at about 15 GW, with OpenAI and Anthropic each taking about 5 GW; the supply chain will respond, and by the end of 2027 that number is estimated to reach 45-55 GW, an increment of 30-40 GW, of which the two giants take about 30 GW. Assume half goes to training, leaving 15 GW combined for inference. Inference is currently modeled at about $50 billion of revenue per gigawatt (a figure from Dylan Patel on Dashpod), and it can also be back-solved from Anthropic's deal to buy 300 MW from SpaceX for $1.25 billion a month; Dylan thinks smarter models can eventually push it to $100 billion per gigawatt. On that basis the two should produce $750 billion to $1.5 trillion of revenue in 2027. The author says that number is absurd: most people agree the two will do $150-200 billion this year, and next year he can barely imagine $400-500 billion, but $750 billion to $1.5 trillion is ‘two Walmarts’ or ‘two Toyotas’, a stretch in credibility, and he does not think it can be reached. He bets revenue per gigawatt comes in far below $100 billion or even $50 billion, possibly only a small fraction of it. From the infrastructure side it looks the same: assume 40 GW lands in 2027, current rent is about $20 million per megawatt, implying a 3-year payback, so those 40 GW require $800 billion paid to infrastructure providers, in 2027 alone. He does not think that can be collected either, which means rents have to fall and someone somewhere has to take a loss. Conclusion: in 2027 the supply chain will deliver a lot of compute, most of it in the second half, and he bets this pushes the market from shortage to glut. He stresses he is not saying the AI bubble will pop, only that we will soon be flooded with compute — 2026 is agentic demand matched against 2025 supply, supply will catch up and probably overshoot; but after that maybe the next stage of growth ignites and demand balloons again, for example persistent AI.

item.title: Stalin Was Just the Bookkeeper of the Revolution, and Then He Became General Secretary
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-13-empirehist-斯大林在革命里只是个管账的-后来却成了总书记/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-13-empirehist-斯大林在革命里只是个管账的-后来却成了总书记/
item.description: In 1917, while Lenin and Trotsky were on the streets calling for insurrection, Stalin was doing the organizing and fundraising nobody else wanted. He became General Secretary later not by oratory, but by sitting at the table.
item.content:encoded:
In 1917, while Lenin and Trotsky were on the streets calling for insurrection, Stalin was doing the organizing and fundraising nobody else wanted. He became General Secretary later not by oratory, but by sitting at the table.

This episode covers the groundwork before Stalin took power: Georgian origins, seminary, a failed bank robbery. Medium information density, but it makes clear why he was able to rise.

5:28 Even his birthday was something he changed himself
The parish register, the seminary certificate, the tsarist police file and his own handwritten questionnaire from the 1920s all say 18 December 1878. But the birthday he announced after taking power was 21 December 1879 — off by one year and three days. Bob Service offers one judgment in his biography: forgery was too easy for him. Service also has an unprovable but persuasive speculation — that changing his birthday helped him dodge conscription when he was young. The thing itself is the theme of the whole episode: this man's attitude toward facts was instrumental.

6:35 How anomalous it was for a Georgian to become master of Moscow
His real name was Joseph Jugashvili, and he was born in Georgia. Georgia is in the Caucasus, next to Armenia, just north of Iran and Turkey, far from Russia; it has its own language, its own alphabet, and its religion is Georgian Orthodoxy, not the same thing as Russian Orthodoxy. The analogy the episode gives is this: a man from a Georgian Orthodox background climbing to the top of power in Moscow is like a mid-20th-century person from an Irish Catholic background, from some remote place like Limerick, becoming master of London. For Georgians at the time, being ruled from Moscow meant being colonized.

8:43 His father refused to change trades, then started hitting people
His father Bessarion (nicknamed Besso) was a cobbler with his own workshop in Gori, and by most accounts a good craftsman. But he refused to keep up with the times: he kept making Georgian-style soft leather high boots while the market had already shifted to European shoes. He did not adapt; he became bitter, drank heavily, and the violence fell mainly on his wife Ekaterina (Kiki) and little Joseph, who was nicknamed "Crazy Besso." Stalin later told his daughter Svetlana a scene: his father was drunk and beating his mother, he grabbed a knife and threw it at his father, missed, his father charged, and he ran to a neighbor's house and hid for several days until his father's rage passed.

11:52 Smallpox, a carriage, and a left arm that was too short
Around age six he caught smallpox, severe enough that his mother thought he would die — two older brothers had already died in infancy, and the family was too poor to afford a doctor, so they could only call a local folk healer. He survived, but his face was permanently scarred, and every official photograph was retouched. Later a runaway carriage hit him and broke his arm, and the left arm never healed properly, staying visibly shorter and stiffer for the rest of his life. The episode puts it this way: smallpox did not take him, his father's violence did not take him, and the carriage did not take him either. His mother was extremely devoted to him and had ambitious plans for him.

16:07 He wrote poetry, and he was good at it
Two things happened at once in his late teens: he began writing quite good poetry, and he entered the seminary. The episode reads one poem: "The pink buds have already blossomed, toward the pale violet; brushed by the breeze, the lily of the valley bends over the grass. Flowers, my Georgia. May peace come to my native land, and may you, friends, make our homeland famous through study." Anita says that in the original Georgian it is quite beautiful. It shows two things: he was a proud Georgian, not a Russian; and in the tsarist context, writing about a "homeland" like this was already close to sedition.

19:09 The seminary was the tsar's Russification machine
In 1894 he won a place at the Tiflis Theological Seminary. The sign over the school said Georgian Orthodox, but in practice it was under the control of the Russian Orthodox Church, one of the tsar's institutions for "Russifying" the borderlands. Students were kept under close surveillance, with constant reports written: are these people good tsarist subjects, are they talking sedition. And right under that surveillance, he was reading banned books, including What Is to Be Done? and other big questions about freedom and the individual. Anita's comment in the episode is: the surveillance here was not done well enough.

21:11 He gave himself the name of a bandit
On the banned list was a Georgian novel, The Patricide by Alexander Kazbegi, whose protagonist is a mountain outlaw named Koba. He took that name as his own alias, and his classmates at the seminary called him by it. The episode calls this a kind of "name determinism": he first took the name of a bandit hero, and then he really did become a bandit. The turning point from seminary student to bandit began when he saw with his own eyes two mountain bandits publicly hanged in the center of Gori for shooting a policeman over a stray cow — he was forbidden to go watch, but he went.

24:16 They robbed 250,000 rubles and could not spend a single one
In 1907 he and a group of friends ambushed a bank carriage in Yerevan Square in Tiflis, almost within sight of the seminary: some stood up high and threw bombs down, others fired in the street, and the man organizing, funding and directing it from behind the scenes was Stalin, under the alias Koba. They got away with 250,000 rubles packed in linen bags. But the bank had already published the serial numbers of its largest-denomination notes, so not one ruble of that money could be spent. It was the first time he left a police photograph on file, but he did not go to prison for it and essentially walked away untouched.

item.title: Outbound Reply Rates Near Zero? Don't Blame the Copy First — Check Who You're Sending To
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-13-ycsp-外联回复率接近零-先别怪文案-先查你在发给谁/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-13-ycsp-外联回复率接近零-先别怪文案-先查你在发给谁/
item.description: Outbound is like finding a needle in a haystack: get the person wrong and even perfect copy won't land. The YC partner's debugging order is — check the recipient first, then the company, then the subject line, and only then the copy.
item.content:encoded:
Outbound is like finding a needle in a haystack: get the person wrong and even perfect copy won't land. The YC partner's debugging order is — check the recipient first, then the company, then the subject line, and only then the copy.

Eight tactics in 12 minutes — dense, but every one is an action you can take immediately. For founders stuck at single-digit outbound reply rates who don't know what to change.

0:00 Send a hundred by hand before you talk about automation
The most common founder mistake is opening a tool, blasting a thousand emails, and getting zero replies. The real loss isn't the zero replies themselves — it's that you learned nothing from them. The problem could be the copy, the company targeting, the lead filtering, deliverability, or the subject line, and you can't tell which. So the advice is to do at least a hundred outbound attempts manually before automating, and genuinely manually: spend time researching one specific person, what her problem is, what would grab her attention, read her LinkedIn and her company page. That homework is where high-converting outbound ideas come from.

1:04 Picking the right person matters far more than polishing copy
Founders often spend hours tweaking email wording while barely thinking about who they're sending to. Outbound is like finding a needle in a haystack: you have to find the person who has exactly the pain point you solve, or the most carefully polished copy won't land. One winter batch company selling infrastructure products should have been selling to senior engineering leaders, but its actual list was full of dev rel managers, GTM managers, and even customer success managers — hundreds of emails sent, naturally no replies. Those wrong titles were never going to buy, regardless of how well the email was written.

2:06 Work backward from closed customers to the target title
How do you find the right title? Look at your existing customers first, then at the sales process: who pushed the last deal to close, who signed the contract, who paid the money — list all their titles and go find people with similar profiles. You can also look at who has replied to your outbound. If you're still at the very earliest stage, with neither customers nor replies, ask yourself: who in the organization benefits most from buying your software. Example: selling employee device security monitoring software, the chief security officer could get fired in a data breach, so he'll be interested; an engineering manager would probably rather not be monitored, so he's not a good target.

3:09 List-building tools will hand you the wrong companies
Another common mistake is searching in Sales Navigator and getting back a pile of results that look like a match but are the wrong type of company — search tech companies, for instance, and you often get a bunch of IT implementation consultancies. So use list-building tools very carefully, and verify company by company whether they're really your customer. As you do more outbound, you start noticing the clues that a company needs your product — intent signals. Job postings are a great observation point, since they reveal a company's priorities; company growth is another common signal: selling compensation planning software, companies under 100 people probably haven't introduced job levels yet, and companies over 500 have probably already set compensation bands, so crossing the 100-person mark is a great signal. Every product has signals like this; your job is to find your own.

4:09 Shake your first customers out of your personal network
For closing your first few customers, starting from your personal network is much easier and converts at a much higher rate. Really shake the tree — make sure you've covered everyone you know: your personal network first, then ask friends, family, investors, college roommates, people you met at a coffee shop for intros — literally anyone you can think of.

5:10 Executives don't care about your product features
The single most important thing in the email is clearly stating how you can help the other person. Figure out the three things keeping your buyer up at night: what gets him fired, what gets him promoted, and why he should believe you can help. When buyers read the email and think ‘this is exactly my problem’, they're likely willing to take the call, even if they don't yet fully understand or trust your solution. The fact is executives don't care about your product features, don't care that your upload speed is blazing fast, and don't care that your database is written in rust — what they worry about is hitting their quarterly targets. Keep the product description to one sentence at most; save the details for the first call.

6:14 A good email reads like a peer wrote it, not like a pitch
The email from the founder of Aptin, a YC company in the S24 batch, is held up as an example: the tone is very casual, it sounds like a peer, no jargon, no trying to look impressive, like something a friend sent. He builds credibility with the first line — ‘I used to be a software engineer at Tesla. We got crazy good at using SMS to convert the people who visited our website into car buyers.’ The ending has a very clear call to action: would you be open to running an experiment to see if AI can reactivate leads and lift conversion. The email also mentions that he noticed the phone number collected in the signup flow on their website, which makes it feel personalized; and it barely explains how the product works at all — it only talks about how he can help the other person solve a problem.

8:20 On LinkedIn, mutual connections are the number one predictor
If email is about the subject line, LinkedIn is about your profile — it determines whether people accept your connection request and whether they reply. Key points: a photo boosts trust; turn the top banner into an ad for your company, stating clearly and concisely what the company does, avoiding jargon; rewrite your one-line headline and about section into a short company description; move up what buyers care about (relevant and impressive experience, say) and cut the irrelevant — if the about section is a pile of hobbies and interests, it's harder for buyers to see how you can help them. Another place worth investing in is mutual connections: the number of shared contacts is the single biggest predictor of whether someone accepts a connection request, so build up relevant mutual connections with your target audience — it takes time, and you should turn it into a habit of using your full connection quota every day.

item.title: World Models Are Not Video Generation: Atlas Makes 3D Control an Input
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-13-a16z-世界模型不是视频生成-atlas-把-3d-控制做成了输入/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-13-a16z-世界模型不是视频生成-atlas-把-3d-控制做成了输入/
item.description: Language models process tokens; world models process physical space. Atlas's key move isn't generating longer video — it's putting cameras and reference images into 3D coordinates as inputs, turning generation from a slot machine into directing.
item.content:encoded:
Language models process tokens; world models process physical space. Atlas's key move isn't generating longer video — it's putting cameras and reference images into 3D coordinates as inputs, turning generation from a slot machine into directing.

23 minutes, medium information density, but Justin draws the line between world models and video generation very clearly. Worth hearing for anyone working in 3D, robotics, or VFX.

1:05 Atlas is a model release, not a product release
Justin clarifies right at the top: Atlas is not a product, it's World Labs' foundation model; products come later. It does three things — generate worlds that don't exist, reconstruct from real spaces, and run simulation inside reconstructed spaces. Generation can start from text or an image, and then you can directly fly a camera through that world; reconstruction can take just one photo, or a hundred or more, and the more photos the more accurate the reconstruction; simulation is aimed at VFX and robotics. That ordering itself says World Labs doesn't intend to build a consumer app first — it wants to stand up a horizontal foundation model first, then let products grow on top of it.

4:09 Reference images are pinned into 3D space, not fed to the model
Video models tend to drift and hallucinate their own direction after around ten seconds of generation. Justin says Atlas's answer is spatial context: the reference images you give it aren't ordinary images, they're grounded in 3D space, and you can specify ‘put this one here, that one there’. When generating video you're also not just giving a text prompt — you're directly operating the camera, telling it to fly this way and that way, achieving precise pixel-level control. So even at a minute of generation, it's not pulling a slot machine — you are generating, directing, and controlling what the model outputs.

7:10 Atlas moves the 2D/3D fork earlier
Compared with Marble, World Labs' first product, Atlas is a completely rebuilt model stack. Marble put Gaussian splats at the center: video, 3D scenes, and meshes all had to pass through a Gaussian representation before being rendered back to images or video. Atlas breaks that dependency: the architecture is more unified and easier to scale, and the 2D/3D fork happens earlier. Generating 2D or video output is no longer bottlenecked on a Gaussian scene — the model produces 2D pixels directly; only in applications where you actually need 3D does it get lifted to 3D.

8:10 Gaussian isn't obsolete, it's just no longer mandatory
Justin doesn't think Gaussian has been outgrown — it's a tool, and you use it in the right place. VFX's final product is a 2D image or video, and may not need explicit 3D at all. But in real-time applications and on embedded devices, explicit 3D representations like Gaussian and mesh still have a place: in the future you might stream pixels in real time from a server farm, but we're not there yet, and it would be very expensive, so for client-side rendering, mobile, and VR devices, Gaussian or mesh is still useful. Its other role is plugging into existing workflows — people in games, VFX, design, and architecture already have pipelines built on 3D representations, and rather than making them switch to fully AI-native all at once, it's better to let AI enter their workflows.

11:13 Simulation fills the last stretch of robot training
On the value of real to sim for robots, Justin says the first thing is evaluation: a robot ultimately has to work in a specific factory, on a specific machine, in a specific environment, and you have to make sure it works in exactly that environment. So simulation is useful in the last stretch of training and evaluation — build a simulation as close as possible to the final use case, then either fine-tune a pretrained robot foundation model directly in that simulation, or run evaluations to confirm it works. That gives you a path different from ‘collect lots of demonstrations or teleoperate by hand’. He also describes a more aggressive version: take a few photos or some casual video on your phone, reconstruct the space with Atlas, describe the task in natural language, and let an agent build the simulation and do RL fine-tuning, giving you a robot adapted to that space within minutes.

14:16 OpenAI dropping world models may be an innovator's dilemma
The host asks why OpenAI turned that Sora-era direction — ‘video generation models are world simulators’ — into a consumer product, and now isn't doing world models. Justin says he won't comment on OpenAI's internal strategy, but offers one explanation: there may be an innovator's dilemma — you're holding something as strong as the LLM and you're leading in that direction, so investing in the next thing isn't necessarily worth it. World Labs' judgment is that there's another class of model here, with a lot of opportunity, and they want to be the ones who seize it.

18:21 Bullet time from three iPhones came out far better than expected
Asked about hard physics, Justin says he hasn't tried a black hole and guesses it wouldn't be too impressive. What really surprised him was bullet time: three iPhones on tripods shooting in sync, then using Atlas to freeze the frame and reframe a fly-around. He cites the official example — a strawberry dropping into oat milk, time frozen at the instant the milk splashes up, flying a full circle around it, and the effect is completely insane. This capability needs only three input viewpoints. That shows Atlas's value isn't only in ‘generating new worlds’ — it's also in turning a small amount of real footage into shots that traditionally required a large camera array.

19:21 3D is underrated on the input side
Justin says 3D has value in two places. On the output side, everyone has already talked about it — sometimes you just need explicit 3D assets to drop into a workflow or game engine. But 3D's value on the input side is underrated: even if the final output is a 2D VFX shot, giving the model a 3D control surface helps the director decide what kind of scene the model should output. You don't want to write ‘push in, pull out, move left’ in text — you want to grab the camera directly and have it zoom exactly the way you want, which text simply can't describe. So Atlas makes camera control a native input type: one of the modalities is the camera.

item.title: Making a furin site isn't hard at all — admitting it isn't rare is
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-13-twiv-造一个-furin-位点根本不难-难的是承认它不罕见/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-13-twiv-造一个-furin-位点根本不难-难的是承认它不罕见/
item.description: Deep sequencing shows that a few genomes in every thousand of a coronavirus population carry insertions, and a furin site has been hit independently at the same position at least three times — the probabilistic argument for a lab origin doesn't hold up.
item.content:encoded:
Deep sequencing shows that a few genomes in every thousand of a coronavirus population carry insertions, and a furin site has been hit independently at the same position at least three times — the probabilistic argument for a lab origin doesn't hold up.

The first half is the quantitative methodology of viral recombination and insertion; the second half is the real target of this episode: dismantling the lab-origin argument with numbers. Listeners who want the argument can jump straight to 52 minutes.

6:07 They changed the GFP sequence and the recombination rate went up
The team first built an OC43 reverse-genetics system and made a pair of viruses: each carries a frameshifted GFP, so infection with either alone yields only fragments, but coinfection lets recombination stitch green fluorescent protein back together. They expected that changing the nucleotide sequence of one of the GFPs would lower the recombination rate; instead it rose. Paul says there is only a hypothesis for this, no data — one possibility is that once double-stranded RNA forms, the strand-transfer events of recombination become more likely because the duplex "breathes." This counterintuitive result later became the reagent starting point for the whole paper.

11:12 Knock GFP out of frame and let insertions reveal themselves
Measuring insertions and deletions is far harder than measuring point mutations, because they were thought to be rare and sequencing depth was insufficient. Their approach was to put the GFP gene into the viral genome and deliberately knock it out of frame, preceded by a start-codon peptide that is in a different frame from GFP, so the virus does not glow green; it turns green only when that site acquires an insertion or deletion of a particular length that pulls GFP back into frame. This lets them count event frequencies and also pick out green viruses, read back their sequences, and infer the mechanism. This is where figure 1 of the paper comes from.

13:15 Knocking out NSP15 made insertions go down, not up
The original hypothesis came from prior work suggesting that NSP15, a nuclease, affects deletion rates — think nuclease and you naturally think deletions, not insertions. But the experiment went the opposite way: viruses with NSP15 showed a greatly increased rate of acquiring insertions that pull GFP back into frame. Paul says the deletion rate numbers were not good enough this time to quantify, but the insertion result was black and white, and they were very surprised at the time — it was this accidental result that opened up the entire line of research.

22:26 Every base sequenced a million times before you talk about frequency
They moved from picking green viruses to brute-force sequencing: concentrate about 10 milliliters of virus down to 1 milliliter, load a portion onto a sequencing chip, and produce hundreds of millions of reads, so that every nucleotide in the genome is read at least a million times, with roughly 30 human genomes' or 3 million viral genomes' worth of data per virus stock. Paul stresses that depth has to match the number of virions in the sample — sequencing hundreds of millions of times when there are only a thousand virions in the tube is meaningless; they calibrated to sequence roughly a few percent of the viruses in the sample.

27:32 Eleven nucleotides is the threshold for judging origin
Short insertions (three to six nucleotides) can arise randomly in a viral genome, so their origin cannot be determined, and they were excluded from the analysis. They calculated that if an 11-nucleotide stretch matches the viral genome perfectly, the probability of that being pure chance is below 5%, so they restricted the analysis to insertions of 11 nucleotides or more. The result: more than 90% matched the viral genome perfectly or nearly perfectly, and in OC43 wild-type virus had 87 times more insertions than the NSP15 mutant, most of them derived from the positive strand.

36:41 Insertions aren't rare events — they're a few per thousand
Vincent says that for years he was told insertions are rare, but the data suggest this has been happening all along. Paul responds that "rare" is a relative term: one in a million is rare, but if you have ten million of them, it is common. The insertion frequency they report is a few genomes per thousand — roughly five to ten genomes carrying an insertion per thousand virions. That frequency is lower than the point-mutation rate, but not by much. The reason it seemed rare in the past is that the vast majority of insertions are deleterious or even lethal to the virus and get purged at low multiplicity of infection, so you cannot isolate them.

55:05 Making a furin site isn't hard at all
Mechanistically, a furin cleavage site needs at minimum two arginines, RXXR, and can even be cleaved with a single arginine plus other amino acids in support. Six of the 64 codons encode arginine, so multiplying the two fractions, about 1% of random 12-base sequences encode an RXR motif. A coronavirus genome has roughly 30,000 different positions where an insertion mutation can occur. So this is not some enormous engineering challenge.

57:08 Lightning strikes the same spot at least three times
Put the frequency of insertions, the number of insertable sites, and the size of the viral population together, and the probability of a furin cleavage site appearing at one particular position in a coronavirus genome is not astonishing — and it roughly matches what deep sequencing actually measures. In their deep-sequencing data, which does not cover the whole population, they have already found new furin cleavage sites at least three independent times at the exact position of the existing SARS-CoV-2 furin site. Paul says the numbers in the paper are an underestimate: they only focused on the spike region for PCR, and they required insertions to match the viral genome perfectly to rule out PCR artifacts, which very likely also excluded some real natural sites.

item.content:encoded:
Rome turned sea battles into land battles with a boarding bridge called the corvus, cancelling Carthage's advantage in seamanship; but Carthage brought in a Spartan to rebuild its army and captured a Roman consul in return.

This episode tells the First Punic War as a war story with mechanisms: the crow boarding bridge, the sacred chickens, mercenaries, war elephants — all backed by concrete images and numbers, at high information density.

2:03 This was not a war between two equal powers
The host opens by calling this a clash of ‘the two great powers of the western Mediterranean,’ and Eve MacDonald corrects him on the spot: at the war's outbreak Carthage was not necessarily a military power of that rank. Carthage had money, controlled the sea routes, and had centuries of alliance networks in western Sicily, but it had no strong standing army — it relied on allies and mercenaries. What actually made Carthage into a power capable of fighting Rome as an equal was this war itself. So the story Roman sources tell over and over, of ‘Roman adaptability,’ is only half the story; the other half is Carthaginian resilience and adaptability, without which there is no explaining why this war lasted more than twenty years.

15:29 Mercenaries at Messana dragged both powers into war
The trigger was not the ambition of Rome or Carthage but a band of Campanian mercenaries called the Mamertines. They had seized Messana, and after being defeated by Hiero II, king of Syracuse, they split in two: one faction asked Carthage for help, the other asked Rome. Carthage acted first from its base in the Lipari Islands, and Rome followed — and not with a small intervention, but a full invasion with two consular armies. Eve points out that the Roman sources' claim of an ‘accidental empire’ is highly suspect, because the Romans showed up at Messana at the scale of an invading force. Polybius treats the Romans' first crossing of the sea into Sicily as the starting point of Roman imperial expansion.

28:14 The corvus turned a sea battle into a land battle
Carthage was a naval power: its rowers were skilled, its ships built fast and well, and the Romans even built their own warships to Carthaginian standards. But the Romans added one thing: the corvus, meaning ‘crow,’ a boarding bridge that could hook an enemy ship. Once hooked, the Carthaginian ship could not move, and Roman marines simply crossed over and fought a land battle. At the Battle of Mylae the Carthaginians clearly did not expect this, and took heavy losses. Eve also cautions that the details of the corvus leave many unanswerable questions in the sources, but ancient historians all treat it as decisive. By the Battle of Cape Ecnomus the corvus was again credited as the chief factor, and Rome thereby opened the sea route for its invasion of Africa.

38:40 Carthage hired a Spartan to rebuild its army
After the Roman landing in Africa the advance rolled on, and it looked as though Carthage was finished. Carthage's response was to recruit a new army in the eastern Mediterranean and to bring in a Spartan commander, Xanthippus. He reorganised the Carthaginian army and reworked how the war elephants were used. Eve notes in particular that the Carthaginians had not used war elephants before; it was only after seeing the Indian elephants Pyrrhus brought that they realised they had a smaller African elephant of their own they could use. Xanthippus's reforms worked: the Roman army was destroyed and the consul Regulus was captured. This was Rome's first devastating defeat in the war, and it became a key event in later Roman memory defining the relationship between Rome and Carthage.

43:11 The captured consul went back to Rome to argue against peace
Carthage sent the captured consul Regulus back to Rome to negotiate peace. In the Senate Regulus said not to surrender, that Carthage was there for the taking. By agreement, if peace was not made, he had to return to Carthage and remain a prisoner. He went back, and died in captivity. Eve says the various horrific versions of how he died are not actually mentioned in the credible sources, so it is hard to judge how much is later embellishment; but what is certain is that he died in captivity in Carthage, peace was refused, and Rome fought on. This passage is a classic moment of Roman self-congratulatory rhetoric.

46:27 The sacred chickens would not eat, and Rome's fleet was finished
In 249 BC the Roman consul Tiberius Claudius Pulcher took his fleet to fight Carthage off Drepana. By Roman ritual, the sacred chickens on his ship had to eat for the battle to proceed; if they did not, it was a bad omen. The chickens would not eat, so he threw them into the sea, saying that if they would not eat, then let them drink. Roman sources present this as the most serious act of sacrilege, and the Roman fleet was then defeated at Drepana. Eve says that once Roman sources start stressing a commander's arrogance and contempt for tradition, it usually means something bad happened. After this defeat Rome did not send out a fleet again for eight years.

50:48 Hannibal's father tied Rome down with guerrilla war
After Drepana Rome vanished from the sea, and Carthage gained freedom of action on the western coast. In 247 BC Carthage sent a new commander, Hamilcar Barca — Hannibal's father. He brought a force Polybius calls the Mix-Hellenes, made up of soldiers of Greek, Libyan and Phoenician descent from North Africa, and waged guerrilla war against Rome, occupying the high ground above Drepana and Panormus with considerable success. Eve says this was the first time in the war that Carthage's army fought Rome this well. He also seized the temple complex at Eryx, sacred to the goddess the Carthaginians called Astarte, and both sides fought fiercely over this holy site.

57:20 The rams from this war still lie on the seabed
The Battle of the Aegates Islands in 241 BC was the last battle. The Roman fleet hid behind the islands and ambushed a Carthaginian fleet heavy with supplies meant for Hamilcar. Eve says that if you go up to Eryx today, on a clear day you can see the Aegates Islands perfectly, and Hamilcar very likely watched this disaster unfold from land. More remarkably, the site of this sea battle has been preserved underwater: over the past twenty years underwater archaeologists have found large bronze rams on the seabed near the island of Levanzo, some inscribed with the names of Roman consuls, some bearing Punic inscriptions and carvings, along with Monte Fortino helmets and amphorae.

item.title: A Bunsen Burner Doesn't Reduce Plate Contamination, and Vegetables Protect the Heart by Another Mechanism
