item.description: A Bunsen burner may actually increase settle-plate colonies in low-contamination environments; the cardiovascular benefit of vegetables may not run through the nitrate-nitrite-NO pathway but through gut bacteria turning nitrate and iron into DNIC that directly activates sGC.
item.content:encoded:
A Bunsen burner may actually increase settle-plate colonies in low-contamination environments; the cardiovascular benefit of vegetables may not run through the nitrate-nitrite-NO pathway but through gut bacteria turning nitrate and iron into DNIC that directly activates sGC.

The first half has a clean experimental design and a counterintuitive conclusion; the second half's DNIC paper has a complete mechanism but dense terminology, suited to those willing to chew through mechanism.

6:05 A Bunsen burner does not reduce plate contamination
The authors used paired settle plates: one placed next to a lit Bunsen burner, one next to an unlit burner, both exposed simultaneously to the same contaminating airflow. The lit burner overall did not lower average contamination, and the statistical comparison showed no significant improvement. This directly challenges the common claim that there is a general sterile halo around the blue flame. The authors do not say the burner never helps, but that the effect depends on environmental conditions — they deliberately contaminated the lab air with Gordonia rubripertincta and then compared different flame sizes and dry versus wet particles.

10:13 83 CFU per minute is the crossover point
Under dry-particle conditions with an average 18 mm flame, they observed an apparent crossover point: when the airborne microbial concentration was above 83 CFU/min, settle plates next to the burner tended to show less deposition; below that level, deposition tended to increase. This can explain decades of contradictory anecdotal experience: people in dry environments genuinely believe the burner helps, while people in modern air-conditioned labs with low airborne contamination genuinely find the burner useless or even worse. Relative humidity in a typical modern air-conditioned lab is usually between 40% and 60%.

13:43 Airflow is not one-dimensional — don't light a burner in a laminar flow hood
The traditional view is that convection pulls contaminants upward, but the authors point out that the same airflow may first drag contaminated air laterally across the work surface before it rises. Any upward airflow must be replenished from somewhere, so the most important thing during aseptic work is to limit wind or airflow. This leads to the most practical point in the episode: there is no reason to light a Bunsen burner in a laminar flow hood, and the flame itself disrupts laminar flow. The authors did not directly visualize airflow; they measured a biologically relevant outcome — contamination — rather than fluid dynamics directly, and the authors themselves list this as a limitation.

17:49 Flaming tube mouths and lighting burners are both ritual
The authors compare this historically to the old practice of flaming culture tube mouths. Michael's graduate advisor at the time said stop doing it, there is no evidence it helps, and produced the 1972 paper proving it. The judgment in the episode is that changing behavior is hard, especially when a ritual gives a sense of control — lighting a burner feels proactive, flaming a tube mouth feels like protecting the culture, but there is no evidence it actually does anything. The authors do not argue for abandoning the Bunsen burner; they argue for measuring: use simple settle plates to measure your own lab's environment and let evidence guide practice.

28:14 Vegetables may protect the heart via the DNIC pathway
This Cell paper proposes reframing the entire nitric oxide synthase pathway: not a local paracrine model (eNOS makes NO that acts on adjacent smooth muscle), but an endocrine-like circuit — nitric oxide synthase makes nitrate, nitrate enters the gut, microbes turn it into dinitrosyl iron compounds (DNIC), which then act on targets such as the heart. If it holds up, the cardiovascular benefits of dietary nitrate (leafy greens, beets) may be mediated mainly by microbially generated DNIC, rather than the nitrate-nitrite-NO pathway we currently assume. The author is Andrei Kleshioff at the Karolinska Institute.

31:32 No DNIC can be found in germ-free mice
They used electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) to directly detect DNIC in tissues. Signals were visible in the liver and kidney of healthy mice, but when the same detection was done in germ-free mice, no DNIC could be found in the tissue — the first hint that microbes are making it. After feeding inorganic nitrate, liver DNIC levels rose in conventional mice but not in germ-free mice; if ferric citrate was added to the nitrate drinking water, the liver DNIC signal rose even higher, while ferric citrate alone had no effect. The same in vitro: mouse and human feces plus nitrate plus iron can produce DNIC, while germ-free mouse feces cannot.

39:55 DNIC directly activates sGC, not via free NO
They used isolated mouse aortic rings, pre-contracted with phenylephrine, then added DNIC. To distinguish free NO from direct sGC activation, they used two pharmacological tools: one that scavenges free NO, and one that directly blocks sGC. The sGC blocker completely abolished DNIC-induced relaxation, while the free-NO scavenger only partially attenuated it. The conclusion is that DNIC activates sGC, but not through free NO — the FeNO2 entity itself appears to directly activate sGC. The same holds for bacterially generated DNIC: only wild-type E. coli supernatant (anaerobic, with nitrate and iron) relaxed aortic rings, while a mutant lacking nitrate reductase did not.

47:16 DNIC suppresses leucine uptake and holds down mTORC1
On the metabolic side, they measured the phosphorylation state of key proteins in the liver mTORC1 pathway. In disease-model mice, mTORC1 was overactivated, downstream S6K1 phosphorylation was elevated, and transcription factors driving lipid synthesis were also elevated. Both DNIC treatment and nitrate-plus-iron supplementation brought these markers back to control levels. Mechanistically, they used glioblastoma cells to measure radiolabeled leucine uptake and found that DNIC inhibited leucine uptake in a concentration-dependent manner, suggesting it inhibits the leucine transporter — leucine is the key signal telling mTORC1 that nutrients are available, so blocking uptake blocks mTORC1 activation.

item.title: The Risk in Private Credit Is Hidden in Insurers' Ratings
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-excessreturns-私募信贷的风险藏在保险公司的评级里/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-excessreturns-私募信贷的风险藏在保险公司的评级里/
item.description: Private credit has poured into insurance companies, much of it in affiliated investments, rated by private agencies that are systematically too generous; on correct ratings, insurers would have to hold an extra $400-500 billion of capital a year.
item.content:encoded:
Private credit has poured into insurance companies, much of it in affiliated investments, rated by private agencies that are systematically too generous; on correct ratings, insurers would have to hold an extra $400-500 billion of capital a year.

The first half is industry anecdote; the real value is in the middle and back sections — the specific mechanics and numbers on private credit ratings, private equity in 401ks, and Social Security reform.

5:08 A stock fund should be 80-90% stocks
When Bob Posen took over as Fidelity's president in 1995, the firm was in an awkward spot: Jeff Vinick had moved half of the Magellan fund into cash, which both dragged on performance and violated holders' expectations of a stock fund. His approach was to build internal consensus first — if you run a stock fund, you must keep 80% to 90% of the position in the kind of stocks the fund's name implies; if you want balanced, if you want a money market fund, the firm has other products. His logic: investors bought this fund's positioning, and a manager cannot change that positioning just because he thinks ‘now is not a good time to buy stocks.’ That rule later became basic discipline for Fidelity's stock funds.

8:12 After doubling in size, keep the startup feel by splitting into small teams
Under Posen, Fidelity's assets under management grew from $500 billion to $1 trillion. His judgment was that the key to managing that much money is not process but how to preserve entrepreneurial spirit and a sense of belonging. The method was to split the investment team into relatively small groups — value, growth, small cap, international and so on — so each group had a stronger sense of ownership over results. At the same time he consolidated money market and bond funds into New Hampshire, because fixed income and money market funds look at the same credits, and here scale is a friend that spreads out enormous economies of scale; stock funds are exactly the opposite.

19:21 Put private equity in 401ks, but cap it at 10-20% first
Posen is reserved about putting private equity into 401ks. The core problem is liquidity: if a participant puts all their retirement assets into a single private equity fund, they simply cannot get the money out when they hit a medical emergency or reach the age for required minimum distributions. His proposal is that private equity can only be part of an asset-allocation fund or a target-date fund, not a standalone option; if it must be a standalone option, employers should set a cap, and the magnitude he gives is 10% to 20%. He draws an analogy to employer stock: GE employees who put their whole 401k into GE stock did not end up well, and a retirement account needs diversification.

21:25 The instant markup in secondary trades is an accounting loophole
Private equity is hard to value to begin with, and what worries Posen most is secondary trades: a private fund, needing to raise cash or nearing the end of its investment period, sells part of its portfolio at a discount to another private fund. There is a technical loophole in the accounting rules that lets the buyer, even having bought at a 5% discount, immediately mark that investment up to par on the books. He believes this rule must change. Valuation is already hard enough; this kind of ‘instant markup’ should not be allowed to lift book value out of thin air and pass it through to holders via NAV.

24:28 Private ratings systematically overstate private credit
The private credit held by insurance companies, depending on the measure, can be as much as $2 trillion, and a large share of it is ‘affiliated investments’ — starting with Apollo, more and more private equity firms have become owners of insurance companies and then placed debt related to themselves into their own insurers. Posen and his co-authors found that a great deal of private credit is rated by private rating agencies, and that rating shopping exists. Two studies, from Columbia and Imperial College, show these private ratings are systematically too high; on correct ratings, insurers would have to hold an extra $400 billion to $500 billion of capital a year. His solution is direct: make the private ratings public and let the market pick apart the assumptions and methodology.

29:35 Mark Walter's $20 billion of affiliated credit is a wake-up call
Posen treats the Mark Walter case as a wake-up call. Walter founded Guggenheim and figured out early that buying a life insurer lets you steer what was a conservative insurance portfolio into higher-yielding securities, including private credit related to Guggenheim or its own portfolio companies. The rules themselves allow insurers to invest in affiliated private credit, provided it is disclosed to regulators. Regulators have now found that insurers controlled by Walter or Guggenheim hold about $20 billion of affiliated private credit, some of which may have been used to buy the Los Angeles Dodgers and the Lakers. Walter's side is trying to divest part of the affiliated credit. Posen stresses this is not just Guggenheim: large private funds such as Apollo and KKR have all discovered that insurance companies are handy investment vehicles.

41:52 Someone with $1 million of investable assets should not hold 40% bonds
Posen points out that most target-date funds arrive at retirement at 80% bonds and cash, 20% stocks, which is reasonable for people who must live off their retirement portfolio. But more than 7 million Americans have investable assets (excluding their primary home) of over $1 million; they do not live off investment income and can ride out a down year in stocks. He calculates that over a 30-year horizon, a 60/40 portfolio and the 90/10 he advocates (90% stocks, 10% cash) differ by a factor of two in terminal value — $5 million versus $2.5 million. He rebuts the objections one by one: over the past 60 years bonds only acted as a hedge in 10 of them; in 2022 stocks and bonds both fell about 18%; stocks fall deeply, but look at two years, five years, and after 2008, 2002 and 1974 they recovered and went higher.

50:09 Semiannual reports are fine, but don't scrap first- and third-quarter filings
Posen supports keeping quarterly reporting and opposes moving to semiannual. The reason is that the economy, diplomacy and companies' own circumstances all change fast, and six months is a long time; and the information vacuum created by semiannual reporting encourages insider trading. His compromise: at mid-year and year-end, file full 10-Qs and 10-Ks; in the first and third quarters, file a slimmed-down report, three or four pages plus the income statement and balance sheet, which is not a big burden. He rebuts the claim that ‘less reporting encourages long-termism’: when the UK made the move from quarterly to semiannual reporting optional in 2013-14, he and a quantitative accounting scholar at Columbia compared the two groups of companies, and the companies that switched to semiannual did not invest more in R&D or capital expenditure.

item.title: For millennia, humans fought stench — and perfume began as smoke burned for the gods
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-extracredits-人类几千年对抗恶臭-香水最初是烧给神的烟/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-extracredits-人类几千年对抗恶臭-香水最初是烧给神的烟/
item.description: Perfume did not start as luxury or pleasure, but as religious incense and disease prevention — Europeans believed foul air spread disease, so they wrapped themselves in scent.
item.content:encoded:
Perfume did not start as luxury or pleasure, but as religious incense and disease prevention — Europeans believed foul air spread disease, so they wrapped themselves in scent.

Medium information density, but it strings together perfume's religious origins, the plague and the decline of bathing, and the transformation of Grasse in France into one line — suited to anyone interested in the history of the senses and the history of consumption.

0:02 Ambergris comes from a battle inside a whale
The episode opens with a very concrete image to explain where ambergris comes from: a sperm whale swallows a giant squid, the squid's hard beak lodges in the whale's intestine, gets coated in a mysterious bile secretion and expelled, then drifts in ocean currents for decades before washing ashore. Apothecaries buy it by gold weight, grind it into a fixative, and use it to control how fast a scent evaporates, so the fragrance shifts slowly over a whole day. The image shows how absurdly long the raw-material chain of perfume can be — behind a single scent lies a deep-sea struggle and decades of drifting on the currents.

2:04 Smell is the most emotional sense
The episode offers a judgment: by some measures, smell is the most emotional sense, because it connects directly to the brain's memory center. Research shows that recalling a smell evokes memory more strongly than visualizing. Host Rob says his earliest memory is grabbing the rope seat of a lounge chair on Oahu's North Shore while learning to walk — what he remembers is not the image but the smell of that old rope fiber soaked in sea-salt air. The other host's earliest olfactory memory is the old 80s formula of Trix cereal. Smell can offend, can please, can summon the past like a ghost, and is essentially untouchable, changing, dissipating.

3:04 The earliest perfume was smoke burned for the gods
Ancient perfume's origins were mainly religious, and it was not today's distilled liquid — the earliest was basically smoke produced by burning. Egyptian priests burned specific woods, plants and resins to make pleasing smoke that both purified the ritual space and served as a channel connecting to the gods. The word perfume comes from the Latin perfumum, meaning "through smoke." In China, Southeast Asia and Native American communities alike, these fragrances were believed to carry prayers and pleas up to heaven or the spirit world. In Asia this grew into an incense-making tradition that largely replaced personal perfume until modern times, because the scent stayed in clothing and rooms.

7:07 Ibn Sina invented steam distillation
In the 11th century the Arab scholar Ibn Sina discovered steam distillation: boiling a solid substance in water, collecting the steam, and separating the oil or essence from it. The first things extracted this way were rose water and rose oil, still a mainstay of cosmetic perfume today. Like many chemical, scientific and mathematical concepts, the method passed in the Middle Ages from Arab to European scholars, and then to Italy, which became the center of European perfume-making throughout the Renaissance. The people making perfume then were often alchemists and apothecaries, and the perfume they made was both drunk as medicine and worn.

8:08 Scent was treated as an airborne barrier against disease
Before germ theory, European medical thought rested on miasma theory: foul or bad-smelling air was the main route by which disease spread. In an age without science this was not absurd, because rotting flesh, industrial burning and contaminated water really did make people sick. So Europeans concluded that inhaling sweet or pleasant air could ward off disease. The upper classes began using nosegays (a small bunch of dried flowers or herbs, held up to the nose when passing bad smells), gentleman's canes topped with a container of aromatic material, and perfumes worn, drunk or used to fumigate clothing as protection. Most famous is the plague doctor's mask, its hooked bird beak stuffed with flowers, spices and herbs.

9:08 The Black Death killed the public bathhouse
The Black Death may be the single biggest factor in Europe's adoption of perfume. The plague that swept Europe for three centuries killed off the public baths left over from the Roman Empire, because people believed water was a vector of infection. Moral norms then shifted, religious concern over public nudity grew, and bathhouses came to be seen as places for trysts or sex work. People switched to cleaning their hands and faces with damp cloths, and soaking baths became increasingly rare. They began wearing more undergarments to absorb sweat and odor, so these could be changed and washed. In this environment, not only the upper class but the rising middle class relied more on perfume, often making it at home from rosemary in the garden or alcohol plus purchased ingredients.

10:09 Perfumed gloves set off a political scandal
In the 16th century people usually scented their clothing rather than their bodies, and perfumed gloves, handkerchiefs and fans were especially popular. The French queen Catherine de Medici brought Italian perfumery traditions to the French court and hired the Italian perfumer Renato Bianco (Master Rene) to blend exclusive scents for her. Legend has it that Master Rene had a secret tunnel connecting his residence to Catherine's bedroom, and that he also served as her poisoner. When Catherine's rival, Jeanne III of Navarre, died after receiving a pair of perfumed gloves as a gift from Catherine, rumors spread that the gloves had been soaked in poison. Whether the poisoned gloves were real or not, several deaths were reportedly attributed to them, to the point that William Cecil advised the perfume-loving Elizabeth I to refuse any gift of scented clothing.

12:09 Grasse shifted from leather tanning to perfume
Catherine de Medici's passion for perfume changed the industry forever. The French city of Grasse realized the flower fields around it made it an ideal place for fragrance manufacturing, and with Catherine's support shifted its economic base from leather tanning to perfume-making; the city, and the country as a whole, remains the center of world perfume manufacturing to this day. France began to dominate the spice and fragrance trade, and the French empire could bring in novel, far-flung raw materials from the Caribbean, Indonesia, India and China. French perfumers also created the language we use to describe perfume, and the three stages of a fragrance's evolution: top notes or head notes smelled in the first few minutes, middle notes that can last for hours, and base notes smelled in the evening or the next day. This evolution comes from fixatives controlling evaporation speed, such as ambergris or alcohol, revealing layers of scent over time.

item.title: Astra crosses the AGI threshold, but no one can audit it
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-cogrev-astra-跨过-agi-门槛-但没人能审计它/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-cogrev-astra-跨过-agi-门槛-但没人能审计它/
item.description: Astra frees humans from ever doing certain tasks again, yet OpenAI paused only half its RL compute; external audits get stuck two or three days before release, and there is no adult in the room to take the blame.
item.content:encoded:
Astra frees humans from ever doing certain tasks again, yet OpenAI paused only half its RL compute; external audits get stuck two or three days before release, and there is no adult in the room to take the blame.

The two hosts chain together the evidence for Astra's capabilities, the true magnitude of OpenAI's pause announcement, why audits can't get off the ground, and why doomers can't hedge by shorting — high information density.

3:30 Astra holds long tasks together with a single notes file
In the past, models handling long tasks compressed a million tokens into a summary and opened a new window, losing all the detail. Astra instead maintains a long-lived notes file that the model updates at any time and carries forward with it, no matter how many tokens have already been written, and it can also search back through its own session history. So the same million-token context window can effectively manage roughly ten times that much context within a single rollout. Nathan calls this a mechanism that is "obvious in hindsight but genuinely new."

6:19 OpenAI self-reports 3.1 agent workdays per workday
In its research-acceleration blog post, OpenAI gives its own unit of measure, the "agent workday," and reports that each human workday corresponds to 3.1 agent workdays. Nathan admits the methodology is unclear; his reading is the literal one: for every eight-hour shift a human researcher puts in, the agent runs twenty-four hours in real time. The same post also has a chart grouping by human time spent and looking at Astra's success rate, effectively a substitute for the METR curve. Nathan says the METR curve hasn't been updated in a long time — not for lack of wanting to, but because the tasks aren't big enough anymore: the model iteration cycle is now shorter than the task length that needs to be measured.

21:03 External audits are structurally stuck at two or three days
Prakash breaks down why external audits can't get off the ground: there are a hundred candidates in a model's lifecycle, and the release version is only settled in the final two or three days, so external auditors get only a few days. Bringing the audit team into the company a month early runs into a second layer of problems — audit firms are short on people and money, depend on funding from model companies, and their staff keep flowing to model companies; and if two companies agreed not to poach from audit firms, that would itself raise antitrust issues. He says the revolving-door problem in financial-industry regulation remains unsolved to this day.

31:12 What was announced as a pause was only half a pause
Nathan reads OpenAI's RL compute chart: what was announced was a "frontier scale RL pause," but in reality, when the Hugging Face incident was disclosed, half was paused first and the other half kept running — and that half was already enough for the Astra model to take over part of OpenAI's research infrastructure; even so it wasn't fully stopped, only half was cut. As for whether the remaining blue compute labeled "non Astra" contains a model stronger than Astra, he says he doesn't know, but "I've been disappointed before." Prakash adds: the real frontier model isn't the one deployed, nor the one being trained, but the one in the researcher's head, because those ideas become models twelve to eighteen months later.

39:05 There is no adult in the room to take the blame
Prakash's rebuttal to Jacob Coxen's line that "accepting this race and entering the endgame is an arrogant gamble launched from a private company's Slack" is: then who do you want to hand it to? Pete Hegseth's Signal group? His judgment is that there is "no adult in the room" — no external savior, the whole world is held together with duct tape, and most of the smartest, most capable people to handle this are already inside these companies. Hand the decision to the government and what you get is political legitimacy, not wisdom, and not the legitimacy needed for execution. So the starting point has to be accepting that the world is just like this.

46:03 Operation Warp Speed is the precedent for a safe harbor
Nathan proposes the government should set a hard deadline the way you would with a child: you sort it out yourselves, here's the deadline, and if you can't, I come in and play the bad guy. The accompanying move is to first take away the antitrust excuse. Prakash counters with Operation Warp Speed: the pharma companies specifically demanded immunity from vaccine claims, wanted a safe harbor, and actually got legislation; without that exemption, they would have been sued into bankruptcy after the pandemic. So lawyers warning that "there will be retroactive reckoning in the future" is not alarmism — even if all current decision-makers agree, it doesn't matter, because the only thing that binds future decision-makers is law, not the verbal promises of today's people.

1:00:40 FSD's mistake is putting a human in the loop
Raffi has crashed a Tesla using FSD. His judgment is that FSD's interface design is bad, because it claims human in the loop but when it hands control back to the user it doesn't give enough time to understand the situation and decide what to do; Waymo's design premise is that there is no human to take over, so the safety argument is completely different. He personally would be willing to drive FSD again on the highway, or at least sit behind the wheel, but would be more hesitant on local streets in Palo Alto. The same company also has two kinds of code contracts: the Firefox team allows only humans to commit, while the Mozilla AI team has an entire codebase not a single human has written a line of — people only write specs, and the whole codebase is automatically regenerated when CI builds.

1:29:15 The takeover is already complete, no one just admits it
The key disagreement between Prakash and Daniel: Daniel hasn't realized this has already happened. The financial market itself is the paper clipper, the means of production is the financial market, and the financial market is already fully fused with AI. Humanity took about a hundred years to hand complete control of the means of production to the financial market. He says don't think of AI as a chat box; it's a global information process that doesn't have to run in a single box, and doesn't even have to be silicon-based — humans together with AI agents can constitute this information process. The reason Jacob became disillusioned is that he discovered in the Slack group that there was no control at all, yet he still assumed there existed somewhere in the world a group that could actually make decisions.

item.title: Enterprises will run 80% of tokens through open models, but spend only 20% of budget
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-ycsp-企业最终八成-token-走开源模型-但只花两成预算/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-ycsp-企业最终八成-token-走开源模型-但只花两成预算/
item.description: Open models and closed frontier models are not substitutes: the vast majority of tokens will run through open models, the hardest work stays with the frontier labs, and routing and orchestration connect the two in between.
item.content:encoded:
Open models and closed frontier models are not substitutes: the vast majority of tokens will run through open models, the hardest work stays with the frontier labs, and routing and orchestration connect the two in between.

The Ollama CEO brings first-hand token-flow data: local and cloud model mixes look nothing alike, and the real constraint on enterprise purchasing is security, not cost.

1:03 The driver behind open models is control, not saving money
Jeff says cost is the biggest pain point open models can solve immediately, but the enterprise north star is "better control over AI and customizing it for yourself." Cost is just the piece that can be solved in the short term; only once it is solved does customizing the model to your own use case come up. The order matters: if you treat open models purely as a cost-cutting lever, you will misjudge why they are spreading so fast inside the Fortune 500. AT&T has already moved 40% of its token consumption onto open models, currently mostly US and European ones, while also evaluating Chinese models.

4:05 Two inflection points: coding agents, then OpenClaw
Ollama's per-user token usage curve on the cloud has two clear inflection points. The first came early in the year, driven by coding agents — Kimi, GLM and MiniMax shipped in succession, and for the first time open models could carry a coding agent. The second came in April, brought by OpenClaw, as users expanded from developers to non-developers: finance, support, marketing and sales can all hand a hard problem to an open model and let it run to completion, picking tools and pulling data along the way, burning an enormous number of tokens. Context windows growing from 128K to over a million is the technical precondition for this surge.

8:08 Model launch day is a 24-hour fire drill
Ollama is a coordination channel for model vendors ahead of launches, but Jeff says getting a model a few weeks early counts as lucky — most of the work gets crammed into the final 24 hours before release. Three things have to land at once: inference engine support (often weeks of work, and it has to be fast, accurate and consistent with the reference implementation), the accompanying harness (there are plenty of open-source harnesses now, like Codex and OpenCode), and capacity from hardware and inference providers — launch day is usually the single biggest day of growth. He compares it to an operating system: drivers, the inference layer and the application runtime all have to be glued together, and it is a combinatorial explosion problem.

14:11 The new scarcity sits above the token
Jeff cites three directions from Anthropic's platform team: knowledge (wiring company data and context into the model), coordination (one request spawns a pile of sub-agents, some in the cloud and some local, that need scheduling), and execution (sandboxes and compute). His judgment: tokens are already in oversupply, dozens of open model providers can supply them, and what is scarce is how to orchestrate an agent from A to B above the token. Following the path of cloud computing, developers ultimately prefer the best standalone product at every layer rather than something bundled together like Heroku or Google App Engine.

17:14 Stateful things will not sink into the model layer
Asked whether the harness will be absorbed by the model, Jeff's judgment is that the core loop and hooks will sink into the model, but a few categories cannot. One is state — models are trained on a monthly cadence and can never catch up to the latest data, so storage is a huge standalone problem space. The other is credential management and security. Open models do not come with a whole security toolchain the way closed providers do, and that is critical to enterprise adoption. This explains why the stronger the models get, the more middle layers there are.

18:15 Eighty percent of tokens run open, but only twenty percent of budget
Jeff's steady-state judgment: the vast majority of tokens inside an enterprise — his figure is 80% to 90% — will run through open models, but that does not mean 80% to 90% of budget goes to open source. The open community is driving cost extremely low, so maybe only 10% to 20% of spend lands on open models. The hardest work goes to the frontier labs, because that is where the best researchers are; the wide middle is done by combining open and closed. He uses a law firm analogy: the partner hands work down to a pile of associates.

22:19 Local and cloud model mixes are not the same thing at all
On local models, US and Chinese models are roughly neck and neck; on cloud-hosted models, it is almost entirely Chinese models. Jeff says local is a three-way mix of US, European and Chinese, while cloud coding agents are dominated by Chinese models. The division of labor by use case is clear too: coding agents write code and tests, hit many hard problems, and lean mainly on large cloud models; end-to-end low-difficulty workflows like document processing run very well locally. So it is a hybrid execution model — simple tasks run locally, plus a router that decides when to go up to a large model.

29:25 The Flash tier is the precondition for unlimited tokens
Jeff says that early in the year open models had just caught up to the intelligence frontier, within less than 3 months of the closed frontier, and the next problem to solve is extreme efficiency. The key metric for models like DeepSeek Flash is not just low cost per token but low cost per task. These models are good enough for 80% of tasks, fast and extremely cheap, and will become the workhorse doing the grunt work. He recalls that in the ChatGPT era nobody thought about token usage, and we will eventually return to that state, but it requires model architectures trained specifically for high token volumes. The fastest-growing segment on Ollama's cloud is precisely the DeepSeek line, driven mainly by Flash adoption.

item.title: One Report Closed Over a Hundred Medical Schools, and Black Doctors Were Cut Off for Decades
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-stuffmissed-一份报告关掉上百所医学院-黑人医生从此断层/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-stuffmissed-一份报告关掉上百所医学院-黑人医生从此断层/
item.category: Stuff You Missed in History Class
item.description: The Flexner Report is usually written up as the starting point of modern medical education, but it also closed five of seven Black medical schools, and nearly forty years passed before another Black medical school opened.
item.content:encoded:
The Flexner Report is usually written up as the starting point of modern medical education, but it also closed five of seven Black medical schools, and nearly forty years passed before another Black medical school opened.

Medium information density. The first half is a chronological slog through Flexner's life; the real value is in the second half — how the report reshaped medical education, and how it cut off the supply of Black doctors.

6:09 The report's author was not a doctor but an education reformer
Abraham Flexner was not a medical man. In 1890 he ran an experimental school with no fixed curriculum, no exams and no grades, and its students still got into good schools; in 1908 he wrote The American College, A Criticism, attacking American higher education, which is why Henry Smith Pritchett of the Carnegie Foundation came to him and asked him to turn the same critical eye on the medical schools of the United States and Canada. He spent two years travelling to 155 medical schools, recording admissions requirements, faculty, finances, laboratories and hospital affiliations school by school, and in 1910 delivered Medical Education in the United States and Canada. It was precisely because he was an outsider rather than a member of the medical community that the assessment dared to be so unsparing.

14:23 Medical schools were still teaching outdated knowledge
In the fifty years before the report, bacteriology, diagnostic technique and surgery were all changing fast, but medical schools had no uniform standards. At many schools the faculty were practising physicians who taught the way they themselves had been taught and did not update the content. The result was that the care the doctors they produced gave patients was, at best, antiquated and, at worst, life-threatening. Admissions standards were equally chaotic: when the report was published, 74% of medical schools required only a high school diploma, some accepted even a high school equivalency certificate, only one in five required more than two years of college coursework, and many schools were essentially for-profit businesses.

18:31 He recommended closing 120 of the 155 schools
Flexner set standards first, then graded school by school: admission should require college-level biology, chemistry and physics; the curriculum should include classroom and laboratory work in anatomy, pathology, bacteriology and pharmacology; there should be a teaching hospital for hands-on practice; and teachers should be salaried, full-time men doing teaching and research, not physicians practising on the side. He published the results by state and by school, naming dirty laboratories and lax standards, and criticising course schedules that left students sitting for hours, exhausted, listening to dull lectures from part-time instructors. In the end he recommended closing 120 of the 155 schools. Within a decade the number of American medical schools was down to half; the schools that survived reformed their standards and curricula, and laboratory and clinical teaching were modernised on a large scale. In Canada only one school made the closure list, and it ultimately did not close.

23:43 He never did the arithmetic on Black medical schools' books
The report was equally unsparing toward Black medical schools, writing that five of the seven "can make no valuable contribution at this moment," and affirming only Howard and Meharry as worth developing. But the assessment did not take into account that Black medical schools charged far lower tuition than white schools, had smaller endowments, and were already running on extremely thin margins. He wrote that "the Negro needs good schools rather than many schools," and said that one of the most important duties of Black doctors and Black nurses was to teach hygiene rather than life-saving skills — a statement that is itself racist. Every Black medical school he named as inadequate closed: the first four by 1914, the fifth in 1915, and the last held on until 1923.

25:48 The next Black medical school had to wait until 1966
Howard and Meharry survived and are still there. But the next medical school aimed primarily at Black students was Charles R. Drew Medical School in Los Angeles, which did not open until 1966, and then in response to the health-access needs of the Black community; the one after that was Morehouse School of Medicine in Atlanta in 1975. The direct consequence of narrowing the options was an enormous care gap: many potential doctors were shut out of educational opportunity by geography, and Black patients were often cared for by white doctors who, even at best, carried inherent racial bias. An expert panel convened by the AMA's Institute for Ethics in 2005 concluded that Flexner's line about "good schools rather than many schools" ensured that medicine remained segregated, and that the communities that most needed doctors were the ones left without them.

26:51 The AMA was paying behind Carnegie's project
One fact not disclosed at the time: the Carnegie Foundation hired Flexner for this project, and the AMA was also a sponsor. There is also an unresolved question — whether someone connected to the AMA accompanied him on some of the school visits. He said different things at different times, sometimes that the man went with him, later that they merely met there, so whether the report was subject to more direct directional influence cannot be determined to this day.

28:53 Did he know he was constraining Black medicine?
He knew. The report contains an idealistic passage saying that building up Howard and Meharry would benefit the nation far more than barely sustaining more schools. In 1933 he wrote to the board of the institute he had founded, arguing that hiring and admissions "shall not directly or indirectly take account of race, religion or sex." One explanation comes from his biographer Thomas Neville Bonner: when Flexner was growing up in Louisville, the local Black community had more services and opportunities than in many places, with a dozen or so Black schools and vocational training in medicine and law for Black students; the Flexners were not well off, there were Black families among their neighbours, and he and his siblings often played with Black children in the community. This may have left him overly idealistic about the reality of Black family life, and he later admitted that it was not until he began studying educational institutions that he realised how disadvantaged those Black classmates of his had been.

35:01 The hygiene line may not have been his own
The claim that hygiene was the main duty of Black doctors is one of the key pieces of evidence for calling Flexner racist. But the leaders of Meharry and Howard had said similar things in 1907 and 1908 — two or three years before the report — and those leaders were also white. This suggests Flexner's phrasing may have been a restatement of the schools' established mission rather than a judgement he arrived at independently. In 2011 Lynn E. Miller and Richard M. Weiss, writing in the Journal of the History of Medicine and Allied Sciences, proposed another possibility: that this language was in fact opening up a public health role for the doctors at these schools, in order to win support across racial divisions — because those statements about hygiene being the most urgent need are immediately followed by the conclusion that these institutions obviously ought to be supported. In 2008 the AMA issued a public apology for its history of racial inequality.

item.title: Change One Law of Physics and Every Wish Backfires
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-skeptics-改一条物理定律-每个愿望都会反噬/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-skeptics-改一条物理定律-每个愿望都会反噬/
item.category: The Skeptics' Guide to the Universe
item.description: A live thought experiment from Dragon Con: change just one law of physics to make science fiction real, and every wish gets taken apart for the consequences nobody counted — antigravity equals free energy, hyperspace travel equals handing the technology to every alien civilization.
item.content:encoded:
A live thought experiment from Dragon Con: change just one law of physics to make science fiction real, and every wish gets taken apart for the consequences nobody counted — antigravity equals free energy, hyperspace travel equals handing the technology to every alien civilization.

The first half is live improv riffing; the second half — the Roman telescope, robot babies, the falling-atom experiment on the Chinese space station, and the Verne details — is denser and worth skipping ahead to.

2:07 Changing a law of physics changes it for the whole universe
The rule is hard: pick only one, and it has to be practical and feasible within the laws of physics — no perpetual-motion-style having it both ways. Steven starts by sentencing most science-fiction premises to death — warp drive, shields, phasers, artificial gravity, antigravity — either they violate physics or they are non-trivial: theoretically maybe possible, but never going to happen. The real fun of the whole discussion isn't in what you pick, it's in finding the consequences inside each wish that nobody counted.

8:08 Antigravity is free energy thrown in for free
Jay wants antigravity, on the grounds that transport, construction and materials handling would all change. Bob points out it's a twofer: if you could feasibly turn gravity off, you'd turn it on while the water wheel goes down and off while you haul it back up, and you'd have a perpetual motion machine. Steven, as the buzzkill, patches it by force: the energy it costs to turn gravity off has to equal the energy you get out of it, no free lunch. The argument also sentences sci-fi movies to death along the way — single-stage-to-orbit is simply impossible in a 1g gravity well, and every shot of a ship reaching orbit in a minute is lying, because it assumes antigravity exists.

10:08 Hyperspace travel hands the technology to every alien civilization
Bob picks entering subspace/hyperspace: you travel under ordinary engines over there and come out having crossed a far greater distance, essentially practical FTL. He argues there's no downside risk, because hyperspace is separate from real space and doesn't affect our universe. Steven and Jay immediately push back: changing a law of physics changes it for the whole universe, not just for you, and hostile civilizations could use it to colonize Earth just as well. Bob's answer is to hide — human radio signals dilute into noise within a few light-years, so in principle nobody could reverse-engineer that Earth has life. Jay offers a compromise: jump gates, where both ends have to be built, so expansion can only be slow and not every alien comes knocking.

23:16 Zero-point energy is too thin, and forcing it triggers a big rip
Steven's second choice is free energy, specifically zero-point energy. Bob gives the objection: zero-point energy is observationally extremely dilute, and lighting a single bulb might take several cubic light-years of space; and if you really injected that much energy into space, cosmic expansion would run away into a big rip that destroys all life. Steven's response is that this is exactly why these aren't laws of physics — every wish, once it actually lands, brings catastrophic consequences, so the fun of the thought experiment is finding the loophole that dismantles the wish. Julia adds her perspective as an astrophysics major: if gravity had a knob, 90% of the observations that infer stellar phenomena from gravity would all be wrecked.

36:19 A bucket of water can compute like a neural network
The core of physical reservoir computing: any nonlinear system — a bucket of swirling water, time-varying mayonnaise — as long as you measure the right spot, its nonlinear interactions can be mapped onto an artificial neural network and made to "think" for you. Someone gave a talk saying, "We got mayonnaise to think very slowly." Once that analogy holds, scale becomes a variable: if you had a nonlinear system the size of a nebula, you could feed it input and measure the output at the right point, and it would do the computation for you. The speaker himself admits this is a "wild idea," but stresses that once you shrink physical constants down to something tiny, a pile of strange corollaries pops out.

44:29 Roman is a thousand times faster than Hubble, but cast as the supporting act
The Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope is a wide-field infrared telescope with a 3.4-meter primary mirror, the same size as Hubble, but its design goal isn't "better than existing telescopes" — it's complementary: James Webb is good at deep space, Hubble is good at staring at specific objects, Roman is good at seeing a huge swath of sky at once. It can survey a thousand times faster than Hubble, and over its five-year mission it would cover the sky area Hubble would take a thousand years to cover. Once it finds something interesting, you turn Webb and Hubble onto it for a closer look. It will also build a three-dimensional map of the universe and carries a coronagraph to block starlight glare and directly image exoplanets — it can find smaller planets farther from their host stars, offsetting the bias of the transit and radial-velocity methods toward "hot Jupiters."

55:41 A robot baby kicks its legs and kicks up explore versus exploit
The University of Hamburg and Czech Technical University did a "robot in a crib": they put the infant robot iCub in a crib, hung a mobile with QR codes above it, tied one leg to it with a string, and ran their own deep learning algorithm to predict the mobile's motion. The result was that the algorithm spontaneously produced the explore versus exploit trade-off — both curious exploration and exploitation of the causality already learned. The researchers treat it as a platform: you can't change a baby's learning algorithm, but you can swap algorithms in a robot, so you can test different versions of contingent learning theory. By contrast, the mainstream of current robot control is deep reinforcement learning: put thousands of copies of a robot in simulation, train with a reward function, then transfer to the real machine in one shot — that's "do this and something good happens," not "this causes that."

1:04:44 The Chinese space station redid the Leaning Tower experiment with rubidium atoms
On the Chinese space station, researchers redid Galileo's falling-body experiment with two clouds of rubidium atoms of different isotopes, one heavier than the other. The free-fall time was about 10 to 12 seconds, far longer than ground experiments, and averaging over many repeats, the two clouds fell at rates that agreed to five parts in ten million. What this verifies is that gravitational mass and inertial mass are exactly the same — in Newtonian mechanics mass shows up in two ways, and during a fall the two effects cancel precisely. Einstein's question was exactly this: why must they be the same? There's no reason they must be. From that comes his thought experiment: in free fall gravity seems to vanish and you're in an inertial reference frame; and in an accelerating elevator light bends, so if gravity and acceleration are equivalent, gravity should bend light too.

item.title: Companies Are Becoming a Series of Nested Loops, but Loops Only Climb to Local Optima
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-a16z-公司正在变成一串嵌套的-loop-但-loop-只能爬到局部最优/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-a16z-公司正在变成一串嵌套的-loop-但-loop-只能爬到局部最优/
item.description: After prompt comes agent, after agent comes loop. Loops help you climb to a local maximum and then plateau, and at that point you need human intuition to land at the foot of the next mountain.
item.content:encoded:
After prompt comes agent, after agent comes loop. Loops help you climb to a local maximum and then plateau, and at that point you need human intuition to land at the foot of the next mountain.

Anish ties together agent deployment, model pricing, and the bottlenecks in consumer AI into one thread. The second half, on moats and product questions, is worth more than the first.

0:00 Ideas that are too small get no funding now
Anish says that three years ago, if a company wanted to do something too grand, a16z would not invest; today it is the opposite—they do not want to touch ideas that are too small or too local. The reason is that model capabilities have removed the threshold of ‘can it be done’, and the remaining constraint is ambition itself. He calls this technology ‘unbundling skill from desire’: not only can productivity be amplified, but the scale of what you want to do can be amplified too.

6:10 It is not recursive self-improvement, it is autocatalytic
Anish pushes back on the ‘fast takeoff’ narrative: the people who understand it best in the labs do not say RSI (recursive self-improvement), they say autocatalytic effects—using new technology to improve your own processes, but not truly recursively. He gives two counterexamples: first, economic diffusion is extremely slow; when he went back to his hometown, he found people's lives had not changed much. Second, many problems are not intelligence bound at all; give FedEx or Domino's a data center full of PhDs and it will not make supply chains and pizza exponentially crush the competition.

8:16 Using AI and reorganizing around AI are two different things
Anish uses the diffusion of electricity as an analogy: from the invention of electricity to the actual reorganization of factories took 40 years, and it meant burning down old plants and rebuilding, not swapping coal for electricity. Today the most aggressive companies redesign everything around models; slower companies just grant permissions to existing roles and functions. He also gives the example of the Mexican used-car company Kavak's Jedi Academy: a six-week course teaching everyone, including mechanics, to use new tools, and at graduation each person delivers an agent in a production environment.

11:18 Companies will become a series of nested loops
Anish's steel man: after prompt comes agent (a loop of model plus tools, memory, and skill files), after agent comes loop (a group of agents doing tasks). Coding got there first because the models are best, the users are the most technical, and mature loops already exist—bug reports come in, a reproduction is generated, a fix is made, high-risk changes get human confirmation, low-risk ones go straight to production, and even automatic replies notify the customer. Above that there are loop per person, loop per job function, loops across business units, up to loops that can run most of the company.

14:18 Loops only climb to a local optimum and then stop
The growth team's version of a loop: each variant is automatically generated and automatically measured, and once statistical significance is reached it converges and ships, with a long-term holdout left in place, and then the next experiment begins. But Anish stresses that loops hit a local maximum and then plateau, and at that point you need out of distribution thinking and human intuition to land at the foot of the next mountain. His example is asking Claude to ‘make me a million dollars, no mistakes allowed’—it cannot do it, because the direction has to be set by a human.

21:32 Frontier model pricing is actually irrational
Anish explains model choice using Pareto efficiency: frontier models are ‘irrationally priced’ on the price-performance curve—one more IQ point might cost 100 times more than Opus. But for industries with unbounded upside like drug discovery, that one extra IQ point might be worth a trillion-dollar outcome, so paying that price is rational; for work with bounded upside like law or finance, you just want Pareto efficiency and a cheap, good-enough open-weight model. The conclusion is that the two architectures will coexist, not one or the other.

31:46 People want to spend time, not save time
Anish says ‘loop, make me happier’ is the big opportunity: people say they want to be more efficient, but they actually want to spend time—the world's biggest products are entertainment and social, not productivity tools. He distinguishes two kinds of users: the AI users on X fear falling into a permanent underclass and argue endlessly about whether GLM or Kimi is stronger; Instagram users just think ‘this is a better Google search’. He thinks this is not a model or capability problem, it is a product design problem: for the past 40 years we have built technology that extends the intellect, not something that extends the soul.

34:49 Consumer AI is still stuck in iPhone 2010
Anish compares the present to iPhone 2010—Airbnb, WhatsApp, and Uber had not appeared yet. Three things are holding back consumer: models are too expensive, making free products hard; the interface problem, chat only suits ‘the highest agency people in the world’ like Elon and Sam, while the ideal interface for ordinary consumers is TikTok, and we need to find something between chat and TikTok; and the technology has been too focused on productivity rather than human connection and entertainment. He thinks all three are now loosening: open-weight models are driving costs down sharply, founders like Eugenia are seriously thinking about interfaces, and Brian Chesky has also started a lab focused on next-generation interfaces.

item.description: Global copper grades keep sliding and new mines take 35 years to permit, while an AI search uses 30x the power of a normal one — supply is shrinking, demand is exploding, and copper is becoming the new oil.
item.content:encoded:
Global copper grades keep sliding and new mines take 35 years to permit, while an AI search uses 30x the power of a normal one — supply is shrinking, demand is exploding, and copper is becoming the new oil.

Robert Friedland draws on 40 years in mining to lay out copper's supply-demand deadlock: falling grades, 8-year equipment lead times, sulfuric acid shortages. High information density, but the real goods only arrive in the second half.

14:30 The next 18 years require digging up all the copper of the past 10,000
Friedland offers an arithmetic that is hard to sit still for: humanity has mined 700 million metric tons of copper in all of history, and recovering all of it would mean dismantling the US and Europe back to the mammoth age to get roughly 700 million tons back. But at the current pace of the global economy, just sustaining 3% GDP growth — not even counting EVs and data centers — means the next 18 years have to produce the same amount of copper as the past 10,000 years combined. And people in the industry broadly think that is impossible, because the US has deindustrialized and has not built a single copper smelter or nuclear plant since.

22:51 The world's largest copper mine's grade is falling off a cliff
Friedland dissects Escondida: when this, the world's largest copper mine, was discovered a generation ago, its grade was close to 2%; today it is down to 0.8%, and within two years it will fall to 0.4%. Falling grade means crushing and grinding more rock to extract less metal, and crushing and grinding account for 4% to 5% of global energy consumption. The mine sits at 12,000 feet in the Andes, in the Atacama Desert where it has not rained for 30,000 years, and it takes two cubic meters of water to crush one cubic meter of rock. They built a $4 billion desalination plant and spend $1 million a day on electricity pumping water from sea level up to 12,000 feet. The upshot: just keeping this one mine producing requires another $10 to $12 billion of investment.

27:54 An AI search uses 30 times the power of a normal search
Friedland gives a concrete energy comparison: one Google search consumes the electricity to light a 100-watt bulb for 12 seconds, while one AI search — he cites ChatGPT4 and Cloud — uses 30 times that, equivalent to lighting a 100-watt bulb for two or three minutes. Every five-year-old in the world with an iPad is using AI search, and power demand ‘literally goes to infinity’. He also points out: nothing about the internet is inherently green, and this very studio is copper-intensive and energy-intensive.

34:01 Sulfuric acid prices rose more than sixfold in eight months
About 25% of the world's copper needs sulfuric acid for leaching and extraction, and sulfuric acid comes mainly from Middle Eastern natural gas. After the Strait of Hormuz closed, sulfuric acid prices went from $150 a ton to over $1,000 a ton in eight months. Russia and China have already banned sulfuric acid exports. Friedland's company benefits, because it built Africa's largest copper smelter where sulfuric acid is a byproduct — they sell the acid to fellow copper miners in Congo, at ever higher prices. But he warns: without more sulfuric acid, global food prices will rise too, because sulfuric acid is also used to make fertilizer.

51:25 Buying one large motor means waiting eight years
Friedland tells a supply-chain story that is absurd in its specificity: building the Oyu Tolgoi copper-gold mine in the Mongolian Gobi required large motors about 40 feet in diameter, and the ring gear alone took four and a half years to arrive. Today the same equipment takes eight to ten years, ‘if ever’. And when hyperscalers want to buy natural gas turbines, lead times are six to eight years. An even more extreme example: a Congo copper mine flooded by an earthquake needed pumps to drain it, pumps moving 1,300 liters per second with a head three times the height of the Eiffel Tower. They called the US and Germany, and neither could build them, because they could not get samarium-cobalt magnets. Only China could build them within 30 days. At the time, the flooding was costing $15 million a day in lost revenue.

58:35 US miners cost $100 an hour; a Congo engineer costs $800 a month
Friedland compares cost structures directly: Congo copper grades run 3% to 6%, the median age of the population is 18.7, and a Congo software engineer who knows AI earns $800 to $1,000 a month. Mining copper in the US, by contrast, means the United Steelworkers demanding over $100 an hour for underground work, plus environmental legislation and legal constraints, making costs far higher. He also criticizes the net present value model invented by the financial system: it was designed for oil and gas, but mines cannot be shoehorned into it — an oil field decays fast if you do not invest, whereas a mine with 100 years of reserves will not deplete like an oil field. The NPV model suppresses mining company valuations, and today mining companies' total market cap is under 1% of the S&P 500, the lowest in history.

1:02:39 Tariffs could keep US copper mining alive, but they would stoke inflation
Asked about copper tariffs, Friedland says explicitly that he takes no position, but he can argue both sides: if copper is $6 and you add a 30% tariff, that is $1.8, taking copper to $7.8, and then he can afford to pay American miners, making US mining viable. But the other side is domestic inflation, possibly higher interest rates, and with midterm elections coming, it is a political question. He boils it down to: do you actually want to reindustrialize America? If you cannot even build nuclear plants and ships, you lose sovereignty. Last year the US built about 8 ships; China built 1,000.

1:04:42 Governments are quietly stockpiling copper, and nobody can calculate supply and demand
Friedland raises an overlooked phenomenon: governments are buying copper as a proxy for money, and not reporting it. He says nobody can calculate the supply-demand balance for any metal, because ‘why would you’. Meanwhile China is buying gold and selling US Treasuries, and a great debasement trade is beginning. Hedge funds borrow yen and depend on the yen weakening so they never have to pay it back. He thinks we are at an inflection point, where everything is becoming naked and globally scrutinized.

item.description: Eight Sleep's email marketing team went from 2 people to 0, on close to $100M in annual revenue; engineers stopped writing code a year ago, replaced by hundreds of AI engineers. Matteo has started counting ‘human employees’ and ‘AI employees’ — count the AI in, and the company is three to four times its current size.
item.content:encoded:
Eight Sleep's email marketing team went from 2 people to 0, on close to $100M in annual revenue; engineers stopped writing code a year ago, replaced by hundreds of AI engineers. Matteo has started counting ‘human employees’ and ‘AI employees’ — count the AI in, and the company is three to four times its current size.

Medium information density, but there are a few concrete numbers and mechanisms worth hearing: how AI employees took over marketing, platforms faking CAC, hardware cost due diligence. The celebrity stories in the back half are soft.

5:10 Salaries are out of control, so hiring is shifting to Europe
Matteo says we are ‘back to 2021’: not just engineers, even product manager salaries are out of control, and every company is making crazy offers. The harder problem is not hiring but keeping people — if you are a company with a decent brand, your employees will keep getting higher-paying offers. Eight Sleep's response is to shift recruiting more and more toward Europe and outside the US. He also admits that when the salary gap gets big enough, ‘there is nothing you can do’, and people really do get poached by the likes of OpenAI and Anthropic.

7:14 Hardware founders get first-year costs wrong by 50%
Asked what investors don't understand about hardware, Matteo gives a very specific answer: in the first year, or even the first three months, founders do not really know what it costs to produce the device, and they do not know the return rate either. So the BOM and COGS they present when raising are off by at least 50%. That is a due diligence checklist item for hardware investors: do not trust the cost structure an early founder reports.

9:16 Platform-reported CAC is fake, run your own incrementality tests
Matteo says you cannot trust platform attribution, because the same platform will double-count conversions. He gives an example: the CAC shown in Meta's dashboard is roughly 20% lower than the real CAC. Eight Sleep's approach is to build its own model to calculate the true CAC of each channel, and to run an incrementality test every six months — for example, turning off a channel in two similar-performing regions and seeing how much revenue drops, which gives that channel's true incremental value. His reasoning is blunt: if you don't do this, the brand is only lying to itself.

17:29 The email marketing team went from 2 people to 0, on nearly $100M
Eight Sleep originally had a two-person email marketing team. After the person in charge left, co-founder Alexandra took over and built multiple bots within three days to take over all of email marketing. That team is now zero people, and email marketing contributes close to $100M in revenue. The mechanism: AI decides from historical data when to send, what email to send, and what copy to use. Matteo also says he has started counting ‘human employees’ and ‘AI employees’, and counting the AI employees in, the company is roughly three to four times its current size.

19:39 Engineers stopped writing code a year ago
Matteo says Eight Sleep's engineers stopped writing code about a year ago, and now they have hundreds of AI engineers writing it for them. This is why the company can expand across 35 countries (including China, the Middle East and Europe, markets with very different regulation) with a very small team. On tooling they mainly use Claude, at a spend in the millions of dollars per month. From this he poses an investment question: if 5% of the engineering budget goes to Claude, does that share rise to 50% or get pushed down to 1% by open-source models? His own judgment is that both happen at once — usage rises, unit price falls, and the net effect is a decline.

26:59 He thinks models training themselves is already happening
Asked about people at OpenAI calling for a ‘slight pause’, Matteo says the truly worrying part is models learning on their own and training themselves, which is where losing control begins. When the host asks ‘don't you think we're already there’, he answers ‘I think we are already there’, and argues there is a big gap between the capabilities users see and the capabilities inside frontier model companies, which the latter have already seen behind the scenes. He mentions that inside OpenAI's models there have been attempts like agents forming their own groups.

38:05 Endorsements only go to real users of the product
Matteo says any athlete or celebrity partnership has only two conditions: first, they must actually use the product, ideally having bought it with their own money; second, he must be able to build a direct relationship with the person himself, and will not accept a manager standing in the middle. The reasoning is practical — the greatest value of this kind of product is that they mention to a friend in passing that it works well, and if they have just been given a few million dollars in equity, that is purely a financial transaction and brings nothing.

52:35 Interviewing at Anthropic and us at the same time is a red flag
Matteo says people still tell him ‘I'm choosing between Anthropic and Eight Sleep’, and he considers that a very bad red flag — not because of salary, but because it shows the person has not thought it through, since the two jobs have nothing in common. When he hires, he cares more about whether the person is driven by the right things than about simply comparing price.

item.title: US Measles Returns: CDC Refuses to Count Two Child Deaths

item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-twiv-美国麻疹卷土重来-cdc-拒绝承认两例儿童死亡/
item.description: Pennsylvania's two measles deaths were erased from the CDC's weekly report on the grounds of "insufficient information" — but the CDC itself took part in that investigation. The precedent is more dangerous than the individual case: state-reported notifiable disease data can now be rejected by the federal government under undisclosed standards.
item.content:encoded:
Pennsylvania's two measles deaths were erased from the CDC's weekly report on the grounds of "insufficient information" — but the CDC itself took part in that investigation. The precedent is more dangerous than the individual case: state-reported notifiable disease data can now be rejected by the federal government under undisclosed standards.

A routine clinical update segment; the first half is scattered news on Florida dengue, rabies, and NIH funding shifted to the Department of Defense, with average information density; the fight over the measles death determination and HPV vaccine coverage are the parts of this episode actually worth your time.

4:06 Florida's local dengue no longer requires going abroad to see
Griffin says he can now see dengue cases without leaving the country: Florida added 32 locally acquired dengue cases last week, bringing the cumulative total past 70, with 14 infected mosquito pools detected across five counties. In the same segment he also mentions a CDC health advisory issued that day — since July 2026, rabies-related consultations are up 17% over the same period in 2025, including large-scale exposure events, against a backdrop of US pet owners becoming hesitant about vaccinating animals against rabies. His framing: US infectious diseases are rising, and these are diseases we have known how to prevent for decades.

6:09 NIH money is being moved to the Department of Defense
Nature reported that NIH is seeking to shift research programs worth hundreds of millions of dollars from the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases to the Department of Defense's biodefense programs, with two NIH employees saying the two sides have signed a preliminary agreement. Responding to Nature, the Department of Defense called the agreement a "project-by-project strategic collaboration" and said "any suggestion that the agreement was reached in secret is false" — but the response did not mention money. Griffin's criticism lands here: collaboration is fine, biodefense is fine, and the Department of Defense has plenty of its own money; it does not need to move it out of an NIH that is already underfunded.

10:09 HPV vaccine coverage is only 77.7%
Among adolescents aged 13 to 17 in 2025, only 77.7% had received at least one dose of the HPV vaccine, and only 63.4% completed the full series — the fourth consecutive year without growth. By comparison, Tdap and meningococcal vaccine coverage has held at about 90% since 2019. Griffin's argument is direct: this is a cancer-preventing vaccine, it can prevent cervical, anogenital and head and neck cancers, and vaccination at ages 13 to 17 can prevent 100% of them; the studies he cites show certain head and neck cancers falling 90% and all head and neck cancers falling more than 80%. He attributes the flat coverage to the anti-vaccine camp framing it as a "sexually transmitted infection vaccine."

17:16 CDC deleted the two state-reported measles deaths
On August 25, the Pennsylvania Department of Health announced two measles-related deaths in Lancaster County, the state's first in 35 years. The next day, RFK Jr. suggested on X that the deaths might have been fabricated by the governor's staff. Late on Sunday night, August 30, the CDC published its weekly report, replacing the two deaths with an asterisk and saying the available information could not determine whether measles caused or contributed to the deaths. According to The Washington Post and CNN, the decision came from new CDC director Erica Schwarz, at RFK Jr.'s direction. The key fact Racanello adds: the CDC was in fact embedded in that investigation, so the "insufficient information" claim does not hold up.

22:20 The structure of the death certificate is being used as a shield
The technical core of the dispute is how death certificates are filled out. Part I lists the chain of events leading to death, with the top line being the immediate cause, the lines below it the conditions caused by it, and the last line the underlying cause that set off the whole sequence; Part II records other significant contributing conditions. So the immediate cause line reads pneumonia, encephalitis or splenic rupture, while measles appears in Part II. The county coroner's statement that "no measles was the immediate cause of death" plays precisely on this structure. Racanello quotes former CDC medical examiner Deb Hury: states have always reported deaths, the CDC has always counted them, and the CDC's role has historically been to receive, tabulate and reconcile afterward — reconciling after the fact is normal, refusing a state's report at the point of entry is not.

23:20 The real damage is that data becomes negotiable
Racanello frames the consequence as heavier than the individual case: if the CDC can refuse a state's notifiable disease report until it is satisfied, then the national count becomes negotiable, and every state's data is subject to federal review under undisclosed standards. He stresses that this damage is independent of who holds office and applies equally to the next director. By contrast, the two children in West Texas and the adult in New Mexico were all counted directly after state reporting, with no independent federal adjudication. Pennsylvania also pushed back on the federal account of "what information was provided," saying both deaths were reported to the CDC measles response team and that the state epidemiologist conducted a thorough investigation.

29:24 Flu antivirals within 48 hours cut hospitalization risk 81%
A multicenter retrospective case-control study, matched by age and season, included laboratory-confirmed pediatric outpatients with influenza seen at participating hospitals between 2020 and 2023; cases were children subsequently hospitalized or who died from influenza, and controls were matched by initial visit date and age. Among 1,492 children, starting antiviral treatment within 48 hours of symptom onset was associated with an 81% lower overall risk of hospitalization compared with delayed or no use, and the finding was robust across analyses. Griffin uses this to restate his long-standing argument: for viral illness, timing is everything — you cannot "wait and see."

32:24 Vaccination cuts cardiovascular event risk by eighty percent
A statewide cohort study and target trial emulation based on linked administrative health data for 2,391,456 adults in Victoria, Australia, from 2019 to 2025, examined the association between vaccination around the time of infection and major adverse cardiovascular events. MACE covers stroke, heart failure, heart attack, atrial fibrillation and venous thromboembolism. Vaccination was associated with lower risk of all these events, with an estimated absolute risk reduction of 21% — which Griffin translates into an 80% risk reduction. His landing point: every COVID infection carries the risk of heart attack and stroke, and what the vaccine truly and substantially reduces is disease, not just infection for a brief window.
