item.content:encoded:
The CDC refused to count two Pennsylvania measles deaths in the national tally, citing "insufficient information" — but the CDC itself took part in that investigation. The precedent is more dangerous than the individual case: state reporting has become negotiable.

A clinical-update format: the first stretch is a quick pass over outbreak data, and the two densest segments are the measles death controversy in the middle and the cardiovascular benefit of COVID vaccination.

4:06 Florida now has locally acquired dengue
Griffin says he can now see dengue cases without leaving the country: in the past week alone Florida had 32 locally acquired infections, more than 70 locally acquired dengue cases cumulatively, and 14 virus-positive mosquito pools detected across 5 counties. In the same segment he notes a CDC health advisory issued that day — rabies-related consultations since July 2026 are up 17% over the same period in 2025, including mass exposure events, against a backdrop of U.S. pet owners becoming hesitant about vaccinating animals against rabies. Put together, these two things show not an isolated flare-up of some pathogen but that the United States has abandoned lines of defense against preventable diseases it mastered decades ago.

6:09 NIH money is being moved to the Department of Defense
Nature reported that NIH is seeking to transfer hundreds of millions of dollars of research projects from the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases to the Department of Defense (referred to in the piece as the Department of War) biodefense program, and two NIH employees told Nature the two sides had signed a preliminary agreement. The Department of Defense responded confirming it had signed a research agreement allowing "project-by-project strategic collaboration," and said "any suggestion that this agreement was reached in secret is false" — but the response never mentioned the money. Griffin's follow-up is direct: biodefense itself is fine, the Department of Defense has plenty of money, and it does not need to reach into the pockets of an already underfunded NIH.

9:09 HPV vaccination has not budged in four years, at only 77.7%
The MMWR adolescent vaccination coverage survey shows HPV vaccine coverage among 13- to 17-year-olds has not risen since 2021, stalling for a fourth straight year: in 2025 only 77.7% had received at least one dose, and only 63.4% completed the series. By comparison, Tdap and meningococcal vaccines have held at about 90% since 2019, with far smaller geographic variation than HPV. The HPV vaccination gap between rural and urban areas exists at every poverty level, whereas the rural-urban gap for meningococcal vaccine appears only among adolescents below the poverty line. Griffin's comment: this vaccine can 100% prevent cervical cancer, anogenital cancers and head and neck cancers — why isn't it being done.

15:15 Congo Ebola: only 15% of new cases come from known contacts
MMWR used a set of "operational indicators" to assess control of the 2026 Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo over the 21 days from July 31 to August 21: the average proportion of alerts investigated within 24 hours was 83%, against a target above 90%; an average of only 10.6 contacts were identified per confirmed case, against a target that should exceed 20; only 15% to 20% of newly confirmed cases had previously been identified as known contacts, against a target above 90%, meaning most cases are occurring outside known chains of transmission; and 59% of Ebola deaths occurred outside Ebola treatment centers, when that number should be zero. Griffin's conclusion is that the outbreak is far from controlled, with 6,757 confirmed cases and 3,267 deaths cumulatively.

17:16 The CDC removed state-reported measles deaths from the tally
On August 25 the Pennsylvania Department of Health announced two measles-related deaths in Lancaster County, the state's first in 35 years; the next day RFK Jr. suggested on X that the deaths might have been fabricated by the governor's staff. Late on Sunday night, August 30, the CDC published its weekly measles update, replacing the two deaths with an asterisk and saying the available information could not determine whether measles caused or contributed to the deaths. According to The Washington Post and CNN, the decision came from new CDC director Erica Schwarz, at RFK Jr.'s direction. Vincent points out the key fact: state and local health departments do the case investigation, apply the case definition and report to the CDC; the CDC has no independent investigative authority and historically has only received and aggregated, checking later. And this time the CDC was itself embedded in the Pennsylvania investigation, so the "insufficient information" claim does not hold up.

19:18 Nobody routinely screens the dead for measles
A commentary in SIDRAP dismantles the "measles wasn't the direct cause of death" line: clinically there is no admission swab, no routine testing before delivery or surgery, and no laboratory reason to go looking for measles virus in someone without symptoms; CDC guidance for clinicians is to look first at clinical features — fever, cough, rhinitis, conjunctivitis, rash — and only then mention testing. So a positive measles result in a death investigation usually means there was already a clinical or epidemiological reason to test. The piece concedes the probability of an unrelated death coinciding with an unrelated measles infection is not zero, but it is small enough to move a reasonable person's judgment substantially. In the Pennsylvania case specifically: the mother also became severely ill after another child was infected with measles, delivered about a month early, and the infant was born not breathing and could not be resuscitated, with measles virus detected in lung tissue.

22:20 The structure of the death certificate is being used as a shield
Much of the dispute stems from how death certificates are structured, something most people have never had reason to learn. Part I lists the causal chain leading to death, with the top line the immediate cause and the lines below it the conditions that produced it, and the last line the underlying cause that set off the whole sequence; Part II, in the words of the National Center for Health Statistics handbook, is "other significant conditions contributing to death." So the immediate cause line says pneumonia, encephalitis, or in this case splenic rupture, while measles appears in Part II — measles caused the splenic rupture, and the splenic rupture killed the child. Treating "the immediate cause wasn't measles" as evidence that measles was irrelevant mistakes the structure of a form for a medical conclusion.

24:20 The real damage is the precedent, not these two cases
Vincent lays out the consequence clearly: if the CDC can refuse to accept a state's statutory report until it is satisfied, then the national count becomes negotiable, and every state's data is subject to federal review under undisclosed standards. Former CDC medical examiner Deb Hury told STAT that states have always reported deaths and the CDC has always counted them. Pennsylvania also pushed back on the federal account of "what information was actually provided," saying both deaths were reported to the CDC's measles response team, that the state epidemiologist conducted a thorough investigation, and that, according to the Pennsylvania health commissioner, the CDC was in fact embedded in that investigation. Griffin adds: whichever team is in power now, someday the other team will be, and the federal government should not be touching the data.

item.title: The AI Doom Narrative Is a Psyop, and the Target Is Open Source
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-11-allin-ai-末日论是场心理战-靶子是开源/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-11-allin-ai-末日论是场心理战-靶子是开源/
item.description: Anthropic asks public markets to underwrite it at a trillion-dollar valuation while its safety lead endorses the claim that AI may end civilization — not an internal contradiction, but regulatory groundwork aimed ultimately at open source.
item.content:encoded:
Anthropic asks public markets to underwrite it at a trillion-dollar valuation while its safety lead endorses the claim that AI may end civilization — not an internal contradiction, but regulatory groundwork aimed ultimately at open source.

The first half is the sparring over Doomer PR and IPO disclosure; the second half's breakdown of OpenAI's math breakthrough and Nike's collapse is worth more.

0:00 The resignation letter wasn't spontaneous — it was organized PR
Jacob Coxon quit Anthropic after only six weeks and posted that the people building AI genuinely believe it could kill everyone by the end of this decade. Sachs points out this was not spontaneous: the account had almost zero followers and zero posts before, yet got hundreds of millions of views in a day; within the first 15 minutes three Doomer organizations amplified it, all funded by the same big EA donor, who also co-led Anthropic's Series A. More tellingly, the Wall Street Journal story went out minutes before the tweetstorm — meaning the reporter had been briefed under embargo. Sachs says if Coxon really came on the show, the first question would be: who introduced you to the Wall Street Journal?

6:12 The company didn't distance itself — it amplified him
A normal company facing a whistleblower immediately pushes back and distances itself. Anthropic did the opposite: Evan Hubinger, who runs alignment, publicly replied that Jacob is right, that they genuinely believe AI could kill all of humanity, and that he personally puts the probability above 10% over the next decade. Sachs argues this exposes the contradiction — what he said matches the company's internal Doomer agenda exactly, which is why he got internal support. Chamath adds the knife: the company can't distance itself, because the moment it does, that whole internal bloc blows up.

10:18 Asking for a trillion-dollar valuation while saying the product could end civilization
Sachs lays out Anthropic's IPO dilemma clearly: you are asking public-market investors to underwrite your company at a trillion-dollar valuation while your safety lead says the core product is unsolved and could end civilization. That is at minimum the seedbed of product-liability litigation. Chamath uses the Philip Morris analogy: we know cigarettes kill you, we'll say so, but we won't disclose it, we'll still go public and let you buy the stock, and we'll figure it out later. Sachs calls it "a time for choosing" — either publicly deny that Coxon is a Doomer operation, or admit Bernie Sanders is right and development should be frozen, in which case how do you IPO at a trillion-dollar valuation?

22:45 The real target of regulation is open source
Sachs is blunt: this is a Doomer psyop, and the end goal is open source. Because FDA-style regulation won't say "ban open source" — it will say "the same standards apply to open and closed models" — and Dario has already testified in the Senate that models are dangerous if they can't be centrally monitored and rolled back. Once open-model weights are released they can't be rolled back, so the standard landing is equivalent to banning the release, use and hosting of those weights. Freeberg adds: open source has no corporate structure to file regulatory paperwork, and open source is precisely what cut AI costs by 50x and benefited everyone. Chamath's version: once open source is banned, you get a monopoly in partnership with the federal government.

39:17 AI can't even nail autocomplete yet
The core anti-Doomer argument isn't theoretical speculation but everyday experience: autocomplete still isn't good, and AI can't even handle a chore like "bring the toiletry bag upstairs." If it can't finish one mundane task, why believe it can kill all of humanity? They call this humanity's insurance against AI taking over the world — company decisions still require humans to wake up, drink coffee and sit in the same room, and there is a natural 16-hour window between decisions.

50:45 What's truly damning is that retweet endorsement
From a legal standpoint, the key isn't Jacob Coxon's resignation tweet but Evan Hubinger's endorsement retweet — he is still a senior alignment executive at the company, running one of the safety teams, and his co-sign plus the "greater than 10% probability" figure is what made it go viral. If it were only Coxon, the company could call him a disgruntled employee; but an executive endorsement turns "was disclosure adequate" into a real question.

1:00:12 OpenAI solved the math problem with brute force, not divine inspiration
The Navier-Stokes solution used roughly 130 billion output tokens, with 10,000 agents communicating with each other, equivalent to between 50,000 and 500,000 years of human work (estimated at 40 words per minute of typing). AI had no flash of insight humans couldn't have; it just did a huge amount of brute-force work, and every step of the message chain is recorded and human-readable. The conclusion is that AI is a leverage tool, not a math god above humans.

1:15:40 De-identification doesn't remove the method itself
De-identification can strip personal information and company-specific information, but the general method for solving a math problem is itself IP. A user iterates on that method inside the tool, and that conversation can be de-identified and used for training, making the model better at math. This is the network effect of closed models: they can see what the whole world is doing, and this observation system feeds them more data than anyone else, constituting a long-term advantage over customers.

item.description: Alliance Bernstein relocated from New York to Nashville, saving roughly $85 million a year, without forcing a single portfolio manager to move — the savings come from real estate and personnel, and the bet is on hiring people New York can't reach.
item.content:encoded:
Alliance Bernstein relocated from New York to Nashville, saving roughly $85 million a year, without forcing a single portfolio manager to move — the savings come from real estate and personnel, and the bet is on hiring people New York can't reach.

A 32-year JPMorgan veteran explains the structural shifts in asset management: active to passive, ETFs replacing mutual funds, private credit entering 401ks. Medium information density; the second half is worth more than the first.

9:18 When passive squeezes active, cut costs before talking growth
The Alliance Bernstein Bernstein took over was hitting the biggest industry headwind since the financial crisis: money moving from active to passive, fees compressing across the board, institutional sales commissions sliding from 20 to 25 cents a share all the way down to a few cents or less than a cent. The firm itself had just been through a collapse — post-merger AUM had touched nearly $900 billion intra-quarter, and by 2012 only $380 billion remained; in 2006 roughly 70% was equity assets, and by 2012 only 30%. His predecessor, brought in from Goldman Sachs, restructured, replaced parts of the teams, and equity performance began to recover, which is what got the firm back to net inflows. Bernstein says what he brought was not firefighting but a more global perspective and an emphasis on distribution.

21:39 Moving to Nashville saves $85 million a year, and nobody is forced to move
The firm was debating whether it could still afford a New York headquarters, and ultimately chose Nashville from five candidate cities — the reason being ‘wanting to be a big fish in a small pond’, which Charlotte or Dallas couldn't deliver. The move saves roughly $85 million a year, part real estate and part personnel. The key design: no portfolio manager is forced to relocate, because the firm is a ‘price taker’ for that kind of talent. As a result, nearly 100 portfolio managers chose to move. The challenges are concrete too: Nashville is the capital of healthcare services, and locally it is hard to find international tax accountants and technology and operations people with traditional Wall Street training; but the firm received a flood of résumés from Atlanta, Chicago, New York, Boston and the West Coast.

25:44 Sell-side research with no cross-subsidy can only be a joint venture
Bernstein says a buy-side firm owning a sell-side research business is a historical accident. Nearly every peer cross-subsidises its research department with equity capital markets or prime brokerage, and Alliance Bernstein had none of those businesses to subsidise with. So they put the research business into a joint venture with Société Générale, and made clear it would eventually transition entirely to SocGen. He specifically mentions the other side's concern was culture — a large French institution facing a group of Americans and Brits — so it had to be done step by step, very carefully. The transition period runs five years from the JV's anniversary, and they are still midway through it.

37:08 Banks are structurally unsuited to holding long-dated fixed-rate assets
Bernstein uses his leveraged finance experience at JPMorgan to explain the structural opportunity in private credit: banks are highly leveraged players running short money, structurally unsuited to holding long-duration, especially fixed-rate, assets. JPMorgan at the time spent a great deal of time and money trying to securitise its loan book, and credit derivatives started from there. Insurance companies and funds are a better home for these assets, because funds don't offer a genuine liquidity option and therefore have no run risk. He states plainly that there is no maturity transformation in credit, and apart from interest and principal there should never have been any liquidity at all.

40:14 Private credit's problem isn't defaults, it's insufficient disclosure
Asked how the industry gets past the first-half troubles this year, Bernstein's answer is education and transparency: tell clients how many names are on the watch list, how many have stopped accruing interest. He says there is currently no mandatory disclosure obligation, but regular updates to clients make them more comfortable, and one should ‘over-communicate in periods like this’. He also frames the problem as structural rather than systemic: defaults are simply the normal state of lending, and models typically already build in 2%, 3%, 4% default expectations; what went wrong was a handful of companies, plus fraud which has always existed; what genuinely went wrong was structure and pricing getting out of balance for a while. His conclusion is that after going through this, now is actually a better entry point.

43:14 Private credit in 401ks: fees are not the obstacle
Bernstein thinks target-date funds and 401ks may be exactly the right place for private credit: demand is highly predictable, professional managers make the decisions, and plan sponsors are themselves sophisticated investors. Alliance Bernstein worked with Brookfield and Carlisle to develop a vehicle that can sit alongside target-date funds, building diversified exposure to private credit, private equity and private real estate. He concedes the industry has been too optimistic about the pace of adoption, that plan sponsors are conservative, and that this will take many years — but in ten years it will most likely be part of large plans. On the fee objection, his response: these are institutional buyers who will drive a hard bargain; and private assets are only a small slice of a target-date portfolio, so the impact on total fees is limited.

47:18 Retirement planning should go through retirement, not stop at it
Bernstein points to Australia's superannuation funds as an example, saying they are thought leaders on how to think about retirement, and that one key practice is designing the glide path to go through retirement rather than stop at it. His reasoning: what most people need least at 65 is to hold mainly short-term fixed income and cash, because they may have another 20 to 25 years to live. More practically, many people haven't saved enough to retire, and will delay retirement and look for supplemental income. He also proposes a specific mechanism: rather than buying an annuity in one lump at retirement, design the target-date fund to leave a pool of liquidity at 75 to buy an annuity, which can significantly lower the cost of the annuity while extending income protection over a longer lifespan.

51:26 AB is the last publicly traded partnership
Bernstein says AB is probably the last publicly traded partnership, a structure rare outside energy MLPs. It means issuing K-1 tax forms, and institutions have an allergic reaction to K-1s, which limits institutional willingness to hold. He describes the stock as ‘a bond with an equity option’ — essentially high-yield debt plus an equity kicker. Asked why not change the structure and make the stock pop, his answer is direct: if they changed the structure and the stock didn't pop, a lot of people would be unhappy; and most shareholders would be negatively affected on taxes, so the board has to consider it, but the honest answer is that it's not a sure thing.

item.content:encoded:
The real mechanism behind the anti-AI proposal is a compute ceiling: pause new frontier training, allow inference only, and make stealing weights impossible with a 1 MB/s external link and a Faraday cage.

High information density, but the topics jump around: AI regulation, robotics, how VCs read people, and the chip supply chain each get a segment — good for listening selectively.

0:00 AI 2040 doesn't stop AI, it delays it to 2040
Many people assume anti-AI sentiment is pushing to ‘stop AI’, but what the AI 2040 proposal actually says is: keep inference on existing models, keep doing capability research, and just push superintelligence from 2028 to 2040. The concrete mechanism is a compute ceiling — pause new frontier training, apply ‘inference-only verification’ to data centers above 10,000 H100-equivalents (roughly $100M of equipment), and physically rip out the high-bandwidth east-west networking inside the data center so distributed training can't run but inference proceeds as normal. New R&D centers would have to be built from scratch inside a Faraday cage, with external connectivity capped at 1 MB/s — stealing the weights would take five years.

0:00 Anti-AI mobilization is nowhere near anti-battery-chicken
Speaker 2 points out a contrast: the anti-flock (anti-battery-chicken) movement converts into real physical action by ordinary people, whereas on the anti-AI side you don't see a 100,000-like video titled ‘here's how to cut power to your local data center.’ Speaker 1 adds that the volume on the anti-AI side comes more from concrete self-interest — ‘I'm an artist, I don't like AI-generated images’ — than from x-risk arguments. Data centers sit in remote locations, behind fences, heavily fortified, far harder to get at than a chicken coop on the street.

0:00 The compute ceiling is the valve easiest to turn
The most effective control lever in the proposal is judged to be the compute ceiling: chip controls plus slower data center construction. The goal is to make models stronger mainly by adding hardware rather than by new algorithms — because algorithmic breakthroughs can be hidden inside secret projects. Speaker 1 notes that Ilya's new lab recently got a large cluster from NVIDIA; even people on an orthogonal research path have to stack compute, which suggests ‘scale is a prerequisite’ is close to consensus in this circle.

0:00 Doomers don't bet, because they wouldn't live to collect
Tyler Cowen demands that pessimists name the corresponding market price to validate their belief, but Deep Dish pushes back: why should short-term existential risk be reflected in market prices? ‘If everyone's dead, the contract that pays out is worthless to me.’ Speaker 5 twists the knife: in the nuclear war era people built bunkers; nobody builds an AI bunker, because everyone thinks it's too totalizing for a bunker to help — so ‘you didn't build a bunker’ doesn't prove you don't believe. Paul Christiano was dug up as being 2x levered long and short 30-year US Treasuries, but that bet also makes money in the ‘good ending’, unlike a doomsday wager.

0:00 The fruit fly agent moves the moral question forward
Google mapped every neuron of the fruit fly, and once the code was open-sourced people started messing with it in every way: someone put the fruit fly agent inside a Rabbit R1, and shaking the device makes its escape circuit light up; someone else had it play Doom. Speaker 1 thinks the real question is the next stop on this road — if you can simulate a human, converse with it, and it behaves like a human, does it have moral status? His own judgment is not to overthink it and not to be in the business of torturing anything. He also mentions having Astra play Balatro with computer use last night, and it felt like giving it a reward rather than torturing it.

0:00 Once the reporter is in the room, he stops being escorted out
Alex Heath describes the core mechanism of his changed status: when a reporter is in the room, you're brought in and then immediately escorted out; now he gets to stay in the room and slowly marinate on it. So his newsletter perspective changes — it's not about landing a scoop, but about letting a large volume of off-the-record conversation settle into a judgment, like the personal agents piece he's writing. He states clearly that confidentiality still matters and he won't leak memos the company is worried about again; ten years in, that's enough.

0:00 A newcomer can hardly replicate his path now
Asked whether now is a good time to become the next Alex Heath, his answer is the opposite: the traditional media environment is structurally challenged, many places aren't hiring, traffic is declining, and they haven't shifted to direct models like subscriptions and streaming. The only viable path he offers is ‘maniacally focus on one thing and become the best in the world at that’ — he himself started by focusing on covering Snap, broke a pile of Snap news, and once noticed, migrated that capability to other companies. And the niche has to be the intersection of niche and matters, not just obscure.

0:00 Fear of being left behind hands new players an opening
A host other than Mitesh offers a counterintuitive mechanism: because people fear AI, they're more willing to try new products — they don't want to be left behind, don't want to become a permanent underclass. The result is that people who've used various AI products for years are still willing to try new things, which keeps creating second- and third-mover advantage. At the same time, once an AI brand gets big it starts accumulating baggage, and people become more willing to share and discuss something new rather than the one they use every day. That leaves a lot of room for startups.

item.content:encoded:
The Oxford Digby 23 manuscript is written in Anglo-Norman, and scholars date it to between 1140 and 1170 by tracking dialect drift — the most complete version of this French epic was performed for the English.

This is a members-only sample episode, medium information density, but it gets very concrete about how a manuscript gets read as "some minstrel's working copy" — good for listeners interested in manuscripts, oral epic and dialect reconstruction.

1:03 The most complete version is an English manuscript
The Song of Roland is a French epic that took shape around the 12th century, belonging to the genre Chanson de Geste (songs of deeds), and it spread with 12th-century French cultural hegemony to regions including Britain. But its most complete and oldest surviving version is not from France itself — it is an English manuscript, catalogued as Oxford Digby 23. This manuscript was originally bound together with a completely unrelated book by someone later, which is why it is called Digby 23 B, and A is that "other book." Nobody knows who bound them together; possibly some monk felt both were his favourite books.

3:05 Every stanza is a camera position
The poem is organised in laisses (stanzas) of varying length, and each laisse is like a camera focus: when the scene or the mood shifts, you change laisse. The whole poem is in decasyllabic meter, cut into four plus six in performance: the first four syllables rise, then a dramatic pause, then the last six syllables fall, overall close to iambic turning into trochaic. Recited over and over this becomes hypnotic, and the poem runs to four thousand lines — hours of recitation.

7:27 At peak emotion, the same action is performed three times
This kind of epic has a convention that is hard for any reteller to handle: when the action is especially intense or the emotion especially strong, it uses consecutive laisses to tell the same action from three angles, a kind of poetic slow motion. For example, Roland's refusal to blow the oliphant is told three times, with almost no gap between them. This is also why it reads like an action film or a comic: scenes cut hard, with no softening transition — for instance, "Roland dies, his soul ascends to heaven" is followed directly by "the Emperor arrives at Roncevaux."

9:29 The performer's name is left at the end of the manuscript
Digby 23 is very likely a real minstrel's working copy. Line 4002 of the poem, its final line, says roughly: "here ends the song of deeds; Turoldus will not tell more." This line appears before Charlemagne's lament, so it reads more like the performer saying: this is too sad, I cannot go on. The name Turoldus does not appear in the poem, and he is not a known scribe, so scholars lean towards him being the owner of this manuscript, the performer of this performance.

10:31 Its pocket-book size gives away that it was for work
The manuscript is only about six and a half inches by four and a half inches, a pocket book you could carry on your person, not a wealthy man's finely bound volume. It is itself heavily worn and not refined, and it contains some small annotations of unclear meaning. Together these features point to a professional performer on the move: he might have travelled alone with an instrument, or been the lead singer or narrator in a troupe, with someone in front of him doing the physical performance. Such people were jongleurs — the origin of the later word juggler.

12:31 The dialect pins this performer to England
The manuscript is not in the French of central France, nor continental French, but in Anglo-Norman, which suggests this performer was probably Anglo-Norman, performing in Britain or at least in Normandy. The dialect features are very specific: continental French O and OU are replaced by U, so Roland becomes Rulant, l'or becomes l'ur; Anglo-Norman French was also losing final soft e. These changes even begin to break the originally strict decasyllabic meter, leaving some lines with only nine syllables or swelling to eleven.

14:34 Accent drift alone can date a manuscript
Scholars' grasp of this dialect is fine enough that they can date the manuscript to between 1140 and 1170 based on the degree of accent drift. The method is similar to scholars reconstructing Shakespearean pronunciation, tracking regular changes in syllables and sounds. Poetry is especially suited to this kind of reconstruction, because meter and rhyme expose which sounds were dropped and which were added. For many jongleurs, French was a second language anyway, spoken with a dialect accent, and they spelled by sound.

17:40 A French epic, an English artefact
Although this is a French poem about an old French king, this manuscript is an English thing, performed for Britons at the time. There is no equally complete other manuscript to compare line by line, but there are abundant records of The Song of Roland being sung before and after this manuscript, and scholars can use them to judge where this performer departed from what the genre should look like. The episode goes on to cover the poem's symbolic system, how its audience was constructed, and what the music sounded like.
